WHY LAMS* CANNOT EDUCATE DOGS.—The fAit Sex, though possessing such unbounded and proper influence over es, notoriously have but little control over their favourites. If a lady takes &dog out for a walk, she keeps constant's, galling to it, leet it should go astray and be lost. The result is ere long that the dog pays not the slightest attention to her, his own sagacity telling him that he need not trouble himself by watching her, as she will be sure to look after him. A gentleman in Danbury has long been annoyed is, his neighbour's hens, wh,ch made a daily practice of roving thronlh his front garden and backyard. And what did this woi thy gentlemaa do? Fle just went patiently and put old hats and hay under his steps and in the barn, and when those hens eame on their marauding expeditions those thee came to scratch remained to lay. He has had all the fresh eggs he wanted thia spring, and has sold 840.60 worth to the man who Owns the hens. E. MARE TWAIN ON BABIES.—Mark Twain was asked to contribute to the paper issued at the fair in aid of abused children in Boston, and responded as follows —"I: do it with pleasure, but I also do it with pain, because I am not in sympathy with the movement. Why should I want a Society for the Preventioa of Crue'ty to 'Children to prosper when I have a baby dowistaire Viet kept me awake several hours last night with no pretext for it but a desire to make trouble? This sesurs every night, and it embitters me, be- came I Seelleiebil'e needless it wan to pat in the other bur- glar alarm, easily and complicated contr:fance which can- not be depenleo upon, because it is always getting out of order and won't go,' whereas, although the baby is always getting out of order too, it can nevertheless be depended on, for the reason that the more it gets out of order the more it i does go. Yes, lam bitter against your society, for I think I the idea of it is all wrong; but it you w'll start a Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Fathers, I will write you a hole book." INTEILECTUAL COMPANIONSHIP TN MARRIED LIFIL— The great charm of marriage is the union of hearts yrhlch secures to either of the pair lifelong syr,pathy and affec- tior. But there, is another great and elevating pleasure which might be found in maned life, and of which the examples, wherever we come upon the etc :ice us with their expression of consummal.e happines. 'There is a union of minds as well as of souls, the intellect of the man and of the woman mutually enlightening and helping its mate. Those who belie .re such an alrance visionary will be sur- prised at the testimony of John S. Mill. This is the Dedi- cation Of his "Essay on Liberty";—"To the beloved and deplored memory of her who was the inspirer and, in fact, the author of all that is best in my writings—the friend and wife, whose exalted sense of truth and right was my strongest incitement, and who. e approbation was my chief reward—l dedicate this volume. LiLe all that I have written for many years, it belongs as much to her as me. . . . Were I but capable of interpreting to the world one-half the great thoughts and noble feelings which are buried in her grave, I should be the medium of a greater benefit to it than is ever likely to arise from anything I can write, unprompted and unassis•ed by her all but unrivalled wisdom.' There is one point suggested oy this Dedication to which we shall devote a few lines. The interdependence of the masculine and feminine minds is due, not to their likeness, but to their diversity. CAR it be supposed ttlaat the philosopher would lament in such terms his intellectual loss in the death of a brother or a friend of his own sex ? There must have been an intrinsic difference in the consti- tution of his wife's mind and of his own which led either to think more justly on certain topic,, and thus to render mutuel service. And there is another reason why perfect mental companionship can be found only between the sexes. The love which casts out all thought of rivalry, and which renders each less anxious to display his or her own grasp of mind than to appreciate the thought of the other, is rarely found except in married life, but is there of the most com- mon occurrence. At once secure of sympathy, and stimu- lated by the desire to keep pace with her consort, the mind works with vigour and elasticity, and the happiness which follows upon mental acqnisition is trebled by the lov;ng praise of the person "whose approbation is your chief re- ward." Woman is not undeveloped man. But diverse. Could we make her as the man, Sweet Love were slain, whose dearest bond is this : Not like to like, but like in differ° nce. 'Set, in the long years, liker must they grow; lie gain in sweetness and in moral height, Nor lose the wrestling thews that threw the world; Me mental breadth, nor fail in childward care, Till at the last she set herself to man As perfect music unto noble word.; And so these twain, upon the skirts of TIME. Bit side by side, full summ'd in all their powers. . Dispensing harvest, sowing the To be, Self-reverent each, and reverencing each: Dlttinct in individual{ties, But like each other, even as those who love. Then conies the statelier Eden back to mem.. Then springs the crowning race of human kind t BILTREEN are EA.GTR AND A TBUSIEB.—A farm- yard near Elizabeth city, New ,York State, was the scene one day in December last of a combat of a most unusual description. According to a glowing account of the battle in an Americaa contemporary, a soaring eagle, towering is his pride of might, turned his far-seeing eye from gazing at the can upon the quiet yard of a farmer named Dough. A stock of fat geese attracted his sight and tempted his palate, and dorm he pounced. The feathers flew, the geese gaggled, and there wars a sensation in that farmyard—and there was a dog there, too. As soon as the eagle struck, the goose ram ander the house, which was some two feet above ground, with the eagle fastened to its back, and the rest of the flock in hot pursuit. And there the fight grew fast and furious. Forty biting and flopping geese on one side and the king of birds on the other. Although outnumbered, the eagle main- tained the fight and dune: to his victim. But soon another enemy appeared—an enemy more terrible than an army of geese--a bull-terrier dog, small of body, but big of heart and full of fight. Although the dog had no natural bel- ligerent rights in a combat between birds, yet he came with a bound, and the eagle had no time to settle questions of military ethics; so he threw himself on his back (eagle fashion) to do his best in this hard fight between tooth and toe-nail. The dog made a lunge at the eagle's breast, and the eagle stuck his claws deep into the dog's shoulder. The blows were simultaneous, and both told. But a terrier never, and an eagle hardly ever, says die. The only witnesses of the grand combat were the geese, who now stood off and looked on, and Miis Martha Brothers, who in the end was I. be the conquering heroine crowned with the laurels of Tie- tory. The battle raged teeth gashed ; claws clawed; eyes flamed. But eagles, like men, contend against odds when fighting against fatai aud so the eagle's great heart sank within him, and turning tail upon his foe, he sought safety in flight. But his r.:treat was slow and full of difficulty, fo-r he had fifteen pounds of bull-terrier swinging behind him. He reached the yard fence. With one desperate effort he sought to scale it. He could reach the topmost round. He, bore a weight he could to. further carry. There they stood ; then it was that Miss Martha Brothers, the true heroine og the fight, came to the front and won .the palm of victory. Seeing a rail, with one fell swoop she came . down with at ,11 head, and le. t him prostrate, strugg.4 crash upon the eagle link in the agonfes of death, the victim of a combination too, powerful to be resisted: He measured nine feet between the tips of his outstretched wings.—Land and` Water.

TROPICAL VEGIBTATION.—A lov,er of nature who sees a tropical country for the first time cannot help but enjoy the bright light and heat, the vegetable glories of flower, fruit, and leaf, called forth by the rain and sunshine—of a clime where winter is unknown. And yet, with all the sun- shine and showers, the tropical blossoms are in a way aria- OCratic and exclusive, and never mingle socially in bosky • Matins, as do our own wildings ; and it is not possible to mune, half-a-dozen of them that could at all compare with the bluebells, or heather, the buttercups, the primroses, forget-me-note, anemones, violets, and rosy lychnis of our own cool moist woods and pastures. During a year's rambles in one of the richest and most fertile of tropical islands I saw nothing really freehand spring-like--nothing like the "green and gold" of daffodils, and the tender young grass of April, or the royal glory of a summer iris, or an autumnal crocus on its mossy bed. This much is ever lacking in the forest primeval ; and even in gardens— Eastern gardens beautifully as they undoubtedly are in ; ' many ways, the sameness, the cloying degree of per- manency observable in the forest, becomes intensified, and so still more unsatisfying. The plants seem always to pre- sent the same aspect; and although most of them are at their best when revived by the rains, just after the dry season, yet the charm of freshness Is destroyed by the number of evergreens everywhere, and the driblets-of bloom I kept up by them nearly all the year round. Still the beauty of tropical gardens is lovely of its kind. You have, or may hPve all the tropical treasures of Kew—palm, hr;, and orchids—around you in the open air; but all this is as the beauty of a lovely woman jaded by over-enjoyment, the whirl of a whole season's gaieties! There is elegance of form and charm of colour, all the refinement of culturod beauty, sure enough. Victoria water lilies, and dainty nymphmas in open-air pools, the flesh-tinted blooms and umbrageous leafage of the sacred lotus also • the noble amherstia, with its pendents of crimson and gold—groveßot feathery-leaved palms—all this, and very much more, is common; but it is astonishing how soon one tires of this plethora of flora charms, and how eager becomes the longing to sniff the homely fragrance of pinks and wallflowers; to. stoop for a violet from a mossy hedge-bank, or a snowdrop even from a cotter's garden. Indeed, there is no gainsaying the fact, as has been pointed out by Wallace and others, that the most lovely and satisfying, the most sociable of all flowers, are those of temperate climates.—" The Gardens of ,he Sun: a Naturalist's Journal on the Mountains and in the Forests and Swamps of Bornoo and the, Suits Archi- pelago," by F. tional amusement.— - ANIMALS WITII SECOND BRAIN' IN 11114 SPINAL CORD. —At the closing session of the autumn meeting of the National Academy of Science of New York, Prof essor Marsh read a paper on the " Dimensions of the Brain and Spinal Cord in some Extinct Reptiles," which, from the report in the IYeto York Medical fleeting, appears to have contained some very interesting facts. Professor Marsh first brought the evidence to sustain his proposition that the older tho type of mammal, reptile, or fish, the smaller the brain. He then called attention to a very curious development in cer- tain fossils, near the sacral region of the cord. In a gigantic reptile, of the jurassic formation, an animal nearly 30 feet in length, the brain was scarcely as large as that of an ordinary dog, judged by the size of the cranial cavity. But the spinal canal presented the extraordinary feature of an immense enlargement in the sacral region, where the bone was so excavated as to form an immense vaulted receptacle, several times- larger than the cavity of the skull. The sacrum consisted of four vertebrse, which were well ossified and of great solidity, and within this was contained, daring the life of the animal, a posterior brain—if he might use the term—which was eight times as large as the encephalon. The point was of very curious interest, not only as a fact of fossil anatomy, but in respect to the physiological in- ferences that might be drawn from it, into which he did not propose to enter. It was so remarkable, indeed, that he took occasion to examine other examples of the same species before accepting it as a general fact of extensive applica- tion. Upon recurring to some younger specimens of the same gigantic saurian, he was enabled to verify the exist- ence of the cavity in every instance, and to prove that sacral enlargement of the cord in extinct reptilians was an extraordinary fact. If it had appeared in a single instance, it must, of course, have been regarded as a phenomenon due to injury or disease; but in all cases, since his attention was attracted to the point by this enormous creature he had found the posterior cavity in extinct reptiles. There was nothing analogous to this sacral enlargement, Prof. Marsh continued,. in existing vertebrates. The aurphiax had abso- lutely no brain—that is, no cerebral enlargement of the cord at the anterior extremity, but there was no enlargement of the spinal cavity at the sacrum which answered to what he had observed in extinct species. In answer to an inquiry I, whether the sacral enlargement was in such a position as to furnish a point of origin for the nerves of the leg, Professor Marsh said that such was the case, and that the animal had very powerful hind legs; but the fore legs were equally strong, and there was no corresponding enlargement.— British Medical Journal. • The Russian Government, according to the Berlin press, has ordered 8,600 tons of rails of Krupp, of Essen, for the Finnish railways. Two of them, James Smith and Angus M.Leod, have since expired, and the third is not expected to recover. A DOUBLE Fayarxrx.—At Sherborne, Dorset, on Sunday morning, Alice Osmond, cook at Mr. Enter's, Barton Farm, was found dead in bed, having been suffocated by fumes from a charcoal stove which she and a fellow-servant named Mary Glover had lighted and taken into their bed- room. Glover, who is very ill, still lives. On Tuesday an inquest was opened on the body of Osmond. Whilst there, one of the jurymen, named Dowet grocer, suddenly fell into the arms of one of his companions, and expired immediately. John Bright, in acknowledging a letter sent to him by a Carnarvonshire farmer on the relations between landlon; and tenant says, "The whole conditions of agriculture in this country are unfavourable for the farmer and for the public. Misfortunes may change them, as they may force the farmers to say something and to exert themselves. I have preached to farmers for nearly forty years, but with little result. American competition may speak to them and to our landlord class with more effect. I hope better days are in store for tie better class of farmers, ' when the calamities are overpast.'" 1111DISCOTHRBD ORDERS 01 ON COMMONS.— Professor Thorold Rogers has furnished the folbewing orders ef the House of Commons, which, he states, are still were- yoked, and consequently binding:-1. 1-p. 14, 1004. If any man speak impertinently, or beside the question in hand, it stands with the orders of the house for Mr. Speaker to interrupt him and to know the pleasure of the house, whether they will furt.er hear him. 2. Ap. 17, 1004. If any superflous motion or tedious speech be offered in the house the party is to be directed and ordered by Mr. Speaker. 3. May 2, 1610. Mr. Speaker may stay imperti- nent speeches. 4. Nov. 10, 1640. When a business is begun and in debate, if any man rise to speak to a new busi- ness, any member may, but Mr. Speaker ought to interrupt him. Professor Rogers remarks that these orders are the product of the best age of Parliament—i.e., between the ac- cession of James 1. and the conclusion of the first session of the Long Parliament. CIIEWITSTO JEWEL FiourranY BY A SALM CLAROYIIA.A.— At Bow-street (London) Police Court, on Monday, a clerk aged twenty-six, of no fixed named Frederick Simpson, abode, was charged on a warrant with stealing a quantity of jewellery. An assistant to Mr. Peacock, jeweller, of New Oxford-street, stated that on the 7th of October, 1872, the prisoner called at the shop and asked to see some watches of a superior quality. There being none in stock to suit him, it was arranged that he should call again in an hour, when more valuable ones would be procured. He called as arranged, and invited the assistant to accompany him to the Bedford Hotel, Southampton-row, with seven watches, a diamond ring, and other articles of jewellery, for the pur- pose of showing them to a lady. Upon arriving at the hotel the assistant was conducted by the prisoner into a drawing-room with folding doors, leading into a bedroom. The nrisoner went into the bedroom, and the witness heard voices speaking. The prisoner returned, and asked that the lady might be excused coming out, as she was unwell. At his request he was allowed to take the watches into the room for the lady to select one from. He came out, and stated that one had been selected. He did not bring the other six out, but asked to be allowed to take the ring and other articles in for the lady to look at. His request was complied with, and witness again heard voices as if in con- versation. A cart passed in the street at the time, and when the noise had subsided the voices had ceased. The witness remained some time, and feeling suspicious at the prolonged silence, opened the door of the bedroom, and found that the property worth over Z 250, and prisoner bad decamped with had only left a bat and the invoice of the goods on the table. The prisoner at the time was dressed as a clergyman. the prisoner was arrested at Lewes Gaol as he was die- charged after undergoing a term of imprisonment for a similar offence. Committed for trial.

The steamer Baltic has just reached the Mersey from New York. During her passage exceptionally severe weather was encountered. Day after day strong gales prevailed, ac- companied by high seas. Intsit ETICTIONS.—The Parliamentary returns issued on Tuesday show that altogether 11,657 persons were evicted in Ireland up to the end of November last year, and 6,017 readmitted as aaretakers or tenants. TOTAL WRIWIS OF i LIVARPOOL STlSAMllR.—lnformation has just been received by cable of the total wreck of the steamer Macgregor at Kumpari, south et Batticaloa, on the coast of Ceylon. The crew, it was mentioned in the message, had been saved. At Port Meadow crossing, Oxford, on Tuesday, a man named Turtle was seen to throw himself in front of the Worcester expresi, which cut one arm, in which he held a pocket-book containing his address, completely off, while it took the remainder of his body a hundred yards, and literally

cut it to pieces. On Monday morning a fire broke out in the first floor of a house in, Pleasant-place, Lambeth, London. Three children were in the top floor, and could be reached in,no other way than through the roof. When they were fond two were already dead and the third so seriously injured that her life is despaired of. Mr. McLaren, who has represented the city of Edinburgh in the Liberal interest fbr the last fifteen years, has' issued an address stating that he has applied for the Chiltern Hundreds. Referring to a statement made by him when re- cently addressing the electors that if he should feel unable from impaired health properly to discharge his Parliamen- tary duties he would resign his seat, the hon. member says circumstances have unexpectedly occurred which seemed to make it his duty Row to place his resignation unreservedly in the hands of the electors. .

BURYING is EMPTY COPYIN.—An extraordinary blunder has just come to light at Devonport. A pauper inmate of the workhouse having died, the body was remored to the mortuary to be placed in a coffin, and, by some error, when the bearers eame to take it away and bury it, they removed an empty coffin instead of that containing the corpse, and it was taken to the cemetery and buried with the usual rites. The mistake was not discovered until another death caused the mortuary to be again visited, when olfactory evidence was afforded that something was wrong, and investigation revealed the facts.

Hall's cartridge factory at Eastwood, near Ilkeston, when a terrific explosiontook place. The building was blown to the ground, and the girls terribly burnt and scorched. In their agony they rushed into a stream of water, but were speedily rescued and sent home on stretchers. Chambers died forthwith, and Kate Ward is dying, but Lizzie Hanley and Ellen l'ollard are expected to live. The inquest was adjourned for three weeks te await the Goyern- meat inspection,

A NOTPL ACT OP PARLIAWINT.—For the first time pro- bably in the history of the British Legislature, an Act of Parliament is about to be passed to effect the alteration of a single small word in a previous Act. The Lord Chancel- lor has just brought in a bill which has for its sole object the changing of " that " into" this" in one of the clauses of the Burials Act of last session. This highly important niece of legislation seems to be necessitated by a mistake perpe- trated by the draftsman who had the task of drafting the Burials Act, which makes nonsense of t e clause as it at present stands, and consequently the blunder has to have a whole new statute all to itself in order to be rectified. ATTKIIPTBD MITRDIHI •ND R08.E1211Y.---Between seven and eight o'clock on Sunday evening two men, who had ostensibly called on matter:, of business, got admission to the house of Mr. Benjamin Saynor, master plasterer, Leeds, and after making a daring attempt to murder Miss Saynor, a young woman of 20, by cutting her threat, they took what money they could find and fled. About seven o'clock the next morning two men who are described as being of similar appearance, waylaid a Leeds pawnbroker on his way from his home to his shop, and after striking him on the head with a bludgeon, inflicting a terrible wound, attempted to to rob him of a large sum of money he was ea:l7in. The ruffians were interrupted and made their escape. ROT IN SHEEP.—The Veterinarian referring to this subject says:—" Many serious losses continue to take place in various parts of the country from this disease, among not only aged sheep, but lambs of this year. During the past month we have made post-mortem examinations of lambs which were not suspected to be the subjects of rot, and found the bile ducts filled with matured, flukes, and the liver itself most extensively diseased, the entire organisation of the animal being amemated and dropsical. In some large flocks, about which we have been consulted, we find that the per- centage of lambs which will be left by the end of the winter months will be practically nil." CRY/a( GLOSIJLES.—Dr. De Klenzie, writing in the Farmer's Review on this subject, says :—The best of the cream globules rise soonest to the surface, because they are the largest, and the flavouring oils rise with them because they are the most volatile; hence it is that the finest butter is that which is made from cream that is skimmed before all of it that will rise has risen to the surface, while that which rises afterwards but tends to reduce the quality. Cream is a singular product; all of it will not rise—would not rise in a month, even if the milk could be kept sweet during that , period, and some of the globules actually sink instead of rise, while others remain in suspension neither going up nor down. Thus the specific gravity of the globules varies, not on account of size only, but also on account of composition; but, in any case, the cream which, under ordinary condi- tions, rises in the first twelve hours, will make the finest butter. ENGLISH Idemmarent.—This very pretty and graceful fern is a plant of wide distribution, and one which occurs withconsiderable frequency throughout Great Britain and Ireland. It varies a good deal in the selection of a habitat; sometimes found upon hedgebanks, it is more frequent upon rocks, and is perhaps most usually founcl upon old walls. In this last-named situation it is not unfrequently associated with the Wall Rue (A. Bract-murari) and Scsly Spleenwort (Ceterach officinarum). In the County Waterford, the old walls in the neighbourhood of the Comeragh Mountains produce large quantities of these three ferns, growing to- gether with the greatest luxuriance, sometimes mingled with small plants of the Hart's-tongue (Seolopendrium oulgare)l or, more often, with some flowering plants such as the Herb Robert (Geranium Robertianum)—the contrast in this ease between the free-spreading foliage and bright pink t owers of the Cranesbill and the darker hue and more formal growth of the ferns is very striking. Great consternation and much excitement was caused in outhport by the suspension. Thel`bank a :ihorttiMe'ago entered upon large and extensive Premises ad joining the Cam- bridge Hall, Southport. It was first fOrmed as almost purely a Southport bank, and a large number of the tradesmen of the town and of -Birkdale and district not only became shareholders, but put their money into it ; therefore,the loss in Southport will be great should the,establishment-not be re-opened. Recently branches have been opened at Orme- kirk, the centre of a large farming district, and at Skelmers- dale, in the neighbourhood of which there are extensive coal tattles.' Negotiations have for some days been going on between the directors of the bank and the directors of Parr's Banking Coinpaay at Warrington, the former wishing to dispose of the concern; but On Monday it was currently .reported that the negotiations had failed. At present the closing of the bank is almost the only topic of conversation in Southport, and knots of people.congregated round the building all day discussing the simple notice on the doors, Bank elosed."

The last balance sheet was submitted to a meeting of the shareholders on February 3rd last. The chairman of the bank, Mr. Walter Smith, IP*, presided at thatlneeting, and made an important statement relative to the position of the undertaking. He said that notwithstanding the depression of trade, which had restricted businese operations, the amounts of the deposits had increased during the year something like £47,000. "It the bank," he added, "were to close to-morrow, they would be in such a position that the depositors would not lose a single penny, and in addition to that, after the claims were met, they would still have money to call in." He went on to observe that all the calls had been paid, and at the present time, with the reserve fund hi hanil and with, the prospects they had in the future, the bank would in a-short time be one of the meat preaperous concerns in Lancashire.—The chairman was questioned on several points. A demand was made for a more detailed statement of accounts, and it was asked if the directors made advances without security. The Chair- man said he could not deny that advances had been made without security, but only to gentlemen whom the directors thoroughly knew, and £250 would cover all the bad debts in the past.—Mr. Alderman S. Breithroyd (one of the directors) confirmed the'faimarable- statement made by the chair- man. A grant of £BOO was made to the direotors for their services.

Since the meeting in.question a new call of .11 per share has been made, which realised £38,000. Ohly half the share capital has bee. called up. The result to Southport, it is feared, will be disastrous, the deposit account being very heavy. The Southport Corporation has £27,000 deposited in the bank, and it was only a week ago that Councillor Otegory proposed to withdraw £lO,OOO to invest in console, but the proposal was not carried. At present no accurate Idea can be given of the liabilities of the bank, which are, however, very heavy; but it is thisught that the assets will generally realise well. The immediate cause of the smelt- sion was the sudden run at a time witen oustonaers had been allowed to Overdraw is a large extent. At meetiag of the directors on Monday morning, a cir- cular was prepared and forwarded to the shareholders regret- ting the stoppage of the bank, and summoning a meeting of shareholders for Wednesday "for the purpose of considering the question of reconstruction or liquidation, as may be decided upon."' Messrs. Chadwick, Queea Insurance-buildings, Liverpool, creditors of the Southport aid West Lancashire Bank, have filed a petition to wind up the affairs of the bank. The peti- tion will be heard on the 28th of the present month., The secretary of the Southport and West Lancashire Bank has issued &notice stating that the register of transfers will be closed until the 14th of February. There is nearly £200,000 to be eilled up on the capital account. EXCITEMENT IN ST. HELENS. Considerable excitement was caused in St. Helens by the report of the suspension of payment. BONES FOR POULTRY.—A writer in the American Poul- try Yard urges upon poultry keepers the necessity of giving to fowls a liberal supply of baked bone and oyster shells, and writes his own experience in a very entertaining man- ner. It is as follows :—" I supposed I did my duty by my hens when I burned bones to ivory whiteness, ground them to the consistency of flour, and fed them occasionally, with the idea that I was giving them egg-shells in a very avail- able form. But I did not considerthat the gelatine, the fat, the ammonia, and other constituents of the bones, which were discharged by the internal heat—leaving only a little pure lime—were really the richest possible food for the hens and the greatest egg producing diet that could be furnished them. My new tenant only bakes them, more or less brown, in an old tin plate on the top grate of the stove oven. This is not a very pleasant process; for, like all scorched portions of the animal frame, they give a pungent, half-suffocating eaten, which tempts you te 'ear de kitchen' till the fresh air from doors and windows has sent the objectionable odours into outer space. But you soon become reconciled to this invasion of ill scents when the fiery combs, the ceaseless cackle, the evident high health of your fowls, and the daily filled egg baskets show you what they have accom- plished. No other food, nor any amount of food, if this is left out, will give von such returns; and this baked bone, pounded on a rock-in your poultry pens and fed with ordi- nary feed, will give results that ought to satisfy the most craving disposition. The hens cluster around that priniitive bone-mill, gulping down the rich morsels with evident de- light ; and since everything necessary for the production of eggs is thus fully furnished there is no undue strain on the tviiotna tfoo br cuessi,nne sos ,wteoaktehnei weakening completeofth e system,satisfaction b of atihl ye aftotwe s- and their owners. You can hardly give too much burned bones to your hens to provide the necessary amount of lime for the egg-shells, which can be obtained by the barrel— and generally without cost, except taking away—at hotels Or restaurants in your nearest city. My new tenant goes eighteen miles for them, and considers them cheap enough at that. The hens eat them when pounded into fragments is eagerly as they pick up shelled corn, and they furnish the needed material for the egg-shell more completely than anything else"

The restoration of Candahar to Afghanistan under a powerful ruler would be the arrange- ment Her Majesty's Government would prefer in re-estab- lishing some settled Government. General Roberts in his memorandum expresses his opinion chiefly that the line -of Herat and Candahar is the one to which the efforts cf Russia wsuld be directed in operations against India, and that we should not, therefore, release our grasp upon Can- dahar ; but as to the rest of Afghanistan, we should leave it, if possible, to itself.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMINTI"..
HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.

PROTECTION IN IRELAND. Earl FORTESQUE asked whether Her Majesty's Government would not, for the sake of saying time ma case where every day was of importance, introduce into that House the Bill for the better protection of persons and property in Ireland which was stated more than a week ago by Her Majesty's Ministers to be urgently re- quired, now that there seemed no prospect of their being able to introduce that Bill in the House of Commons.—Earl GRANVILLE replied in the negative, and the LORD CRAN- CELLOR was amongst the speakers who followed. A BILL FOR TEE CONSERVANCY OF EIVERS AND PRE- VENTION OF FLOODS was brought in by Earl SPENCER and read a first time. . .
-....-. THE AUGMENTATION OP BENEFICFS ACT AMENDMENT BILL WAS read a third time and passed. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY.

Mr. GLAD-ST:ON-8.-Mr. Gladstone returned to the House this afternoon, his appearance being welcomed by a burst of cheering from the Ministeral benches. The right Lon. gentleman brought with him a portentous bundle of papers, which turned out to be a petition signed by 1,700 electors of Mid-Lothian in favour of legalising marriage with a deceased wife's sister.

--Trt-s-T—uTtler. svaat.—The PREMIER, who was again cheered on appearing at the table, informed Sir David Wolderburn that no offer of mediation in Transvaal affairs'llad been received from the Government of the Netherlands or any other friendly Power. THE PRACTICE OF MOVING AN ADJOURNMENT.—Answer- ing Mr. Alderman Lawrence, the PREMIER said the attention ' of the Government had been attracted to the inconvenience of initiating a debate at question time by moving the ad- journment. It was, he admitted, a great and growing I inconvenience. But he could not at the present time give any specific answer as to whether the Government proposed to take steps in the matter, because it might presently be his duty to take a wider and larger view of the whole subject, ' and he reserved particulars till that time. This significant statement was loudly cheered from both sides of the House. IThe Premier dropped another hint in the samer direction when replying to a question from Sir Baldwin Leighton, whe wanted to know whether it would not be desirable to postpone further consideration of the Address until after the Coercion Bill was introduced. Mr. Gladstone said that he could only say for the present—" and," he added, "I answer only for the present;'—that the Government thought it most expedient to encourage the House to proceed with the debate on the Address, which lie trusted was now near its close. CORRUPT PRACTICES AT ELECTIONS.—In reply to Mr. Arnold Morley, the ATTORNEY-GENF,RAL said it was his in- tention first to introduce the Bill dealing with corrupt prac- tices at Parliamentary elections, to be followed by one dealing with municipal elections. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—On the motion for the adjourned debate on the Address, Mr. MCCARTHY moved an amendment praying Her Majesty to refrain from using the naval, military, and constabulary forces of the Crown in enforcing ejectinents for non-payment of rent in Ireland, until the measures proposed to be submitted by Her Majesty, with regard to the ownership of land in Ireland, have been decided upon by Parliament.—Mr. GLanerrown, who seized this early opportunity of taking part in the debate treated the amendment with unusual severity. It was difficult, he said, to believe his own eyes in seeing its terms, not in some of those writings of the hon. member with whick many of them were familiar, but on the Orders of the House of Commons. The naval, military, and constabulary forces were the whole resources at the disposal of the Crown for maintaining order and fulfilling the law. If they were not for the purpose of executing the law for what purpose did Ithey exist? He did not believe that the Speaker, nor any ef his predecessors in the chair, had ever been callel upon to put such an extraordinary amendment. Mr. McCarthy had come sown and asked the House of Commons to insult the Throne by carrying to its foot a prayer that the Queen, who swore at ker coronation to execute the law, should by her arbitrary will renonnce the means of performing that duty. "We are here" he added, "about serious business. and an amendment like this introduces an element almost ludicrous." It was not for the credit of the House of Com- mons that it should waste precious hours which it would better employ in consideration of measures both with regard to the peace and order of Ireland and to the principles of justice to be introduced into the law which governs the land.—This speech was frequently in- terrupted by loud cheering, more particularly in its pas- sages denunciatory of wasting the time of the House.— Lord JOHN MANNERS rose to express the perfect accord with which he and gentlemen sitting near him had heard the views just expressed by the Prime Minister. He thought he could best show the cordiality of his desire to ass•st the Government by sitting down without further remark, which 'he did after the delivery of a speech not extending beyond three sentences—Mr. Dmow complained of the bitter tone" of Mr. Gladstone's speech, A remark from him as to the strength of the Land League in Ireland, and the cer- tainty that eviction would be met by armed resistance, brought up Sir HENRY TYLER, with an Appeal to the Speaker whether Mr. Dillon was in order in uttering these traitorous and seditious sentiments.—The SPEAKER pointed out that the proper course for Mr. Tyler would have been to move that the words be taken down.—Mr Dillon proceeding in the same strain, Mr. NEN/HECATE rose on a fresh point of order, and more than once the Speaker himself interposed to call the hon. member to the point actually before the House. On rising for the third time, the SPEAKER said he must call his serious attention to the matter, and must insist on his confining his remarks to the amendment.—Mr. Dreeoer thereupon brought his remarks to a conclusion.—Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN and Mr. Dery spoke with unprecedented brevity, and at this time the debate grew so languid and the attitude of the Irish members so far modified, that it seemed possible that a division might be taken forthwith—Mr. O'Conmon POWBR introduced some fresh vigour into the debate by replying to Mr. Gladstone's speech, a rejoinder which the Premier was not present to hear.—Mr. PARNELL joined in the complaint of the bitterness of Mr. Gladstone's speech, regretting that he had hurried away into an attempt to stifle freedom of discussion, a way. of putting things that called forth laughter and ironical cheers from the Ministeriel benches. Mr. Parnell, preserving throughout the greater part of his speech a curiously apolo- gettie one, threw himself -upon the consideration of the House, whilst he disclaimed all intention of advocating under guise of practical improvement in tbe land laws the severance of Ireland from the Empire. A passiodate variation from this ' tone, in which he lauded the power of the Land League, called up Sir STAFFORD NORTECOTE with a proteat against , this claim of co-equal authority with the Sovereign. The right hon. baronet, amid loud cheers from the Opposition, said bethought the statement was one that demanded some notice from the Treasury Bench.—The SOLICITOR-GENERAL for IRELAND said the only reason why silence bad been pre- served on the Treasury Bench was that it was thought that the debate had gone on long enough, and that no ' useful object would be served by extending the discussion. Nevertheless, Mr. T. P. O'Connon proceeded to extend it, Ildelivering a long speech in which a remark to the effect Ithat after certain alleged events the Government " had the cheek" to come down to propose coercion, led to the inter- position of Mr.WARTON, who solemnly put it to the Speaker "whether 'cheek ' was a Parliamentary word?" The SPEAKER declining to arbitrate in so novel a case, Mr. O'Coterron proceeded with his speech.—On the conclusion of this address, which waslistened to with great impatience, Mr. LAMB moved the adjournment of the debate.—l.ord HARTINGTON, in a few vigorous sentences, loudly cheered, declarkl that this could not be done without taking the sense of the House. He 'Warned the Irish members that they were irritating the House and the country to is degree that might prove uncontrollable. On adivision, the adjourn- ment was negatived by 223 to 40.—0 f the eight English Liberals who voted for Mr. Parnell's amendment on Satur- day, Mr. Arnold now voted with the Government; others were not present at the division. No further objection being offered from the Treasury Bench, at half-past one the debate was adjourned. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tnasner. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at five o'clock. . There was no business set down for consideration, and this fact, coupled with the extreme inclemency of the weather, accounted doubtless for the non-atiendance of peers, of whom threelirtly were present. The Earl of Coax presented further corresponce relating to the affairs of Afghanistan; and the House adjourned at a quarter past five o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Togitnay. THE SNOWSTORM without did not prevent a considerable gathering of the members of the House of Commons. There I were some gaps in the Conservative ranks; but the Liberals braved the storm in numbers sufficient to give quite an ordinary appearance to the sitting. Mr. Gladstone was not present, Lord Hartington, in the Premier's absence, ipnder- taking the leadership of the House. TEMPLE Batt Mamowter,.—Mr. LARDS:TONERE gave notice to ask the First Commissioner of Works whether he hasany intention or taking steps to secure the removal of the Temple Bar Memorial. • WATER SUPPLY.--In reply to Mr, Ritchie, the ‘Homa dealing dwteh hoped to rbesuapbpl el ytoot the bring sessionSE alir ia metropolis.aßill this THE Ortum TRADE.—In reply to Mr. tease, Sir CHARLES DILICE said the Government were to waitirg • r communica- I tin's of the views of the Indian Government on the opium question before coming to a final decision upon the arrange- ment proposed in Sir Thomas Wade's despatch ef January 31,1E80. ME. MCCARTHY'S AMENDMENT.—Mr. KOLLOY rising to resume the debate on Mr. McCarthy'. amendment to the Address was the signal for a general clearance of the House. Mr. Molloy deserved a better audience inasmuch as his speech was commendably brief.—Mr, BLENNERHASSETT, speaking as an Irishman, and having a: heart the interests lof his country, deplored the action of efr. Parnell and his friends as calculated to alienate frog Ireland the support of Liberal opinion throughout the country,mr. He suggested, amid cheers from the Irish quarter, that Mr. Forster should bring in a measure something like the Com- pensation for Disturbance Bill, to run pending the passing of the Land Bill—Mr. MARIIIf having, in the course of a discursive speech, dealt with the Battle of Hastings, was proceeding to inqaire bow far the Continental history bore on the subject, when he was called to order by the SPEAKER, who pointed out the difficulty of tracing the connection be- tween these topics and the amendment before the House. By way of proving the loyalty of the Land League in the face of calutnnious statements to the contrary, Mr. MARIIII narrated an interesting anecdote, showing how at a Land League dinner he had attended a 'toast was drunk to the health of "The Queen and the rest of the Royal Family." The company insisted upon him (Mr. Marum) reeponding, "which," be said, "though an unusual circumetance, I did." —Mr. O'Dornerm announced that if the axe were waiting for Irish members in the lobby, it would not debar them front doing their duty—a declaration greeted with unsym- pathic laughter by the House.—ln the subsequent courswof debate Mr. sluarne McCanniv expressed his willingness to withdraw his amendment in favour of any other proposi- tion which would embody the protest of Irish members against evictions in a form that would not be regarded by hon. gentlemen_ as open to objection on Constitutional grounds. This offer failing to meet with acceptance, the debate was continued entirely by Irish members until twenty minutes past twelve, when, on a division, the amendment was rejected by 201 to 37. The debate on the Address was again adjourned. The House rose at twenty minutes to one. The Speaker took the chair aehalf-parat 12.

Mr. O'Connor, Mr. Sexton, Mr. Callan, and other Irish members spoke in support of the amenc,ment.—A division was taken, 34 members Tating for the amendment and 173 against.—The Address was then adopted amid loud cheers, the debates on it having lasted for a fortnight.—A commit- tee, consisting of the mover and seconder, Mr. Gladstone and other members of the Government, was appointed to bring up the report on the Address.—A lengthy discussion subse- quently took place on the Basuto war on Sir Wilfrid Law. son's amendment, which was ultimately withdrawn, and the Address agreed to. Previous to the adjournment of the House, at 10 minutes past 11, Mr, Macdonald's bill to amend the Employers' Liability Act was read a second time.

STRIKE OF MINERS AT ST. HELENS. GREAT EXCITEMENT. During the past week St. Helens has been in a great state of excitement on account of the colliers "striking" at some of the collieries in the surrounding districts. The men have unanimously resolved to abide by the Employers Liability Act, out of which the employers have been en- deavouring to contract themselves. The colliers of Hay- dock and Wigan' who turned out at the beginning of the week, resolved that the miners of St. Helens, Whiston, and the neighbourhood should be seen as to whether or not they would join them and stay from work until the masters had conceded to them an advance is their wages. It was rumoured all over the town on Tuesday that there would be an invasion by the Wigan, Ashton, and Haydock miners, and it was also said that the men employed at St. Helens would turn out on Wednesday morning. This, however, proved to be false, all the men or most of them going te their work on Wednesday morning. At noon on Wednesday people congregated in the street awaking the arrival of the Wigan and Hay-deck colliers. A number of colliers with brass instruments walked about the streets playing, and apparently soliciting support, but they were ordered off by the police. At half-past twb a band of music heard in Parr gavelli e signal that the colliers were coming, and in a few minutes about 1,500 of them, headed by a brass band, crossed Raven-street Bridge, marched along Ragen-street and Church-street, now and again rending the air with their shouts. They walked five o • six abreast, and conducted themselves in an orderly manner. They were joined by a large number of St. Helens men,and Mr. Cross, the miners' agent, accompanied them to their destination, which was Whiston and Prescot, where it was said the colliers were at wourk.crlotpwpears3.thhiolui,gahntd ma by somede a that they would go to Messrs. Pilkington's pits, but they marched along Liverpool-road, p stoppage at the Bird in Hand. The Superintendent of Police (Mr. Johnston) with a few officers followed close behind to see that there was no breach of order, and he was informed by Mr. Cross that he need not be anxious about there being any misbehaviour as the men were simply having "a walkout," and he would give Mr. Johnston his head if any harm was done. Mr. Cross then informed the men of the nature of the conversa- tion, and cheers were then given for the superintendent of police. They then went forward to Whiston, where a meet- ing was held, and which was attended by miners in that dis- trict. Mr. Cross urged upon the men to offer no violence to anyone who went to work, and to have no interference with the masters or the men. In a short time they returned, walking in the middho of the road as before, headed by a band, and on arriving at St. Helens they stopped in front of the George Inn, a popular resort of the miners, and subse- quently made their way home to Haydock. On Thursday morning, all the colliers in the town and Whiston turned out, and the streets in St. Helens throughout the day wore a very lively appearance. A meeting was arranged to be held on the fair ground, and for two three hours crowds of colliers assembled in front of the Examiner Office, awaiting the arrival of the Haydock contingent, and others at the other end of the town waited to greet those from Whiston. Between three and four o'clock the sound of amusic a plst era in ltdhe de at ihr r at hp plroouadc h. ch eTehr ienr ge ,waansawaa vgi ne nge or af hands rush was made to the Fair Ground. A platform was erected, on which the speakers and reporters took up their position, and round about this platform about 6,000 people assembled to hear what was to be said on the question uppermost in their minds. On the motion of Mr. Cross, seconded by someone in the crowd, Mr. Charles Downs, a Golborne miner, was voted to the chair. Mr. Cross remarked that they had had a very large meeting at Golborne that morning, and they were all present now. The Cnaintalw, addressing the crowd as the workingmen aft. Helens, Haydock, Edge Green, and the surrounding districts, said they were met together determined upon having an advance of wages and weekly payments. Hear, hear, and a voice : "So let it be.") They were aware that the masters had surrendered the Liability Act, but not until they were made. (Cheers.) But he asked the public were they not entitled to an advance of wages, seeing what the price of coal was? He called upon Mr. Cross to address them. Mr. Caws expressed the pleasure he had in seeing inch a glia,aortgwhene rci Honngacl oli unwr oilas : a clpi dee.onp3l He a. n wascTe heyths eahr foundation not they wade stone9llmehe welcomed their flatr ghee outside friends from near Wigan. They were in one mind ; they had been tortured, and this had caused the men to rebel against the tyrants who inflicted punishment upon them and their children. They had suffdred for the last five years as no other subject of Her Majesty had suffered; 16s. a week was a lower wage than any other labourer in Her Majesty's dominions received, and yet the masters told them they could not advance their wages. The mastershad surrendered the Permanent Relief Fund, but to whom did it belong if not to the men? (Hear, hear.) Why should the masters take their money and have the sole management and regulation of the Funds? He was told that five er six who managed it were j,p debt to it £2OO. Those were not people to look after Weir money. He hoped the men would let the masters see they were not to be chaffed or slighted. Though the people might say "What's all this about?" or that " they are only a few colliers kicking up a row," what could the glass works, chemical works, and the ironworks do without them? They wanted 15 per cent, upon their wages, and they wanted their money at half-past 12 on Saturdays—(laughter)—so that their wives might go to the market and purchase food at first cost, and then they would go to work. Having spoken of the insufficient ventilation in the mines, and re- marked that this could be remedied by putting down other shafts, he asked them to give no occasion for the papers saying on Friday that they bad misbehaved themselves. While he urged them to keep the peace he hoped they would go home and not strike another "knock "until their Nthands had been conceded. (Applause.) Mr. WOODS, of Ashton, addressed the meeting, and said it was a great encouragement to see such a large number pre- sent. Now they had got the Liability Act he urged them to band themselves together in case they had to fight the masters, as it was utterly impossible for a poor collier to endeavour to obtain compensation by law from a wealthy colliery proprietor. He was sorry they had not a sliding scale, so that the wages of the men might rise with the price of coal. He was glad that the masters had consented to meet a deputation of the men with respect to the formation of a sliding scale. If they got one formed on a proper basis it would do away with strikes and lockouts* He was glad to find such unanimity amongst them. There were very few knobsticks, and he believed that the masters would give them the advance they asked for before long. (Applause.) Mr. CROSS said that a coal master called at his house at eight o'clock that morning, and said that he only had 20 men—(A Voice: "That's a lie.")—and he sass willing to give them 15 per cent, and weekly payments, and do any- thing he possibly could if they would go and get as many coals as wenld keep his two or three engines working. (Laughter.) It was a very serious thing, and he asked them to use a little discretion. All hands were held up against that proposal. Mr. Cnoss condemned the action of a colliery proprietor who retained the wages of the men because they had turned Cut. The CHAIRMAN then proposed that they stand out tint they receive an advance. (Loud cheers.) It was a reasonable demand, and the public said so. Th• motion en being put was carried unanimously; as was also another that they be paid weekly wages. A vote of thanks was accorded to the members of the Press, and the meeting then terminated.

div.head: COLLIERS' STRIKE.
div.p: COLLIERS' STRIKE.

Six miners residing in Bradford-cum-Beswick were charged at the Manchester City. Police Court, on Tuesday. with having solicited alms in the public streets. It appeared that the prisoners and others crossed the boundary into city, dragging with them a hurry, on which a quantity of bread and other provisions collected from shopkeepers was piled. They begged further contributions from other shopkeepers and passers-by. Mr. Smith, who defended, argued that the prisoners had in no way rendered themselves amenable to the law, not being in any way disorderly. They were, in fact, upholders of the law, for they were on strike against an attempt on the part of the masters to violate the Em- ployers' Liability Act. Having been driven from their employment by the masters, they had nothing to live upon, and had either to go about in this way or throw themselves upon the Guardians for relief. Moreover, they were not begging in the ordinary way, for all the contribution they received went to a common stock for providing soup kit- chens, Asc. They were discharged with a caution. WinAte.—A special meeting of miners' delegates from, various districts in West Lancashire was held on Monday' afternoon, in the Miaers' Hall, Wigan, to consider the I further action of the men. Delegates were present from Wigan, Leigh, Tyldesley, St. Helens, Hindley, Ashton, Standish, Skelmersdale, and other portions of the coalfields. After a lengthy discussion, the following resolutions were passed :—" That, seeing that a good many of the masters in various districts have agreed to give their employes an ad- vance in wages, we, the miners of Wigan and surrounding districts, are determined not to go back again to our work until we get an advance in our wages equal to the last re- duction in our field prices." " That, if the reports which have appeared in the papers respecting the South Yorkshire minera..having withdrawn their notices as a body is true, this meeting considers that those miners have not kept faith with the Manchester conference." "That we try to get al sliding scale established on a satisfactory basis to regulate wages for the future, and that we earnestly recommend masters to pay wages weekly, and as soon as pos. sible." It was also unanimously resolved "That this meet- ing be suspended until it is necessary to call another."_ On Monday afternoon a large meeting of non-unionists took place in the Circus, Wigan. The following resolution was unanimously carried :—" That this meeting is of opinion that, with economic legislatien,the entire coal mines can be worked with perfect safety; and, also that.the present state of trade warrants an advance of wages." The men seem very determined in their action not to resume work unless at increased wages, which, they maintain, they are warranted in applying for. There is great distress in the district already, and if the strike, which is now simply on the wage question, continues, the suffering must become very severe. . Mairroros mutt MANCEIESTER.—On Monday, large meet- ings of miners were held at Pendlebury and Pendleton to consider the decision of the masters who have conceded their claims under the Employers' Liability Act. Resolu- tions were passed not to return to work without an increase in their wages of not less than 10 per cent., the price of coal having risen tenpence per ton. The masters were waited upon by deputations. from the meetings, but the decision of the Bridgewater trustees is not yet known. Messrs. raking- ton have intimated their willingness to consider the ques- tion, if the men would at once return to work. MERTINO OP YORKSHIRE AND DERBYSHIRE MINEES.—On 'Monday, especial meeting of the South Yorkshire and North Derbyshire Miners' Association Council was held at Barns- ley, when the movement for an advance of 10 per cent, was thoroughly discusaed, attention being drawn to the brisk state of the coal trade, owing to the Lancashire strike. To- wards the close a letter was read from Ashton, in Lancashire, stating that the employers in that district had conceded 114 per cent, to the miners, and 4d. per day to the labourers. The council therefore resolved that notices given to expire in Thursday should be extended, and those who have not given notice to do so at once. MOVEMENT os Tnoops.—ln consequence of the disturbed state of the Laneashire mining district, two troops of the 18th Hussars left Hulme Barracks, Manchester, on Tuesday, for Pendlebury, in order to meet any emergency that might arise. Two additional troops of the same regiment arrived in Manchester on Tuesday from Liverpool. Moors AT ATHERTON.—A body of the 18th Hussars ar- rived in Atherton at noon on Tuesday, to protect the Ather- ton collieries from an apprehended attack by the mob after a meeting of miners at Tvldesley. The Hussars are in the neighbourhood, and likely to remain, awaiting the source of events. At present things remain perfectly quiet. MEETING AT AsOcne.—Delegates representing 4,000 col- liers on strike in the Ashton and Oldham districts met on Tuesday morning, in Ashton, to discuss the terms offered by the employers with a view to the settlement of the dispute. IThe delegates reported that the men had decided in their odge meetings to abide by the original iensand for an ad- vance of 124 per cent., and not to accept the offer of their employers, which is equivalent to only 8 per cent. THII SOUTH YORKSHIRN COAL TRAM'. —On Tuesday large placards were pestod throughout the districts of Barns- ley, Sheffield, and Rotherham, by Messrs. Wells, Birch, Hyde, and Company, of Manchester, owners of the Hoy- land Silkstone Collieries, announcing that the Silkstone Pit, where the men struck against the umpire's award, is open to all workmen with or without riddles. The average earnings, with riddles before arbitration was ss. ad. or without rid- dles under the umpire's award Bs. 24. per day. A conference of the miners' delegates representing the various districts of Lancashire was held at the Mechanics' Institute, Manchester, on Tuesday, when, after a long dis- cussion on the etrike question, it was decided that the secre- tary should be instructed to write to the West Yorkshire, Staffordshire, North Wales, and St. Helens collieries, calling upon the men to restrict their labour' to prevent as much as possible the great influx of coal coining from these districts into the Lancashire market during the present struggle, an I stating that the conference was of opinion that it was advis- able to form one union for all Lancashire. A letter was read from Mr. Macdonald, M.P., advising the members to unite in one union.

The strike of colliers in the Ashton-under-Lyne anti Old- ham districts has come to an end. The men had unani- mously decided to reject the compromise offered by the employers, but an interview took place on Tuesday between the representatives of the masters and the men. The result is an understanding that the men should resume work on Wednesday and the colliers on Thursday. It is understood that the masters have conceded the men-'s demands in their entirety. The decision has given great satisfaction through- out the district. where great distress has been caused by its long continuance.

I Anthough a council medial of South Yorkshire miners at Barnsley on Monday resolved that a strike should follow the expiration of the notices, the men employed at the Old and New Oak Pit have withdrawn their Notices, and their ' example has been followed by half-a-dozen of the largest of 1 the pits in the district. All coal owners and proprietors in Darwen have raised their coal Is per ton., Messrs. Placs and sons, colliery pro- prietors, Hoddlesden, among the number. In consequence of this all the colliers at Hoddlesden have been idle since Monday morning, they refusing to resume work unless the masters will increase their wages in proportion to the ad- vance in the price of coal. Best house coal is being supplied to all the mills, and the supply of this is almost exhausted. One mill (Messrs. Gregson's) was stopped at three o'clock on Tuesday, and others are expected to stop shortly. In anticipation of au attack by rioters on the Atherton collieries, near Leigh, the proprietors (Messrs. Fletcher, Burrows, and Co.) on Tuesday secured the protection of a detachment of Hussars from Manchester. They are nos encamped near the pits. Great poverty is felt in the district, and on Tuesday distribution was made of large quantities of potatoes and bread. There is now a strong probability that within a day or two the strike of Lancashire colliers will come to an end, on terms which have been arranged between the masters and the men. Considerable satisfaction was expressed all over Lancashire on Wednesday, at the turn events have taken, and the early settlement of the di fficuluties which have arisen through the idleness of 50,000 colliers willbring with it an - mixed pleasure. On Wednesday, the colliers at Pendleton and the district, including the large workings of the Bridgewater Trust, Messrs. Knowles aid Co., Messrs. Pilkington, the Clifton and eariireY Coal Company, and others were generally In` Work, and jt was anticipated that on the following day most of the ineit would have returned. . ' .

An interview was held, on Wednesday evening' between betideen 2,000 colliers employed by the executors of Colonel Hargreaves and their employes, at Burnley. It was agreed RI adopt kn Accident Fund in lieu of the Employers' Liability, and it was stated that the terms of the new rulesl and regulations would be issued on Saturday next. -.At meetings of the men of the Wigan district, on Wed- nesday,. a strong determination was manifested to insist upon an increase of wages to the extent of 10 per cent., the present state of trade and the large demand for coal war- ranting the advance, as it was urged; and the Pendlebury, Clifton, and Worsley men have unanimously resolved not to go in until they have their wages raised 14 per cent. There has been a considerable resumption of work at the collieries in the Swinton and Pendlebury districts, and the struggle in that neighbournood may, it is hoped, be regarded as over. From what was said at a meeting of colliers at Tyldealey on Thursday, there has been some defection from the ranks of the turnouts, but the meeting passed a resolu- tion not to go in till a more satisfactory understanding had been come to with one of the firms, said to be the only one which had not conceded the men's terms. At a meeting of delegates held at Farnworth on Thursday, resolutions were passed to the effect that work should be resumed the following morning, and notice be given forthwith for an advance of wages; but at a mass meeting held later in the day, i was resolved not to return to work till an advance had been granted. At many pits in the neighbourhood, however, the men have gone in. In the Skelmersdele dis- trict, on Thursday morning, a mob of about 300 men, many of them carrying cudgels, met colliers going lo their work, and compelled them to return home.

• I Tim durtax QUESTION—Sir C. Drum wished to make an explanation. He was erroneously reported in some of the papers as having stated last night that papers relating to the Greek Question had been laid on the table. He would now state that the Government was in possession of information on the 28th July that all other Powers had withdrawn their objection to the mobilisation of the Greek army. On the 110th July Her Majesty's Govern- ment informed the Greek Government that, although con- sidering the mobilisation premature, they did not wish to press their views upoe the Greek Goveinment. A statement to that effect was made also on the 30th July. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDEESS.—CONTINIIANCE OP 013- sTHEcrioß.—Tbe adjourned debate on the Address was re- sumed by Mr. DAWSON' who justified:his amendment and the persistence with which the Irish members had pressed their views on the House during the discussion on the Address, on the ground of the manner in which practical legislation for Ireland had been neglected for so long a time. They wished to have a distinct recognition of the necessity for re- dressing the inequality between the Irish and English borough franchise which was created by the legislation of Parliament. Bills had been brought in for the purpose for several years, but nothing had been done. In Ireland men were liable to be disfranchised through the omission of their' landlords. The Irish voter was under many other restric- tione and obstructions which did not exist in England, and Dublin stood unique amongst the towns of Ireland for special disabilities. The Buesian peasant on the confines of civilisation enjoyed more control over the affairs of his locality than did the working man in the metropolis of Ireland After speaking for an hour and three-quarters, he concluded by moving as an amendment to the Address to add :—"That we humbly pray Her Majesty to submit a measure for the purpose of assimilating the borough fronchise in Ireland to that in England, as promised in Her Majesty's most gracious Speech last session."—Mr. W. E. Foie/mug complained of th: inappropriate manner in which the subject had been brought forward. In the speech they had just beard no reason had been given why the question of the franchise should be taken up before other measures, and especially before the Land Bill, end there was RR entire absence of argument to justify its introduction as an amendment to the Address. It was quite true that the hon. member had acted strictly within the rules of the House, but it was quite pos- sible so to make use of those rules as altogether to prevent the transaction of business. He put it to the members for Ireland whether the time had not come when they should get to the business of the session. Having regard to the events of . last session the Government c)eild not be charged with neglecting Irish affairs, and he was sorry that they were unable to pass the Borough Franchise Bill, as to which their opinion was unchanged. The reason the subject was not mentioned in the Speech from the Throne was that owing to the other very important Irish timidness before the House it might not be posaible to introduce the bill this session. If it should be possible the bill would be brought forward, but some time must be devoted to English and Scotch business. Irish affairs could not be allowed to "take up the whole of the session, though it seemed probable that they would take up a very large portion of it. The hon. member had suggested that the franchise bill should take the place of another measure referred to in the Speech from the Throne, but the Government being of opinion that exceptional measures were necessary for the protection of liberty in Ireland it could not be supposed that they would postpone the duty in order to make way for any other matter. They were desirous to assimilate the borough franchise in Ireland to that of England, and the moment they cquld do so without interfering with the other mom important Irish business a bill would ba introduced for that purpose. —Mr. GRAY had beard of bills for curtailing Irish liberty, but was rejoiced now to learn that they were to have a bill for the preservation of liberty.—Sir J. AVICENNA supported the amendment, to remind the Government of their promise. —Dr. LYONS thought this was a most inopportune time for bringing forward such an ameudment.—Mr. FINIGIN com- plained that the Government had not told them on what principles their Irish legislation was to be proposed, and the Irish members were therefore driven to bring forward such amendments as the one under discussion. Under the existing law, although the borough of Ennis, which he represented, contained 8,000 householders, the number of registered electors was only 250.—Mr. W. Jeeces said that to bring forward the question as an amendment to the Address was simply a waste of time.—Mr. DILLON said three-fourths of the Irish people were disfranchised, end that fact proved the urgency of the question, and as bill after bill handed In by the Irish representatives to deal with'. the question had been rejected they were quite justified in raising the matter as an amendment to the Address.—Mr. EIRALY believed that the Government had no in- tention of dealing with the Irish franchise. He also ventured to prophesy that the Government would not pass the Irish County Government Bill this session, although it was mentioned in the Queen's Speech, because he had no faith in the sincerity of their intentions. He was not sur- prised at the Government dropping the Irish Franchise Bill last year, because the solicitor General for Ireland was him- self a member for a rotten borough. Mr. BYRNE, supported the amendment, and expressed his opinion that it was only from the Irish members that the Government heard the truth about Ireland. Mr. M`Caarrav suggested that if the Government would give an undertaking to introduce and endeavour to pass through an Irish Borough Franchise Bill this session the controversy might be allowed to drop. Mr. BIGGAR considered that the greatest waste of time that took place in the House was in the re-argument of questions about which there was no room for controversy, and amongst such questions he included that of the assimilation of the English to the Irish borough franchise. Irish members were charged with de- laying important legislation for Ireland, but the Irieh peo- ple had no confidence ,in the promised land reforms of the present Government. If they wanted to facilitate business, they would do well to consult the majority of Irish members as to the order in which the Irish question should be taken up.—Mr. DALY also supported the amendment.— Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN was speaking in its favour at a quarter to six, when, by the rules, of the House, the debate was ad- journed.
The Municipal Franchise (Scotland) Bill was read a second time.

Lord E. FITZMAIIRICH brought in a bill to appoint a Com- mission for the alteration of the areas of local govern- ment in certain oases, and for the rearrangemena of bounda- ries. Mr. McDoxam), a bill to amend the Employers' Liability Act, 1880.
The House adjourned at ten minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tnunsnay.

The House assembled for a quarter of an hour, and after Lord FORTESCUB had given notice of his intention to draw attention on the following day to the State of Ireland, their lordships adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tnuinney.

THE GREEK QUESTION.—Sit CHARLES DILLE, in reply to a question from Mr. Burke, said that the proposal of the Powers that Turkey and Greece should agree to submit to arbitration had been abandoned, but active communications were still being carried on with a view to securing a peace- ful settlement of the question. GRIEVANCES or TELBERAPH CLBEKS.—In reply to Mr. Cowen the Postmaster-General admitted that it was just possible that the telegraph clerks had been unduly re- strained in making their grievances known to the public. He himself, however, was not aware of any such restraints being imposed, and it was not true that the officials at Sheffield and Cardiff had threatened to suspend any employe I taking part in calling meetings. Replying to Mr. Whitley, Mr. Fawcett made a statement regarding the labours of the telegraph clerks in Liverpool. MILITARY REFORIC—Mr. Ciar.natas announced that, after much deliberation' he had decided to submit the re- port of Lord Airey's Committee on military reform to Parliament. THE REPRESENTATION OP EDINBURGE.—Lord R. GROS- VENOR moved for the issue of a new writ for Edinburgh. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—Professor THOROLD ROGERS called attention to an irregularity in the amend- ment of Mr. Dawson on the Irish franchise question.—The SPEAKER ruled that the amendment could not be put as it stood, and it was by leave of the House withdrawn.—Mr. 'SEXTON then brought up the amendment in another form —On a division, which Mr.PAIINELL regretted had not been taken on the previous day, the amendment was rejected by 274 to 38.—Another amendment to the Address was brought forward by Mr. O'KutLy, praying Her Majesty to guarantee to the people of Ireland their constitutional right of public meeting.—lt was intimated by the Purim that in order to save time the Ministers would take no part in the debate.—Mr. Thompson, member for Durham,

ROBBERY BY SERVANTS AT CRONTON.—Eliyabetit Hay- dock, aged 17, and Jane Atherton, aged 16, servants, pleaded guilty to a charge of stealing, at Cronton, on the 30th Nov. a satchel, knife, bag, and other articles, the property of. Wm. Warburton, and an apron, a cloak, and a par of stock- ings, the property of Elizabeth Derbyshire. .Haycock, who had been previously convicted, was sentenced to four niontht.s' hard labour, and Atherton was liberated on her own recognisances, to come up for Indgenent when called upon. • • The sessions were resumed on Wednesday; the Earl of Derby presiding. RIOTING AT CIII.CRETR.—Bertard Docilely OM, JAR Morley, Michael Morris (the elder), Michael Morris (the iyounger), Thomas Finnigan (22), Thomas Eagan (28),ntui Patrick Gilligan (20), all labodrers, 'Were clurrgedo' ,• rioting at Culcheth, en the 4th December, and mai beating, and wounding Alice Rigley.--After the eVidencl. prosecution withdrew the charge u-ainst Morley, who wa, accordingly discharged. All the other prisoners were found guilty. Morris, jun., Gilligan, and Eagan were each sen- tenced to nine months' imprisonment, Doglierty and Finni- gan eight months each, and Morris, sena six months' imprisonment. WOUNDING AT Eccaesrom.—Ort Thursday, Patrick Pan- nell, a labourer, was sentenced to ten months' imprisonment for having, on Nov 13th, at Eccleston, unlavrfullyand ma- liciously wounaed Michael Donnelly. HOT-SE BREA/HBO AT LOWTON.—Geerge Eckersley (18), a collier, Was indicted for having, at Lowton, on November 4th, feloniously broken and entered the dwelling-house of Wm. Leather, ana stolen therefrom a silver lever watch, a gold albert guard, and other articles. He was further charged, together with Wm. Yates, a young man, with having, at Kenyon, on the 11th November, entered the dwel- ling-house of iVm. Mort, and stolen therefrom the sum of £lO in gold ant a quantity of silver and copper coins. The prosecutor offered no evid, tee on the first charge, but both prisoners were found gailty of the second charge. Eckers- ley was Sentenced to 18 months imprisonment, to be fol- lowed bv Pee years' police supervision; and Yates was sent to gaol lot 12 months.

To describe the means used to prevent citizens from serving on a jury, or to intimidate them when they had once been sworn, the phrase "Emparnelling the Jury" might be used. LORD BEACONSFIELD ON THR POSIVON OF APFAIRS.—• At the Greenwich Conservative banquet, on Wednesday night, Mr. Boord, M.P., read a letter from the Earl of Beaconsfield, dated the 18th instant, from 19, Curzon-street, in which the noble lord said:—" England has, at this moment, much to contend against. It is impossible to con- ceal that the country has fallen on dangerous and disastrous times; but I trust to the high spirit and the patriotic pride of its people alike to maintain the Constitution which has given to them an empire which has made them the envy of I the world."
