the dates and particulars of the several documents relating to the trust, and any declaration of trust that has been executed by the present trustees. The return, when completed, will not only be an elaborate but an interesting document. In the "good old times," when Parliament conducted its proceedings I • , secret,. and an inquisitive public had no newspapers , to unfold to them the practices of those high in State affairs and of those who were the dispensers of the national taxes, pensions multiplied as rapidly as court favourites, and with a lavish hand the descendants of favourites were created pen- sioners upon the British public for all time: The William Penn nnd the Marlborough pensions are j ample illustrations of ,the legacies which legislators in past days left to succeeding generations of the En- glish people. Bat the. time , has come when it is meet to inquire • whether those who did the state service were not fully rewarded in their own days for the good they either did or were supposed to have done the nation; and whether there is any justice in the present race of taxpayers being burdened with the payment of pensions to those whom nature has chanced to make descendants of men who were honoured in their own time, and who have personally served. the country in no beneficial capa- city, bat been mere clogs upon the wheels of State. • Bradlaugh has 'unearthed in a pamphlet he -has recently, issued , some singular transactions with hereditary pensiOns,- and one in particular is just now attracting some attention in certain quarters. • Plymouth contemporary recently published an . extract from this pamphlet, stating that a pension granted in'the days of Charles IL to an ancestor of the Earl of Kinnoull was now 'being paid to the present Earl. The amount was stated to be "i 676 being the residue of £lOOO a year, granted in 1662, and. "settled in perpetuity on the Earl of Kinnoull, as the representative of the Earl of Carlisle, to whom the revenues of the Island of 13arbadoes had been granted by King Charles IL" The Earl of Kinnoull, on seeing this statement in print, denied that he was in receipt of any such pension, and Mr. Bradlaugh then proceeded to make good his assertion by giving his authority, viz., the Financial Amounts, Iwhich set forth 'that £676 were annually charged on the Consolidated Fund in the name of the Earl. His Lordship next deputed his agent to make linquiries upon the subject, and the Chancellor of the Exchequer was called upon for an explanation. The agent put it that his lordship's commands were "to make the necessary inquiry to enable him either again to contradict the statement, or, if it be true, to re- cover the arrears of the pension which must have accumulated for massy years." The question was referred by the Chancellor of the Exchequer to the Lords Commissioners of her Majesty's Treasury, to get at the bottom of Mr. Bradlaugh's statement, Their lordships discovered the fast that the pension I was sold in 1817, but "they were not able to say whether even this was the first sale; at all events the• purchasers and their assigns have had the benefit of it since that date, and not the Earls of Yinnoull." Who the purchasers or their assigns are or were is one of the mysteries of the times. The controversy has resulted in bringing to light that a pension, granted more than two hundred years ago, has been made the subject of commerce; and if it has not created a suspicion that other pensions granted "in the good old times" have been treated as saleable ' commodities, it has at least strengthened the position of those who agitate for a thorough and complete investigation into hereditary pensions.

THB' Royal Commissioners on Agriculture have at last made their report, and it was laid on the table of the House of Commons on Monday night. It deals specially with the IriElti land question. Though much of the evidence eol- lected by the Commission, and the fact that the Commis- sioners we're divided in opinion, have been for some time before the public, the report is full of interest to those who have given to Irish subjects consideration. The statements which have been made from time to time in the Press as to the wretched condition of the tenantry in many parts of Ireland are fully borne out by the report of the Commis- sioners, who take cognisance of the existence of two classes of tenants. One class, the Commissioners point out, are in such straightened circumstances, and so dependent upon every turn of fortune being in their favour, that if there was at any time the slightest failure in the harvests, and no rent was demanded from them, they could not manage to exist; and for this class emigration and migration are recommended. The commissioners report that they "are convinced that emigration under a properly- organised scheme and the voluntary act of the people would naturally tend to relieve the congestion of population, where- ever it now exists, and would conduce to the social, moral and material welfare of the emigrants and of the population' remaining behind. Migration would involve the acquisition of tracts of land, and the transfer to them of a part of the population from other districts." This is a recommenda- tion which will net find favour with the Irish 'people, who are devotedly attached to their native soil. There are causes for the people being reduced to such straights, and there must be remedies for them. Absenteeism haa drained the country of its wealth, and the people have been driven to tie themselves to the soil for a subsistence. The capital hitherto carried out instead of being spent in the country has been necessary to provide industries for the employment el that surplus population which the soil alone cannot el:10mM and until the owners of estates recognise that property has its duties as well as its rights, Ireland must continue to sink deeper into poverty and misery. It is but poor consolation to the people of Ireland to be told that, whilst a system of wealth draining, born of absentee proprietorship, is to be perpetuated, their condition is not likely to he improved if they remain in their native land, and that the best thing that can be done for themselves and for their country is for them to seek a livelihood elsewhere. It has hitherto been a recognised principle in economics that jest in proportion as'a country is drainedihy emigra- tion of its working population it is reduced in material pros- perity; but the Royal Commissioners on Agriculture run coun- ter to this axiom and to the well-worn truism contained in the lines of Goldsmith :

fares the land to hastening ills a prey. Where wealth accumulates. and men decay. Princes and lords may flourish, or may fade. ' A breath can make them Ma breath has made; Hut a bold peasantry, their country's pride, When once destroy'd can never be supplied.

There is no reason in the world why Ireland should not, granted the same conditions as obtain in its sister king- doms, be as happy and prosperous as England and Scotland The second class into which the tenants are divided are those which the Commissioners denominate as "the improv- ing tenants." "Great stress has been laid," the Commis- sioners say, "upon the want of security felt by an improving tenant, which, it is alleged, limits not oily the number of persons employed, but also the quantity of food produced for the benefit of the general community. Bearing in mind the system by which the im- provements and equipments of a farm are very gene- rally the work of the tenant, and the fact that a yearly tenant is at any time liable to have his rent raised in consequence of the increase of value that has been given to his holding by the expenditure of his own capital and labour, the desire for legislative interference te protect him from an arbitrary increase of rent does not seem unnatural; and we are inclined to think that by the majority of land- owners legislation properly framed to accomplish this end would not be objected to." What form this legislation should take is a question upon which the Commissioners are divided. What are popularly known as "the three F's " fair rents," "fixity of tenure," and " free sale," constitute the rock upon which the Commissioners split. The following —Richmond and Gordon, Buccleuch, Vernon, W. H. Stephenson, Nigel, Kingscote, H. Chaplin, J. L. Naper, Paterson, B. Price, C. T. Ritchie, B. B. Hunter Ind- well, W. Stratton, Jacob Wilson, W. A. Peel (secretary),—certify that " the three F's " have been "strongly advocated by many witnesses, but none have been able to support these propositions in their integrity without admitting consequences that would, in our opinion, involve an injustice to the landlord." Lord Carlin gafnord janohinMeßsiscres. Stansteld, M. Henry, J. Cowen, J. Clay, d who were in the minority on the Commission, remark in the report that they are in favour of "the three F's." we have already said, it has for some time been generally known that there was a divided opinion in the Commission as to the remedies to be applied, and it will be for the govern- ment to propose, and for the Legislature to adopt, each remedies as the admitted bad condition of the Sister Isle requires.

•f- r t 4 RUNCORN LIBERAL ASSOCIATIOk —On thursat even.. ing a tireting•of the above association took place in Bathe:34 School, for the purpose of electing officers for the ensuing year. In the absence of Mr. R. Shaw, the president, Mr. R. Norman occupied the chair. The following officers were unanimously elected :—President, Mr. Robert Shaw; vice- president, Mr. T. Norraan ; hon. secretary, Mr. T. Handley; hon. treasurer, Mr. G. L. Davies; and secretary, Mr. .1. D. Jones. The general committee was re-elected en bloc. It was decided to have a banquet and public meeting early in February. and the meeting was adjourned to Friday neat to made Lb* final arrangements.

The insertion of a clause in the Employers' Liability Act, by which firms were empowered to contract their Workmen out of the provisions of the measure, seems likely to 'cause no end of trouble. The London and Nerth-Western Rail- way Company have offered their men certain improved arrangements as to their assurance society, on condition that they agree to contract themselves out of the Act, but they have also told their workmen that unless they consent to agree to their terms certain things will be done, which are apparently intended to frighten them intg compliance. It seems a very strange thing for the digeetoil of a powerful company to take action which; to a great extent, is intended to renders measure passed by the people's representatives in Parliament assembled, a dead letter. A barrister in Liver- pool has been consulted by what I may call the Defence League formed by the railway men, and a statement of his "opinion" was published in the Manchester .Examiner and Times of Thursday. He lays bare with no Oder hand the weak points in the proposals made by the directors, and urges the men not to be deluded by such offers. Amongst other things he states that one of the large companies offers its men just double the amount, in case of death, which the Louden and North-Western Railway managers propose to give; or, in other words, £2OO against the Euston gentlemen's 2100. The Liverpool gentleman also hints very broadly that the directors do not intend to engage any men, after a certain date, unless they are willing to take work on their terms, and he seems to be thoroughly convinced that the workmen now In the employ of the company will not be per- mitted to exercise their own free wills as to what course they may choose to take. What has happened during the last week in the county of Lancaster, in the struggle be- tween the colliery proprietors aid their men, ought to prove a sufficient warning to the directors of the London and Nerth-Western Railway Company that their workmen will not quietly suffer themselves to be tyrannously deprived of the privileges they possess as citizens of a great Empire; and that they are thoroughly instilled insejecting or accept- ing any offers Made to them to quietly dispose Of their birthright under an Act of Parliament for any mess of• pot- tage offered them by interested people. ,

BETHESDA I CONGEEGIATIDNAL CHURCH, BITHCOHH. kinetriL TEA MEnirtro.—This annual gathering took Place 'on WedaesdaY evening. About one hundred and seventy eat at tea. Afterwards a meeting was held under the'presi- dency of the pastor, the Rev. J. Di Thomas.--Mr. William Handley read the annual report. On the occasion of their last report there were 90 church members; daring the year 12 had been admitted, one had been removed by deatl4 one by transfer to another church, and three had removed from Runcorn, leaving the number at present on the church roll 109, or a net increase of seven. During the evening a hand- some dressing case and travelling rug were presented to Mr. B. B. Pierpoint, who, for upwards of ten years past, has officiated as organist at the church. 'Votes of thanks were passed to the tea-makers and the gentlemen who had deco- rated the room, and the proceedings terminated. •

NARROW ESCAPE OF DB. MoITRITZ AT RIINCORIL—On Monday night, Dr. Mouritz, of Runcorn, had a narrow es- cape of being drowned. He had been to the Tonnage office at Top Locks, which stands midway between the two lines of locks, and left there about seven o'clock in the evenihg to go to Shaw-street, Newtown. He crossed the gate, and walked towards Waterloo-bridge ; bat the night being very dark, he was unable to see very far, and instead af turning to hisright siieen clear of the bridge, he went forward and fell into the canal. He could do nothing for his own safety, on account:of the large quantity of ice, and his cries for as- iistance brought to the spot a young man, 'named Robert Hampson, who happened to be the Only person in the vicinity at the time. He succeeded in seizing Dr. Mouritz by the coat: collar in the nick of time before he was drawn beneath a flat which was moored near. Hampsan held the doctor above w..ter for about three minutes, when further assistance arrived in the shape of a dock constable, Joseph Booth, and another man,aud they assisted Hammon in taking Dr. Mouritz from the water. Hampson deserves great praise for his prompt help, for if he had been half a a minute later, there is no doubt Dr. Mouritz would have been drowned.

The distress in Runcorn and the district, consequent upon the severe weather, is very considerable, and I hope that all who have it in their power will do something to help on the efforts being made to relieve it. An important meeting of a committee of the Widnes Local Board was held on Tuesday, when a very im- portant resolution affecting the Law Clerk was passed.- 7, Corn.

All who had the pleasure of hearing the lecture delivered In Rtmcora by the Rev. Peter Mackenzie, in connection with the Wesleyan Methodist denomination, must admit that the gentleman has descriptive powers of a high order. Though not a man of the schools, he is exceedingly popular as a speaker. Owing to the original illustratiens which he introduces at almost every turn of his speech, the interest of the audience is constantly kept up from the beginning to the end of any lecture or discourse. Some may strongly object to such an irreverent way of dealing with spiritual subjects as that adopted by Mr. Mackenzie, but it is in- finitely preferable to the humdrum utterances of some of the preachers--well, let me say of those in towns where my lot has been cast. Sometimes one goes to hear a preacher, and though his theme seems to be such as permits him to draw illustrations from nearly every portion of his- tory, profane aid sacred, modern and ancient, from the rich stores 0 general literature, from the passing topics of the time, and from the ever-open page of human life, yet how dull, how prosaic, he will be, with his old-fashioned thread- bare homilies, and statements which a person has heard from the day when he was six years old, if he has been brought up in a religious family. This no doubt often I arises from the pulpit voice and mannerisms which appear to form the stock-in-trade of many preachers, who are as unnatural and artificial in their delivery as if they were mechanical figures. lam not one of those who would say " Cephas is too blunt, Apollos is too flowery, Paul is too argumentative, Timothy is too young, James is too severe, John is too gentle"; and when I see a preacher who is I thoroughly natural and not an aper of the mere priest, lam filled with admiration, and prepared to esteem him very I highly "for his work's sake,"—be he a General Booth, with his banners and his drums, or a James, such as he who at one time occupied the pulpit of Carr's-lane Chapel, Birmingham. I only wish that some phonographic reporter could sometimes hand over the notes of conversations which I hear on the style and matter of ministers who consider themselves pretty much "A lat Lloyd's." After they had perused the manuscript a little of the self assertion would be taken out of some of them. What we want is that ministers should be men among men, and still able to hold their own by the force of their intellectual superiority or perfection of charac- ter. Some persons appear to think that as long as they wear the parsenic long coat and white tie, they are about all right. In speaking of the tie, Mr. Spurgeon makes the fol- lowing remarks, which may be read with interest by some: —"lt has seemed to us to be needful to discard even the white necktie. While it was the ordinary dress of a gentle- man, well and good ; but as it has grown to denote a per- sonage of the clerical sort, or, in other words, has become a priestly badge, it seems best to abjure it. This may be done the more readily because it is also the favourite de- coration of undertakers and waiters at hotels, and one has no wish to be taken for either of these deserving functionaries. Some young preachers delight in cravats of extreme length, and others tie them with great precision, reminding us of Beau Brumtnel, who produced miraculous ties, because, as he said, he gave his whole mind to them. I was much aided in the summary dismission of my tie by an accident which happened to me when I first came to London. I was crossing the river by a penny steamboat, when a rude fellow said to me, How are you getting on at Hitchcock's ?' I could not imagine what he meant; but he explained that he snpposed I was in the drapery line, and was probably at that eminent firm." FLACCUS.

CONGREGATIONAL TEA PARTY AT Mum:n.7. The congregational tea party of the Halh.n Parish Church has been just held in the girls' schoolroom, when, notwith- standing the severity of the weather, some 230 persons sat Idown to tea. The room was tastefully decorated with ban- ners and flags, and was otherwise made to look cheerful and bright. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Mee. dames J. Ashley, Baguley, J. Baguley, Baker; D. Bennett, Brown, Challener, Cooper, Jones, Ormson, Roberts, Rutter, Limner, J. Stokes, W. Stokes, T. Wright, and Miami Ander- son Griffiths, and Wright. After tea the Vicar (Rev. J. Lockwood), who presided overthe meeting, gave an address, In which he expressed his great pleasure and the encourage- ment it gave him to see such a large gathering of congre- gation and friends, in spite of the very unpropitious night, andat the same time thanked the management committee 1 for their kind co-operation in making their tea party so great a success. The churchwardens (Messrs. J. Stokes and J. W. Baguley), and Mr. E. P. Mac Knight also delivered interesting speeches. An entertainment formed part of the proceedings of the evening, which passed off very success- fully. Hearty votes of thanks were accorded to the ladies for presiding, and also to the management committee and performers. The singing of the National Anthem brought the meeting to a close.

RUNCORN PABLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.—No business took place at the meeting of this society on Tues- day night, as the proceedings were adjourned. A Bill cited as The Licensing (Amendment) Act, 1881," was laid on .the table. The provisions of the measure are as follows : " Whereas it is desirable to give the ratepayers a more direct and immediate control over the granting of licences for the sale of excisable liquors than they at present possess; and whereas the provisions in force against the sale et fermented and distilled liquors during certain hoursof the Sunday have been found to be attended with great public benefits and it is important to extend such provisions to the other hours of Sunday. Be it enacted by the Queen's Most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of this present Parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows :-1. Licensing Boards: That on and after the let day of July, 1881, the power of granting, witholding, and transferring licensing certificates for the sale of excisable liquors in houses now vested by various Acts of Parliament in licensing magistrates, shall cease to be vested in, exercised, or exercisable by elected licensing boards. 2. Constitution of boards: That the number of persons comprising a licensing board, their qualification, date of election, district of jurisdiction, continuance in office, aid any other matter relating to the administrative duties of such board shall be regulated by an order or orders in Council. 3. Sunday closing : That on and after the Ist day of July, 1881, all premises in which intoxicating liquors are sold or exposed for sale by retail shall be closed during the whole of Sun- day, subject to the provisions (except as to the hours of closing on that day) of the Licensing Act, 1872. 4. That this Act shall be cited as the Licensing (Amendment) Act, 1881."

THE WEATHER : THOUSANDS OUT OF EMPLOY AT WlD- MES.—During the week the greatest difficulty has been experienced by the manufacturers at Widnes in obtaining a Supply of coal. Some of the works consume an immense quantity, as is evident from the fact-that Messrs. Sullivan alone use about 1,200 tons per week._ .Day by day reports have beep circulated that certain works had stopped. but Oil enquiry these have proved to be false, though the difficulty of keeping the furnaces going, and the possibility of ceasing, work any day, has been readily admitted. At Messrs. Gossage and Sons, where a very large number of men are employed, all the single men are only working three days per weck, and the married ones have received an intimation that if the present state of things continues, a similar decision may be arrivedat in their case. On making enquiries yesterday we were inform.d that the following works bad been stopped :—Messes. Golding, Davies, & Co., N. Mathieson & Co., the Deslta Co., Widnes Alkali Co ,-Messrs. Ifutchinsons, essrs. Sullivans,Messrs. Mort and Liddell, and Messrs. A. Gordon & Co., are all on short t.xne, and the men are ueder notice to cease work any day. Thousands of men are thus thrown out of em- ployment ; and the consequence of such a state of things to the district, if long continued, will be most disastrous.

_ • COX i7EST AT AFTBOBI7B ClTtrat72 SOH A • 001 m 1 .B. 8- cellaneons concert, in aid of St. Mark's Church, Antrobus was given in the schools on Tuesday evening, and notwith- standing the very inclement weather (the snow being in places several feet deep) there was It crowded attendance. The opening glee, "Hark, Apollo strikes the lyre," was. effectively rendered by a select glee party, and was well received. Mr. Isaac Wilkinson sang in a pleasing manner "The hunting squire." A reading, "Taking the census," was given by the Rev. Lyon Burnett (Little Leigh), vrbo was heartily applauded, and in response he read "I want deux fly." Mr. Bebbington, who is very popular in this' neighbourhood, was very successful in his rendering of "Muddle Puddle Porter" and "He was a careless man," for botfi of which he was encored. Miss Percival, Reed House, won the approbation of the audience with her song, "Sweethearts," and, being warmly encored, she sang in ad- mirable style " Comin' thro' the rye." This young lady I also sang with Mr. Bebbington a duet entitled "Hunting- tower," which was loudly encored. Mr. J. B. liaison gave a recitation, " The Quack Doctor," in such a manner that his reappearance was demanded, and he replied with a song, "The farmer's blunder," which was also much appreciated. The only instrumental item on the programme was "The five o'clock 'bus" a pi moforte duet, by the Misses Percival, Reed House, which was warmly applauded. Mr. .Phillips' reading, "Billy Armitage," was well received. Mr. Coppock obtained an encore for his song, "What an Englishman is made of," and, apr)pos of the dreadful night, Mr. Nixon sang "The Pilot." Mr. G. Parr's songs in character (the feature of the evening) provoked much merriment, and added greatly to the evening's enjoyment. The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, the vicar, in a few Well-chosen words thanked those who had bravely faced the stormy weather to attend the entertainment, after which a thoroughly enjoyable evening was brought to a close by the singing of the National Anthem.

SALE OF , A VALUABLE COLLECTICE OF AUTISTIC Pitorzwry.—We would draw the attentioia of our readers to the announcement which appears in our advertising coluinus of the sale by Messrs. Artingstall and Hind, on Tuesday next and two following days, of a rare and varied collection of fine art property. The collection comprises modern and ancient oil paintings from celebrated ateliers, unique and costly specimens of Porcelain, marble statuary, noble cast- ings in bronze of early periods, and many fine pieces of modern date, &c. The collection is well worthy of *the attention of lovers of the fine arts.

ANNIVERSARY MEETING OF GOOD TRAITLARS, AT ST HELENB.—The ninth anniversary of the "Ebenezer" Lodge (752), 1.0.G.T. was celebrated oa Wednesday evening, in the large room of Mr. King's Coffee Rooms, Westfield-street St. Helens. There was a fair attendance, members of other lodges being present. An excellent tea was provided by Mr. King, it was heartily enjoyed. After tea Mr. Haddy,W.C.T., occupied the chair, and, after some introductory remarks, he spoke of the evil resulting from the use of intoxicating liquors mentioning that the records of our police courts could :fiord abundant proof in support of his argument. M a proof that the good templars of St. Helens had not been negligent he said that a short time ago some of the shops in the town exposed whiskey bottles in the windows, with labels attached, stating that a bottle could be purchas,d with a certain number of pounds of tea, but by the action of the Good Templars' those bottles were taken out. (Cheers.) Bro. IL W. Kurkus, D.S., of Liverpool, made an able and amusing speech, and argued that as publichouses did not exist for the teetotallers or drunkards—the former not requiring them at all, and nobody being willing to admit that they existed solely, for, and were supported by the latter, they 'mast therefore, exist for moderationists, who were the very people the teetotallers and Good Templars wanted to get hold of. He mentioned that a coroner by experience proved that the number of deaths occasioned by strong drink in one year amounted to 120,000, being double the number usually quoted. Songs were given daring the evening by Miss F. Aldridge, Miss E. King, Mr. Skaife, Mr. Brockbank,; part songs by Mrs. and Miss Lindon ; recitations by Mr. J. S. Pickeragill and It. Jones • and readings by Mr. T. Pickers- gill and Mr. Hewitt. The usual votes of thanks having been tendered, the rest of the eveniog was devoted to amuse- ments, in which the company joined most heartily. LITATTTRE AT ST. HNLENB ON THE INTERPRETATION 07 THE BIBLE.—The first of a series of leotures, the object of which is to promote thought on religious questions, was held on Monday evening in the Bickerstaffe-street Chapel, St. Helens. The title of the lecture was, " Why do be- lievers differ in the interpretation of the Bible ?" Mr. C. Page occupied the chair, and there was but a small atten- dance. The lecturer opened. by remarking that they were not surprised that nations differed in their religious opinions, as they had different books from which they derived their religious knowledge; but it certainly did seem strange that when one book, which all Christians contended was of Divine origin, the readers should differ in the interpretation of that book. This was not because the book was unintelligible; it was not because the various leaders of different denomina- tions were dishonest, as they were most sincere in their teaching. Men's temperaments could not account for the diversity of interpretation, but the true reason was because of the method adopted by the different believers. He then proceeded to explain the mystic method which sought to find in scripture teaching something beyond the ordinary reading. The dogmatic method instead of deriving the meaning from the book, formed propositions and sought only for proofs of the same from it. From these premises he argued and concluded that the inductive method was the only intelligible one, and if followed faithfully by every reader of the Bible would most certainly lead to definite and true conclu- sions, and those conclusions in the majority of cases would be the same. He studiously abstained from defining any particular position in regard to doctrinal points. He urged his hearers to read the Book for themselves, and to carefully weigh every passage that bore on some particular subject, and after that, by induction, come to some definite conclu- sion. Having spoken of the uselessness of text-preaching, which he said was the most barren of all practices and gave no idea of Bible teaching, he resumed his seat, and the meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks.

TAXING CARE OF HER 'UNCLE'S Mo.—On Tues- day at the Leigh Police Court, a young man named James Farrell, a ship's fireman, applied to the bench for warrants against his brother-in-law, a collier, and the latter's daughter, on a charge of stealing a sum of £l5O under the following circumstances :—Farrell came over from Boston on Thursday week in the lowa, which brought a load of cattle to this country. He had made arrangements that the second accused, a mill girl living at Leigh, and a young woman named Lee, with whose grandmother he had been lodging at lames-at., Warrington, should return with him last Saturday in the lowa from Liverpool to Boston. On Wednesday week the girl was in Warrington, and undertook to take care of money which Farrell possessed to the amount of £l5O. She accordingly took the pocket-book, which contained A £lOO note, a £5O note, and a LIO note with her, to Leigh, promising to meet her uncle and Miss Leein Warrington on Friday night, to be in readiness for proceeding to Liverpool first thing OR Saturday. Farrell, it should be stated, had a portion of the money left him by his mother, and the balance was his own savings, and the entire sum had been entrusted to a priest at Warrington, who had regularly paid interest on it for the past seven years. As his neice did not arrive in Warrington on Friday night, Farrell became alarmed, and visited Leigh on Saturday, finding, on inquiry, that his neice and his brother-in-law bad taken tickets for Dublin, via Holyhead. He telegraphed to the police at Holyhead, and father and daughter were apprehended as they left the train, half-an- hour before the boat sailed for Kingstown. A sum of £l4O was found on the girl, who had been authorised by Farrell Ito spend £lO in clothing herself for the sail to America, where he believed she and the girl Lee might learn to weave, and earn more money than was possible in this country.— The Bench, after hearing the story, decided to grant warrants, the Holyhpad police having declined to hand over the prisoners unless warrants were obtained.—Farrell afterwards stated that he had spent several pounds on the outfit of the ! young woman Lee, and admitted that he purposed marrying r her in America. lie felt sorry for hl. neice, and expressed his belief that she had been influenced in the course she had I taken.

_ THE CHILIAN WAR. • ANOTHER DEFEAT OF THE PERUVIANS. BUENOS AYRES, January 20.—The Chilian army has attacked and completely defeated the Peruvian army, at Miraflores. The Dictator Pierola fled, and the Chilians occupied Lima without resistance, on the 17th. Pierolos, brother of the Peruvian War Minister, was made prisoner. The Peruvian loss in the battle of Chorillos is stated to have been seven thousand killed and two thousand prisoners. Twenty-five thousand Peruvian troops were engaged in the battle of Miraflores. The Chilian loss in killed and wounded in both battles was heavy. The diplomatic body at Lima have urged the conclusion of an armistice, and urged that the person of Pieroia shduld be respected. THE STATE OF IRELAND. Denis Murphey, a farmer, was tried at Kilmallock, Limerick Petty Sessions, yesterday, Tor forcibly entering, and retaking possession of a farm from which he had been evicted. Prisoner was returned for tri.xl.—Bail being re- fused.—Two companies of infantry and one hundred police have been drafted into Kilmallock, to protect Mr. Townsend, the prosecutor, in. the case.

Tile sheriff of the Co'unty Limerick and'about fifty of the Royal Irish constabulary, took possession on Thursday, of five houses, 'the 'Property of M. O'Brien, at Drumaolloger. An immense crowd gathered and attacked the police with stones and bottles. No injuries, however, were inflicted, and the police accomplished their purpose. THE COLLIERS' STRIKE.

Mr. Houghton, the chairinan, spoke in favonr of continuing the strike, and said that coiliers' wages were low through the masters' foolish competition. Another speaker urged the men to be well-behaved, and thus disgrace those who brought the military and extra 011Itce. Ojher speeches were de- livered, and a resolution was adopted to continue the strike. Five thousand persons ttended the meeting. . Sor-ru YORHSEIIRE COAL TRADE: MORE STRIKES.— The colliers employed at Woolley Colliery, between three and four hundred in number, have struck work because the owners refused 10 per cent. advance.—At Hoyland Silkstone Collieries, near Barnsley, the miners employed in the Silk- stone seam have agreed to resume work on Monday next at Is. 40. per ton.—The South Yorkshire Colliery Opera- tives' Association, representing surface workmen, have issued a circular to masters soliciting 15 per cent. adrance from February the 3rd. MR. GLADSTONE ON IRELAND, Mr. Gladstone has written a letter to the secretary of the Blackford Liberal Association in which he says: --T am glad to hear that you are about to hold a meeting far the purpose of strengthening the hands of the Government. If there is anything more important than anything eke at this time, it seems to me an attitude of patient forbearance towards Ireland and the Irish in England. English patience is being tried and will be tried yet more severely, but nothing is to be gained but much be lost by irritation, naturally stirred by thirty or forty of the Irish members of the House of Corn- mons ; we must guard ourselves against the datners of al- lowing prejudices to interfere with our sense of justice. I trust that the people realize the injustice of jumping hastily to conclusioglabout the Land Bill which is in prospect, tile first stage of which it is impossible for the members to be acquainted with.—Yonrs, W. E. GrAnTrown. THE SEVERE WEATHER

Telegraphiccommunication between London and the pro- vinces was, on Thursday morning, somewhat improved, but there was still considerable delay in the transmission of messages. On Thursday morning, the weather continued piercingly cold throughout the United Kingdom, and snore snow fell on the north and the east met, with a north-east wind in Scotland, which caused more drifting. The whole railway system of the north of Scotland is again reported "completely blocked." The thermometer rose in most dis- tricts, but the frost held on. At low water, eprly on Thurs- day morning, the river Mersey between Liverpool and Birkenhead and for some miles higher up was frozen over. On Thursday, the Common Council voted £5OO towards the relief of the distress in the city due to the severe weather. At Stoke-on-Trent, on Thursday, a meeting called by the Mayor was held to devise means for relieving the distress of the large number of out-door workers thrown idle by the severe weather, and a fund for that purpose was started. Tiverton, after being isolated since Tuesday, received the London mails yesterday morning, sixty-three mails being brought in five miles upon men's shoulders.
Tb'e snowed-up train at Brent Knoll, Great Western Rail- way, was extricated yesterday, and traffic between Padding- ton and Bridgewater was resumed. •

The Rev. Mr. Underwood, rector of Burtle, fell dead yes- terday morning in the snow. At Itiddlesborough, snow fell on Thursday night and yesterday, and has drifted in some places to a depth of seven feet. Hundreds of men are thrown out of work.

Owing to the snow drifting, a train on the Kington and Eardsley Railway ran off the line near the latter place yesterday. Two passengers were seriously injured, while others were bruised and damaged. Traffic was much d•layed.
o;ing to the severe frost the Windsor Waterworks engine was broken down, and Windsor, Eton, Eton College, and the barracks are without water.

The Great Western trains were arriving at Exeter more punctually yesterday, but the Plymouth trains were blocked at Ivy Bridge. Yesterday afternoon, the South Western trains from London were in difficulties between Yeovil and Exeter ; and the Dartmoor branch to Plymouth was again blocked. Great destitution exists in Staffordshire and Wor- cestershire on account of the continuation of the frost. All collieries, forges, and brickyards are stopped, and out-door labour of every kind is suspended. Relief committees have been formed in various districts. FATAL FLOODING OF A MINE.

_ None of the eight bodies of those drowned on Wednesday night by the flooding of the New Cathedral Mine, Redruth, have yet been recovered, nor are they likely to be, on ac- count of the quantity of debt-is which will have tobe cleared away before the work of pumping can be commenced. TWO WOMEN FROZEN TO DEATH.
Near Wycombe, two women have been frozen to death on their way to purchase household stores. SEVEN MEN FROZEN TO DEATH.

In the Hungerford district the effects of the snowstorm have been most calamitous. The mail cart driver and two assistants have been frozen to death at Ashbury, and four men in charge of a team at Marlborough lost their lives in the some way. A man was also frozen at Inkpen. In London, yesterday, there were eight degrees of frost. The Thames is more full than ever of drift ice.

Snow has fallen at Falmouth for three days, and was still falling yesterday. Snow has again fallen heavily in Glasgow. Up to ten yesterday morning, no London mails had arrived. Steamers which venture down the Clyde have to pass through a con- tinuous ice floe, progress being very slow. The canal be- tween Glasgow and Howling is entirely frozen, and barges are frozen up. DCNDEE, JAN. 21.—A great fall of snow occurreel through- out this district early this morning, accompanied by strong winds. The Dundee and Aberdeen Railway, which was cleared yesterday Afternoon, is again impassable, three goods trains being stuck between Aberdeen and Stonehaven. The Montrose line, along which only one train got yesterday, is completely blocked, as are also the Carmylie and Bervie branches. On the Dundee and Newtyle line a goods train got fast in a wreath six feet deep, but is now clear. THE IRISH STATE TRIAL. On Thursday, when the State trial was resumed, Mr. L. Dillon addressed the jury for the traversers Gordon and Boy- ton, and, referring to the Attorney General's remark that Gordon, who is a shoemaker, ought to have a stuck to his last," the teamed gentleman retorted that the Attorney General ought to have stuck to his last—the last count of the indictment. The last words for the defence were spoken I by Mr. A. M. Sullivan, M. P. who is a member of the Irish Bar, and appeared for the first time as an advocate in Ire- land. For nearly two hours he addressed the Court on behalf of Mr. Egan, the treasurer of the Land League, and in the course of his speech reviewed the government of Ire- land during the present century, and charged the public journals of Dublin and London with "hounding on" the Government to undertake the prosecution. He warned the jury, if they heard adjurations about "the majesty of the law," to remember that-that was an ancient formula often invoked to lure twelve honest men, and be besought them to Bay by their verdict that the law derived no majesty from its vindictive power of terror of punishment, nor when it was divorced from the sacred principles it was presumed to mirror forth—the eternal equities of God. Mr. Sedet the Heron commenced his reply on behalf of the Crown, and Court adjourned.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—L nom Pitorweriow IN IRELAND.—EarI GRANVILLE referred Earl Fortescue to the Prime Minister to explain why the Pro- tection of Peace (Ireland) Bill was not introduced into the House Of Lords. FLOGGING —Sir W. HARCOURT said that flogging was not ordinarily employed as punishment of incorrigible rogues. Magistrates had wisely abstained from doing go, except for blOntal offences. C. DiLas said the Government were quite prepared to receive communications for a renewal of diplo- matic relations with Mexico. THE LAND LEACIOE.—MI. GLADSTONE, replying I to Sir H. Tyler, as to whether the Gov^rnment, taking inio con- sideration the speeches of members of the Land League, woulclat once adopt stringent measures over certain parts of Ireland, said it would not then be convenient to discuss proposals to go beyond the law, and then to ask for in- demnity. THE ORDER OF BUSINESS.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the first business for Monday would be the motion for the postpone- meat of the orders of the day. On that being carried, Mr. Forster would move for leave to introduce a Bill for the

Preservation of Public Peace in Ireland. On leave being given, he (Mr. Gladstone) would move on Tuesday that the several stages of that Bill should have precedence of all , orders and motions from day to day. ME IletANDs ON TEE Tnalestear..—Mr.,Bamatens called attention to the affairs in the Transvaal, and moved a reso- lution stating that the annexation of the Transvaal was im- politic and unjustifiable, and that the House would 'view with regret any measures taken by Her Majesty's GoVern• ment with the object of enforcing British supremacy over the people of the Transvaal, who rightfully claim their national independence. He condemned the annexation as iniquitous, and contended that it was brought about without the full consent of the people. Hs urged the Go- vernment at once to acknowledge the mistake and to restore to the Transvaallits rlghtful independence. Mr. Cattrwmcnr seconded the resolution, but insisted that it was the duty of the Government to vindicate the honour of England. He thought the annexation a mistake, but he cast the', whole blame on Sir Theophilus Shepstone, who, he contended, did not properly carry out the instruction of Lord Carnatvon. —Sir J. LUBBOCIC objected to the resolution: He thought it hard that after we had spent our money and surificed our lives to be asked to renound the annexation of the Transvaal.—Mr. Fowler urged the Government to retain Her Majesty's supremacy in the Transvaal, and he advised the House to negative the resolution.--Sergeant Starox thought the House -by assenting to the resolution would strengthen the hands of.. the Government —Mr. H. CHAP- LIN, while opposing the resolution, thought the time' had arrived when the Government should sky whether they would give up or support the policy of their predecessors. He condemned the speeches made by the Premier during his electoral campaign in Midlothian, and said his Govern- ment were now sending troops and money to crush the victims of his fatal eloquence.—Mr. GLADSTONE justified his speeches in Midlothian. He denied that he had ever, in the sense implied by Mr. Chaplin, repudiated the annexation of the Transvaal. He thought there would be the greatest danger in now abandoning the Transvaal. With regard to the resolution he thought, if passed, it would increase the difficulty. The Govern- ment were bound by thee declaration in the. Speech from the Throne in which Her Majesty expressed regret that the rising in the Transvaal had recently imposed upon her the duty of taking military measures with a view of prompt vindication of her authority. Hepointed out the resolu- tion was in d irect opposition to that declaration. He stated that a telegram had been received from the President of the Orange Free State expressing its desire to stop bloodshed, to which Her Majesty's Government had replied thit, pro- vided the licrers would desist from their armed operations, Her Majesty's Government did not despair of bringing the dispute to an amicable settlement. —Sir S. NORTE:MOTE de- fended the late Government, and said they acted from moral motives, and they had done their best. He expressed his approval of the answer sent to the telegram just mentioned, and he hoped the House would sustain the Government --- [LEFT SITTING.]

At Bedworth, on Tuesday, Thomas Welge, eighty-five years of age, was choked while eating his dinner. A piece of solid meat in the throat caused suffocatioa. S. HELENS LITERAIIII AND SCIENTFIC ASSOCIATION. —An extraordinary meeting of this society was held on Tuesday evening, a good proportion of those presmt being reporters. At twenty minutes after eight o'clock Mr. Roughsedge arrived with his paper—or rather, half of it, the other half being held in reserve for some future occasion —entitled "The influence of mind upon the body." The paper was briefly discussed by the reporters and two or three prominent members of the society, as was also "the influence of cold weather upon the body." During the evening a respectable solicitor made his appearance and then vanished; another member looked in, but as quickly pulled back his head, remarking that he would go home be- fore his pipe went out., Another came, stayed f ally one minute, bid the meeting good night, and again faced the weather. Ultimately the meeting broke up, it being the most extra- ordinary meeting on record.

div.head: Zellers to the aitor.
div.p: Zellers to the aitor.

-- - . THE WAR IN THE TRANSVAAL. Sir,—l trust there are not many of our countrymen who will look upon the miserable conflict into which we have entered with the Boers of the Transvaal with any othl feelings than those of regret and disgust. The annexation Of the territory of the Republic was the arbitrary act of one official dressed ins little brief auth( city, and was brought about in open defiance of the instructions sent him from the Colonial Office. Sir Theophilas Shepstone was only com- missioned to take temporary possession of part of the Transvaal, and that expressly on the condition that the in- habitants, or the Legislature, signified their desire to be- come subjects of the Queen, instead of which be tiok abso- lute po.session of the whole country, against the wishes both of the people and the Volksraad, who declined even to deliberate on his proposal for the surrender of their inde- pendence. The main plea urged in justification of this high-handed course was this—that the Boers were in danger Of becoming involved in war with the Zulus, and that some contingent peril might arise from that to our colony of Natal. But we utterly stultified that plea; for almost immediately . after the annexation we began an aggressive and unprovoked . War upon the Zulus ourselves. It is greatly to be regret- ted that the present Governmsnt, when it cants into office, - had not the courage to do, in South Africa, what they did in . Afghanistan—that is, boldly reverse the policy of their pre- decessors. Mr. Gladstone did not scruple to brand the an- nexation as both impolitic and-unjust. Why, then, adopt and stand by a proceeding that could be so ch. aracter.ised ? It is very well to talk of the necessity for continuity in our policy. But surely there ought to .be no con- tinuity of acknowledged folly and wickedness. It ought not to be forgotten, at this time, that the entire European population of South Africa amounts to 340,000 souls. Of this number only 120,000 are English, the rest being Dutchmen, .or of Dutch descent. That these latter strongly sympathise with their kinsmen of the Transvaal, is evident from the remarkable address to Mr. Gladstone from _ the Dutch in the Cape Colony, transmitted through Mr. Courteney, M.P., interceding for the Beers, and entreating the Prime Minister to restore their indepeodence. The danger is, therefore, that, by attempting to crush the latter, we should aleniate the loyalty of a large body of our fellow- subjects throughout South African Colonies. Already there are ominous rumours that the men of the Orange Free State clan be scarcely kept back from joining with their oppressed brethren in the Transvaal. But I wish especially to call tha attention of your readers to a remarkable document, an ad- dress from Holland to the people of England. I have a copy before me, sent to me directly from the country, signed by more than two thousand leading citizens of the Netherlands, including members of the States-General, Burgomasters, Professors of the various Universities, clergymen, profee.- sional, commercial, and mercantile men. It is a most re- spectful and earnest appeal to the sense of justice and genero- sity of the English on behalf of people of "their own flesh and blood." I feel confident that this appeal from a sister nation will not be made in vain. No one can question our power to suppress the Boers of the Transvaal. But what possible advantage, or glory can come from such an exploit? Why should we rob those people of their independence? It is impossible that den like Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Bright can have any sympathy with such a policy. Let there be only a distinct expression of public opinion, and we may venture to hope that such instructions will be sent out to South Africa as shall stop further bloodshed by some arange- ment which will practically restore to those people their country and their independence.—Yours truly, HENRY RICHARD.
House of Commons, London.

SEttiOITS CHARGE AGAINST A GENTLEMAN AT WIDNES. At the Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday' last, Mr. Samuel Palin, 68 years of age, formerly dockmaster in Widnes for many years, and at present a churchwarden . in the town, was charged with a common assault on a respectable and intelligent young lady named Miss Minnie V. Davies, of Cholmondley-street.—Mr. Swift, St. Helms, appeared for the defence. Complainant, who gave her evidence very clearly, said until the last few days she was in the employ of the defen- dant as servant. On the morning of the 6th inst., at about half-past seven, as she was going upstairs to clean some boots, Mr. Palin stood at the bottom in his drawers, exposed himself, and then got hold of her. Though she told him to let her go he would not do so. Mrs. Palin then came to the top of the steps and commenced calling her husband foul names, and he let her (witness) go away. Cross-examined by Mr. Swift: Howi long had he been sitting at the fender with his drawers on before this occurred? Some short time —During which you were going about your work? Yes.—Then, when he came down in his drawers you (lid net go away? No, sir. By the Chairman: Has be done that before? Yes, sir; many times.—What time was this? Between six and seven o'clock. By Mr. Swift: How long have you been in this situation? Nine mouths and one week. I complained of nothing but that he put his arm round me. By the Chairman: Had he done that before? No, sir. Mrs. Mary Ann Davies, apparently a lady of good posi- tion, said she was the mother of the last witness. She came home on the morning of the 6th inst., and, in consequence of what she" said, she told her to leave the place, which she afterwards did. She knew nothing of what occurred at the place with the exception of that which defendant's wife told her. By the Chairraan : Mr. Patin did not hear what his wife told her. By Mr. Swift: Does he live far from your house? No: I live in Cholmondley-street, and he lives near the flyer; it is about ten minutes' walk from our house.—What time would it be when your daughter came home? About half- past seven.—And did not she go back to Mr. Palm's? Yes. —By herself? Tea ; I sent her back. She only remained at home a few minutes.—How long did she remain at Mr. Palin's the second time? She came back about eleven o'elock.—So ;that after coming home between seven and eight o'clock she weut back to the house? Yes.—And went about her work and had her breakfast there? Yes. The complainant was then recalled and re-examined by Mr. Swift: You did go back to Mr. Palin's the same morn- ing? Yes.—And finished your work? Yes.—And had your breakfast there? Yes.—And stayed till nearly dinner time? Yes. By the Chairman: Did not you say anything to Mrs. Palin ? No, sir.—Then what happened at dinner time? I went for my clothes. Mr. Swift: I suppose that Mrs. Palin told you to leave? No, sir; she did not. By the Chairman: Were you under notice to leave? No, sir.—Had you had any disagreement with the family? No, sin—Could Mrs. Palin see her husband at the time the , alleged assault took place? Yes, air; and she commenced calling him names.—You do not call her? Mr. Swift: No, sir; it is one of the unfortunate things about the case that she could not be called on either side. It seems to be a very simple case. It appears from the evi- dence that the defendant has made a practice of going into the kitchen early in the morning, and sitting there with his drawers on. On this particular morning complainant was going in the direction where Mrs. Palin was, up the stairs, and was at the bottom of the stairs when this took place. Any exposure must be put out of the ques- tion, as that is not in this charge. The com- plainant does not allege that the defendant said a single indecent word to her; not even that he spoke to her, or said anything at all, but simply put his arm round her and tried to prevent her going up stairs for the moment. I do not know whether he had been down stairs to warm himself or not, but I suppose when this happened he was going up stairs to complete his dressing; but when he got ' to the bottom of the stairs, he saw his wife at the top; and just to tease her, he put his arm round the girl's waist. The young woman does not allege that he did any more; that was the beginning and the end of it. I cannot understand why a summons should be taken out in a case of this kind. Mr. Palin is 68 years of age; he has a wife and grown up children, and I believe that for 4, years he has lived in Widnes, and always borne the character of a respectable man. He was formerly dock master in Widnes for a great many years; and at the present time he is carrying on business as a master stevedore. I put it to your worships, that there is nothing at all in the case; he simply 'put his band on the young woman, without any suggestion of impropriety. The Chairman : Throe is the suggestion, Mr. Swift. Mr. Swift: But she makes no suggestion that he had his hand upon her indecently, in any form.! The Chailman then referred to a particular detail of the evidence. The Complainant's rather: Would you not like to hear what Mrs. Palin says, gentlemen?. The Chairman : You must be quiet • there is a learned gentleman in the case. We should be very glad to hear what she says, if we could admit her evidence. Mr. Swift: Yes, hut the law does not allow it. There is this curious thing about the case,—complainant goes back • to the house, finishes her 'work, has her breakfast there and they all live in the kitchen—and she stays there until nearly dinner time. The Chairman: You call no witnesses?
Mr. Swift: There are no witnesses, so that we cannot call

any. • The Chairman, addressing defendant, said !—I do not see how this girl, Miss Davies,—a virtuous and respectable girl —Could have taken any other course than what she has in bringin, the case here. She has acted very properly; and there is nothing at all to threw any doubt upon what she has stated urain her oath. We believe her statement to be strictly true; that you have acted in a very disgraceful way; —the more discretitable that you are a man of mature years. We fine you 40s, and the costs, or one month's imprison- The prisoner, who took the matter very phlegmatically, IPa't4 the money.

div.p: WARRINGTON PARLIAMENTARY DEBATING SOCIETY.

The second local• Parliament was opened on Monday evening in the Co-operative Hall. The Speaker (Dr. More) occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance of members on both sides of the House. A number of strangers, including several ladies, were also present. The SPEAKER said Her Majesty had been pleased on the reassembling of Parliament to address both Houses, of which speech he had obtained a copy, which he would proceed to read to the House. TIM <annex's seism'. Cientlemen,—lt is with pleasure that I welcome you„on your return to your parliamentary duties, and have recourse to your valuable assistance and advice. My relations with foreign powers continue to be of a friendly nature. You will have heard with regret of the unfortunate difficulties which have arion,n in my South African Colonies. I shall not hesitate to use the means at my disposal for the repres- sion of insurrection and for the assertion of my authority in that portion of my dominions. The skill and bravery of Day troops have brought the war in Afghanistan to a suc- cessful conclusion, and you will be asked to express your thanks to those who have brought about this result. I have withdrawn from Afghanistan a large number of the troops which were engaged in the late war, but Candahar will con- tinue to be occupied by my soldiers, since I am of opinion that such an occupation is essential to the maintenance of satisfactory relations between this country and Afghanistan, and is necessary to secure the safety of my Indian Empire. United action has been taken by the European Powers to procure the cession of a small town called Dulcigno to Montenegro; and His Imperial Highness the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire has, consequently, by force of arms, com- pelled the Albanians to surrender the place. The disquieted state of Ireland has given me much anxiety, and you will at once be asked to renew the Peace Preservation Act which expired some months ago, and to give your assent to a more stringent temporary measure which is necessary that law and order may be restored in that country. When this end has been accomplished it may be desirable that you should consider whether measures are needed to improve the rela- tions between landlords and tenants in Irelaad. The subject of elementary education in Ireland is under the considera- tion of my Government, ond a measure will probably be laid before you dealing with that question. The estimates for the coming year will be carefully prepared, and you will doubtless provide for the Services with your accustomed liberality. The inquiries which I ordered to be instituted into the manner in which the election of members of Parlia- ment had been conducted in various cities and boroughs have shown that corrupt practices have been extensiwly prevalent, and I trust that you will be able to devise effec- tual means for the repression of such practices. A measure relating to Church Patronage will be laid before you, and you will also be asked to consider bills for an alteration in the laws regulating the sale of intoxicating liquors, a Re- form of the Law of Bankruptcy, and an amendment of the . Ballot Act. I have confidence that you will deal with these , and all other matters affecting the welfare of my people in a careful and conscientious spirit.

THE NEW MINISTRY. The SPEAKER: I have now to read to the House the names of the gentlemen who have been chosen by the right hon. gentleman who was appointed by Her Majesty to conduct the present Government:— Premier Mr. W. J. Burgess. Chancellor of the Exchequer Mr. George Woods. Home Secretary Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. Foreign Secretary Mr. J. Graham. Indian Secretary Mr. W. Sileock. Colonial Secretary Xi. W. H. Jenkins. War Secretary • Mr. J. Lee. Irish Secretary Mr. R. W. Francomb. First Lord of the Admiralty Mr. T. VVelsby. Vice-President of the Council Mr. T. Robinson. President of the Board of Trade Mr. W. Dickens. Postmaster-General Mr. J. Hartley. Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster... Mr. W. Westwell. Attorney-General Mr. J. Burgess. Solicitor-General 1 Mr. G. Okell. Political Secretary to the Treasury Mr. C. J. Leigh. Under Secretary to the Treasury Mr. W.Worthington. QUESTIONS. The following notices were given of the questions to be asked next Monday evening:— The member for CARLISLE to ask the Home Secretary whether it is the intention of Her Majesty's Government to include in the licensing bill the principle of local option. (Applause.)—The member for SonTH HAMPSHIRE to ask the Attorney-General whether it is his inted- tion to introduce a bill to abolish actions for breach of promise of marriege. (Laughter and Applause.)— The member for PENRHIN and FAratotrut to ask the Irish Secretary whether the contemplated system of education in Ireland will be undenominational and compulsory ?—The member for CHELSEA to ask the Secretary of State for India what is the precise line of the scientific frontier in Afghan- istan P—The right hon. member for Wasx LINCoLNSHIRE to ask the Prime Minister if it is the intention of the Govern- ment, seeing the present inequality of religious bodies in England in the eyes of the law and justice, to bring in a measure this session for the disestablishment and partial die- endowment of the so-called Church of England ?—The PRIME MINISTER said it was unnecessary to give notice of such a question. It was not the intention of the Government to bring ia such a bill. (Ministerial cheers.)—The member' for WOLVERHAMPTON to ask the Prime Minister for a return of the sales of livings in the Church of England for the year 1880, with the estimated amount P—The member for WEST CUMBERLAND to ask the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster if it is a fact that some of the coal owners and colliery owners of Lancashire, the same being magistrates, have conspired together to defeat the intention of Parlia- ment by compelling their workmen to contract themselves out of the Employers Liability Bill ' • and if in face of such fact he is prepared to remove them from the bench; also to state how many of them are magistrates, and their names ? , —The member for STALEYBRIDOE to ask the Foreign Secre-'1 tary what is the probable amount of expenditure incurred in the late Zulu war, and in the annexation of the Trans- vaal? (Applause.)—The "member for Evastram to ask whether the Government intend to abolish flogging in the army this session? (Applause.)—The member for MIDDLE- SEX to ask the Secretary for Ireland to lay on the table statistics of crime in Ireland since the passing of the 1 "Peace Preservation Act," and for a corresponding period previous to the passing of that Act, skewing the number of ordinary criminal offences as distinguished from those of an agrarian character. The LEADER ot the OPPOSITION : May I ask the bon member which of the two dozen and odd coercion bills which have been passed, he means ?—The Patatm MINISTER: Perhaps it would facilitate things if the right bon. member opposite were to name the two dozen and odd coercion bills. (Hear, hear.)—The LEADER of the OPPOSITION: It would perhaps be too personal to the right bon. member opposite. (Laughter.)—The PRIME MlNtsrgn : I hope the right hon. member won't consider me ih;the matter. (Laughter.)—The member for WOODSTOCE gave notice if in the reply given to the member for South Hamp- shire it was shown the Government had not the couraee to bring in a bill to abolish actions for breach of promise of marriage, of his intention to bring in a bill to abolish such actions.—The member for CARLISLE, to ask the Home Secretary whether the Government intended bringing in a measure for the closing of public-houses in Wales, on Sunday.—The right hon. member for NORTHAMPTON, to ask on what date buck shot was served ont to the Irish constabular in consequence of orders given by the late Irish secretary, the Hon. James Lowther. (Hear, hear.)—The right hon. member for KENDAL, to ask the Home Secretary whether it is the inten- tion of the Government to introduce a bill abolishing vivi- section. (Applause.)--The member for DIFDLEY to ask the Attorney-General if it is the intention of the Government to i bring in a bill to legalise Marriage with a deceased wife's 1 sister. (Applause.) THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS. The member for LerrNcnstow, in moving that an address he presented to Her Most Gracious Majesty the Queen, said the House would receive with a feeling of thankfulness the intimation that friendly rplations continued between this country and the other powers of Europe. (Hear, hear.) Every member would look at the rebellious state of the Transvaal with anxious eyes, and before he gave his sup- port to this part of the Speech he would endeavour to ex- plain his reasons for doing so. He would carry the House back to the state of the Transvaal before the annexation took place. He read that English emigrants and Dutch Boers had settled there in considerable numbers, but that a feeling of jealousy was ever prevailing. It arose from various causes—that slavery existed to a degree; that the Republican Government was feeble, and also in debt; that they were waging war with most of the native tribes; and that the settlers were continually threatened by the since subdued King Cetewayo, and they lived in dreara that he and his dusky tribes would invade their territory. Into this dis- quieted and terrified country the Government sent Sir Theo- philus Shephstone as a helper, adviser, and friend. He stayed there a considerable time anxiously watching the struggle of the Government, calmly listened to those who were in favour of and against the annexation- and he ulti- mately decided that the only way in which he could protect the English settlers and the means by which be could dis- sipate the fears of the whole country was by annexing it to the Cape Colony. The admirable manner in which he per- formed that great work was ably described by the author of the work he held in his hand (" The Transvaal of to-day.'” It read as follows:—"Now it is :impossible to conceive any- thing more admirable for its discretion, more wisely cal- culated a.s to the moment of its occurrence, or more suavely and yet firmly done than this act. There .was not a blow struck, not a shot fired; and the first impulse of nearly every 1 person in the country, whether in principle opposed to an- nexation or not was to congratulate Sir Theophilus Sheph- stop on the skill, tact, and good fortune with which he had put an end to the excessive anxiety, the mental strain, the fears, hopes, and expectations by which thewhnoleow country paralysed. Whether the annexation be eight, Its anonnwrpehgat Itsan th e the In.:cut g itosrelf,rl tact, mndesty, and firmness.' exScuuntpio; liesiorutfartrni• Dutch settlers were attempting to crush the power that swept sway terror in the Transvaal. (Hear, bear.) He (the speaker) held that the Colonial Govern9ent had been trbitrary in calling upon the settlers to disarm. (Hear. hear.) But it was not sufficient jestification—("Oh ")—for heir persecuting and murdering the English settlers— hear, hear,)—and that did not justify them tearing down he British flag—(" Oh"); and he was proud to see that the Ministers of the Imperial Government intended to protect life and property and show those who bad trampled upon our standard that it was an act which this country would not tolerate. (Cheers.) The House would be called upon

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,

to express its thanks to.those who had brought the Afghan war to a successful termination, and he did not think any hon. member would object to be put in a position to demon- crate his appreciation of the skill and bravery which were noticeable features throughout the campaign. (Hear, hear.) As to the late war in Afghanistan, they had put an end to Russian intrigue' which instigated the horde who had in- sulted the British envoy, ant placed the Indian Empire in a safe position. Seeing that had been accomplished by the force of arms, it afforded him pleasure to support that part of the speech which indicated that ministers intended taking precautionary • steps to prevent that becoming agai neces- sary. Knowing that the naval demonstration bad not com- pleted its work, he would only say that it was to be hoped that the plan of its construction had not sunk into obscurity while the fleet had been idling its tune at Duleigna. Refer- ring to Ireland, he remarked that every hon. member was fully cognisant of the state of that unhappy conatry. (Hear, hear.) They all knew that the law was no longer respected, that crime was com- mitted without the slightest fear, that a League existed whose law had superseded the constitutional law, that loyal subjects went about in the fear of their lives, and that the Queen of the country was no longer respected. It was par- ticularly humiliating to this country that, although this lamentable state of things had been existing in its most perfect state for a considerable period of time, Her Majesty's Ministers did not think it necessary to call Parliament to- gether to enable them to receive powers wherewith they could maintain the dignity of the law and of the Crown. (Hear, hear.) If the country had not been sufficiently con- demnatory of their dilatory policy, he felt that a resolution moving a vote of censure upon the Government would not be uncalled for. (" Oh !"and applause.) But he supposed he must give them credit for doing some little, for at the eleventh hour they had the courage to speak, but not before the country had been aroused. Hav,ng defended the House of Lords in respect to the Compensation for Disturbance Bill, the hon. member said be was pleased to see that the Ministry intended calling upon the House to grant them additional powers to remede the present evils existing, so as to maintain the dignity of the law and re-establish the authority of the Crown in Ireland. (Hear, hear.) Other bills would be presented to the House in due course, which, when introduced, would meet, he was sure, with fair con- sideration, and it only remained for Mtn to give his hearty support to the Ministry. (Applause.) The member for BIRKENHEAD seconded the motion, and contended that the Peace Preservation Act suppressed crime during the time it was in operation, and that the first thing which stared Mr. Forster in the face in the pigeon-holes in Downing-street was a draft for the renewal 'of that Act. He maintained that the murders, crimes, and misery which had been perpetrated and existed at the present time in Ireland all rested upon the Liberal party, and the Liberal Govern- ment—(" Oh !" and applause)—of 1880 would always carry the mark of Cain. He hoped the Government would merit the confidence which had been placed in them, and deal with the measures named in the Speech in a careful and conscientious spirit. (Loud applause.) The LEADER OP THE OPPOSITION : It is always a great plea- sure when we are able to congratulate the younger members upon the success with which they address the House, especi- ally upon occasions of this sort; and I must compliment the hon. members who have just sat down upon the very able way in which they have moved and seconded the motion before the house. (Hear, hear.) We are told that we have the mark of Cain, and I can only say to the hon. gentleman that has just sat down cave cattem. (Laughter.) I gather from the speech which has been put into Her Majesty's mouth by her present advisers that she welcomes us back to our duties—that things are quiet at present—" peace with honour." (Laughter and applause.) Having stolen the land and liberty of the Boers, Her Majesty's ministers ob- serve that they actually are in insurrection. After such an application of force on our part to apply the term insurrec- tion to them seems to me an astounding use of the word. Accordingly Her Majesty', present advisers mean to coerce. (Hear, hear.) We have t 5 thank the army in Afghanistan, and we are to keep Candahar. (Hear, bear.) Candahar is, I suppose, to be our scientific frontier. (Laughter.) There is a small town given to Montenegro. It seems to me Her Majesty's ministers are sorry for the Turk, but glad they have got Cyprus first. (Laughter.) Her Majesty's Government, it appears, will certainly coerce Ireland. They may, perhaps, do a little justice—just to go on with. They may probably educate them—for example they educated their party. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Why not educate them. We must now pay up for all this "6 peace with honour," and her Majesty's ministers are won- derfully surprised that corrupt practices have been found at election times. (Laughter and applause.) Indeed Her Majesty's ministers would never have thouedit of such a thing. (Hear, hear.) It appears that they must do some- thing for appearance sake. They will do something for the Church—oh, I mean the Jingoes. They will touch intoxi- cating drink (" No, no," from the Ministerial lets); publicans it seems ate played out. They will try to book the ballot, farmers getting too frisky—(laughter), • the last paragraph being ta-ta. Now, when a Government comes and says to us that a Coercion Bill is necessary, I presume that they have information which is not open to us, and therefore I for one consider it to be the duty of myseleand those who act with me to give the Government support in that direction. But, however, I must ask why the Government did noi renew the bill if they considered it to be so essene tial, before they appealed to the country? (Hear, hear.) The only point upon which I shall make any serious objec- tion is—they may perhaps do a little justice to Ireland, just to go on with. The Government seems to me to be in a perfect maze. ('Oh.") I have heard my young friend opposite, the Prime Minister, called the "people's William." (Laughter). Had I the christening of him I should call him "Permissive Bill." (Great laughter and cheers.) You may do justice to Ireland, may! nay you must, needs must, when a nation drives. (Hear, bear.) I say that we shall give such support as we can. (Hear, hear.) The hon. gentleman opposite taunted us that we found a coercion bill in a pigeon hole. I don't wonder at it. The right hon. gentlemen opposite it seems to Ma keep a coercion bill in every pigeon hole for every possible occasion and for every possible purpose. (Hear, hear.) The right hon. gentleman went on to state that he could promise the Government they would deal with them in no factious spirit, although he should have great pleasure to put his friends to the torture, and remarked that by the action of the gentlemen on the cross benches they bad been relegated to the cold shades of opposition. They had often been told that if they scratched a Russian they would catch a Tartar. He would borrow the words and say if they scratched a neutral they would soon come to a Tory. (Laughter.) The time would come- when the dark clouds of Conservatism would be rolled away from this benighted land,—(hear, bear)—and the gigantic selfishness of the aristocratic order would be kept within reasonable bounds, and when they would be forced to do justice to this great community and in their turn give in their help and their suffrages to peace, retrenchment, and reform. (Cheers.) After a few words from the member for Wigan, The COLONIAL SECRETARY said he had hoped during the recess the ex-Prime Minister would have furnished them with a little volume such as "The Parliamentary joker's companion." (Hear, hear.) A work of that character would have been a great boon, and would have secured a ready sale. He bore willing testimony to the great treat which the Leader of the Opposition gave them during the recess, and was in the midst of a quotation when The right hon. member for DROGHEDA rose to ask whether the right hon. member was in order in criticising the action of any member of that House in another place? A sharp discussion ensued in which the 'Leader of the Opposition depreciated what he considered to be factions in- terruption. The COLONIAL SECEVITARY pointed out that the English and Dutch systems of colonisation were utterly opposed, the English system being to make friends of the natives and whereas the Dutch system was one of extermination. The right hon. member for Dnomenne, in a vigorous speech, charged the Government with inconsistency in reference to their statement as to the united action of the Powers, and remarked that it appeared the lying spirit still existed and that to a very considerable extent. (Applause.) Turning to Ireland, the right hon, gentleman deprecated the introduction of coercive measures and main- tained that the paragraph in the speech referring to such measures was in is opinion a disgrace and discreditable to the Government, and concluded by stating that he could give no supnort to the Speech in its present state. The member for Duman UNIVERSITY supported the motion, and in reference to Ireland, expressed his opinion that there was no better land bill in the world than the Ulster tenant right. The mernoer for STALIMSRIDGE had no confidence in the Conservative ministry just formed. (Loud apol use.) lie felt they were only inclined to support their own interests and to support the aristocracy. The Government did not wish te make the Irish people more loyal, their only object they had in view waste embarrass And persecute Irishmen. He concluded by gusting the words of Lord Beaconsfield who said the Conservative ministry was an organised hypocrisy. (Loud cheers.) The member for MIDDLESEX having spoken in favour of the motion, The liouee adjourned on the motion of the CHANCELLOR of the ExCiennumt.
