HOLY TRINITY CHURCH TEA PARTY, Jstraightforward tradesmen, the gentleman whose guests they were that night would occupy a very high place. (Hear, WARRINGTON. hear.) The rev, gentleman then in very complimentary THE VICAR ON THE CHURCH. terms proposed what all present regarded as the toast of the The members connected with the Holy Trinity Church evening, "The Health of the Mayor," which was heartily , drunk with musical honours and to which his worship Sankey-street, held their anneal tea party and entertainment briefly and appropriately responded. in the Public Hall, Rylands-street, on Monday. There was The other toasts were "The town and trade of St. Helens," not a very large attendance either at the tea or the enter- " The Magistrates," "The Chairmen of Committees of the tainment, probably owing to the severity of the weather. Council," and "The Vice-presidents." This aspect of the hall was agreeably relieved by a number At his worship's request reporters were not present in their of flags and bannerettes which were hung around. Trays official capacity. were given by the following :—Rector of Warrington and the Vicar of Holy Trinity; Mesdames Quekett, Sharp, Owen, Nunnerley, Hoult, Davies, Leigh, Dobson, Siddoll, Ellison, Beamont, Chandley, Lythgoe, Will cocks, Made', Ridgway, Hatton, Kendrick, Skinner, H. B. White, Halton, Grierson, Wellhead, Lewis Reynolds, Lamplugh, Craik, Woods, Booth, Pugh, Gill, Dainteth, Richardson, Gilbert Riley, Pratt; Misses Harding, Riley, Pierpoint, Garven, Gaskell ; Messrs. J. Sharp, Brimelow, Jeans, R. Davies, John Harding, W. Bargees. Sherratt, Artingstall, G. Riley, R. Halton, Dun, E. Davies, Nelson, Draper, P. Stubs, J. Tinsley, J. Crosfield, W. Milner, T. Morris, and J. Halton. The chair was occu- pied by the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, vicar. The Cwarawan remarked that he was unable to account for the poor attendance, unless the counter attractions of skating and the Parliamentary Debating Society had kept many away. Referring to Church matters, he said there was a tendency among many people to get into a panic about the state of things existing in the Church, and he would there- fore deal with the position which it occupied. The position of the Church of England with regard to doctrine was definitely put in the sixth article, where it was distinctly stated that Holy Scripture ought to oe our guide and rule of faith. The position of the Church on matters of ceremony and ritual was no less clear. The 34th Article said that those matters were of secondary or minor importance andi4ight be changed according to the times and men's manners. He thought it Was the duty of clergymen to be guided in these things by the people among whom he iniaistered and influenced by their wishes. The Church occupied a rational position on these questions and eught not to be mistaken. There was a disposition on the part of many people either purposely or through ignorance, to represent the people, of England as if she had formed some secret alliance with the Church of Rome. There could not be any (position more contrary to the truth. An examination or,history would show them that the movement known as the Reformation took place within the Church and was hostile to the Church of Rome That was before Nonconformity had any existence. It was rather late in the day for some of their Nonconformist friends to say that they were the only good organisation of what was called Protestantism in this country. He would like to ask what the Nonconformists could offer to Churchmen better than what they had already. Were they more Scriptural? He would like to know where in the fear corners of God's Word did that system known as Congre- gatiolhalism exist? The exclusion by the Baptists of children from the privilege of Church membership and the Christian covenant was contrary to the teaching of the Word. The Nonconformists were adopting one by one many things in the Church. In fact, Non- conformity was becoming, more a political difference, and he could only ae..sign a political difference for their continued separation. One reason for standing by the Church was the growing secularism and the disposition which there was to disassociate religion from our national institutions and from education. There had been an attempt to disassociate religion from the sacred functions of Government and from the ceremony of marriage, which they wculd make simply a secular contract. These were movements upon which the Church hadtaken an unequivo- cal and decided stand. The rev, gentleman then dealt with the meaning of the word Protestant, which, he said, in its ordinary sense meant opposition to Rome. But the Church '..ef England was a great deal more than that: she was Christian. (Applause.) Rev. J. LOUCH, after referring to the smallness of the attendance, said he dare say there were many who, like him- self, thought, and with reason, that these tea parties were a kind of party manifestoes. They could not think that that party would take a turn like that held there last Monday, of which he had read a report. He had read a great deal of that report with much pleasure. He was pleased with the proverb that Bishop Gregg gave to his hearers, telling them that it was a Spanish one—that they who stop to throw stones at every cur that barked at them would never get to the end of their journey He (Mr. Louch) was not going to throw stones; it would be dangerous to attempt it; and when there was a Presbyterian' an Independent,a Wesleyan, a Reformed Episcopalian, and a bishop in the bargain, he Gould not think of doing it. Itwould, in fact, be like leading a forlorn hope to hope to meet an array of that sort; but he must say a word to try to throw off from their backs the water which this formidable array met to throw upon them. He was very pleased with the first part of Mr. Yonge's speech, and he began to think that Mr. Yonge was not very far from being a High Churchman. He talked a great deal about unity—so much so that Cardinal Manning could not have argued more eloquently against schism. They believed that the Church of England was the old historical church of the land, and they saw no reason now that it was so broad and comprehensive why any Noncon- formist should not be able to find a place within its borders. Mr. Yonge had said something which grieved him very much—that secession from the Church of England was the only honest course for people of Evangelical conviction and belief. He considered that Mr. Yonge when he said that cast a slur upon the greatest body of churchmen in the Cherch—(hear, hear,)—and he has no right to make such an observation. He wondered if Mr. Yonge agreed with the political principles of the Bishop of Manchester, and did he think that the bishop WAS net an honest man because he didn't withdraw from the Church and did not hold Ritualistic views. The Bishop had said on oae occasion, what he (Mr. Louch) thought could not be said with reference to any Nonconformists, that the Church of. England was benificient, liberal, national and comprehensive. He maintained that those terms applied to the Church of England were true and because of that he was a member, and had no intention of seceding. (Applause.) He was very pleased with the work done in Trinity Parish. Let them go on doing their duty quietly and he was sure they would be successful and fully satisfied with themselves. (Applause.) Daring the evening an efficient glee party sung several glees, and songs were rendered by friends assisted by Mr. Antonie, of Manchester, who was very successful in his comic sketches. Mr. Hargreaves Gill gave an able per- lormance on the fairy bells.

div.head: ILIYOR' BANQUET AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: THE ILIYOR' BANQUET AT ST. HELENS.

- - On Wednesday evening Mr. Alderman James Harrison (the Mayor of St. Helens) entertained the other member I of the Corporation, local magistrates, and a number of pro- I minent townsmen at a grand banquet in the Council Chamber of the new Town Hall. Extensive preparations had been made in the room and its approaches, and a tem- porary staircase was erected from the large hall for the use of those, in attendance on the guests. The Cotincil Chamber presented a very elegant appearance, a number of choice' plants from the conservatories of Mr. Brewis and several other gentlemen being placed upon the tables. His Worship had issued invitations to about 80 gentlemen of whom there were over 60 present: They included Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Lieutenant-Colonel Gamble, J.P., Dr. Heginbotnatn, J.P. SIT CRDAY JANUARY
THE WEEKLY RETURNS. _ _ _

The MASTER (Mr. Mackey) reported two old men had died in the house during the week, one of them rather sud- denly, but it appeared that several members of his family had died in a similarly sudden manner. There were three cases of scabies and six of whooping cough in the house. There were 502 persons in the house on the last day of pre- ceding week, admitted since 22, discharged 9, dead 2, re- maining 513, compared with 483 in the correspon Hog week of last year. Vagrants relieved during the week, men 95, women 20, children 5, total 120 ; imbeciles in the Work- house 48.

div.head: PAYMENT OF SCHOOL FEES.
div.p: PAYMENT OF SCHOOL FEES.

Mr. SVALLirrorox moved that the school fees of 42 children, whose cases had been considered by the committee, be paid in accordance.with the recommendation of the com- mittee. Mr. BROWN seconded the motion.
In reply to a question from Mr. Winstanley, it was stated by Mr. Wallington that many of those cases were renewals of old ones. The motion was adopted.

div.head: THB PAYMBNT OF ARREARS OT BATHS.
div.p: THB PAYMBNT OF ARREARS OT BATHS.
The CL anK said he should be obliged to ask the Board to let him summon the townships in arrears with their rates.

A GUARDIAN asked what townships were in arrear. The CLErtx : They are the usual bad characters, Newton and two or three more. (Laughter.) Mr. WINSTANLEY thought that was very bad ingratitude, as he had paid in the first call before it was due. Major CARTWRIGHT : IS it true, Mr. Clerk, that it is a hard matter to get the money from Newton? The CLERK: It is. lam afraid that they get interest on the money themselves. (Laughter.)

div.head: TRH BARRACKS.
div.p: TRH BARRACKS.

The Barracks Committee reported that Mi 93 Walton com- plained that the pauper help the had at the Barracks was insufficient, and the committee recommended that two women in receipt of out-door relief be employed at the Barracks for two days per week. Mr. BROWN moved, and Mr. WALLINGTON seconded, the adoption of the report. .

Major CARTWRIGHT objected to the recommendation, arguing that there was sufficient labour there with the assistance they had already got, and that of the older chil- dren, if properly utilised, to do all the work. Mr. LONGSHAW said the matron of the Workhouse had been asked if she could spare paupers from there to go to the Barracks, and she had replied that she could not do so. Hr. Wirrs-rawmis. asked how many women had been ordered into the house that day. The CLERK said that not one in ten of those ordered into the house would come in. Mr. Bnows urged that the committee had fully gone into the matter, and decided that assistance was necessary until they removed to the new premi.es, at Padgate. Mr. Wiwararmur said there was no more additional ex- pense on the children than if they had remained in that house.

Major CARTWRIGHT was surprised at such a statement, and said he wished gentlemen who came there would talk about what they knew. He accused Mr. Longsh tvr and Mr. Winstanley of not visiting the Workhouse very often, and said that the latter only came when there was a small con- tract to be given in which he was slightly interested. Mr. WINSTAHLRY said he came to the meeting on the day the contract was to be let at the urgent request of the Major, and the Majbr, therefore, should not cosnplain that he came that day. Major CARTWRIGHT : I complain because you do not come oftener. Mr. WINSTANLIT : You have no right to say that I came because the contract was to be let. It was a very improper observation. (Cries of " Chair, chair.") Mr. Ham, said they should get the Barracks Committee out of the mess.

Mr. WINSTANLAT : What mess? Major CARTWRIGHT : Perhaps it is Benjamin's mess. Mr. HALL said he meant the mess at the barracks, as he thought things were not looking so well there as they should do. Mr. HARRISON thought the Board should assist the Cam- mittee. After some further discussion, in which it was pointed out by the Clark that there was no officer at the barracks paid entirely by that Board, and that the Board had led the Local Government Board to believe that they would appoint one to do the work, the report of the Committee was adopted.

THE PENKETH BIGAMY CASE. Rebecca Clarke, who was remanded from the Occasional Court House a week ago, on a charge of bigamy, was brought up at the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Rigby and Mr. Artiugstall. She WAS defended by Mr. Moore; and Mr. Percy Davies prosecuted on behalf of the relatives of the second husband, now deceased.—Mr. Davies, in opening the case, said the maiden name of the prisoner was Rebecca Maden. She was 21 years of age when she married the man Walter Clarke [Prisoner: Beg- ging your pardon, I was 19.] on the 18th July, 1881, and she was described in the certificate as a spinster, and by pro- fession a dressmaker. The parties were married at the Baptist Chapel, Madeley, where she was then living. Her husband was a coal miner, and they lived together for some four or five years, but the behaviour of the prisoner was so bad that he was obliged to leave her. • He went to America, And two years After the prisoner followed him. They lived there as man and wife till 1876, when they returned to England, cohabiting together until 1878. One Saturday afternoon in that year the prisoner's husband came home with his fortnight's wages, which amounted to £2 Os. 3d., and placed the money on the table. The pri- soner took it up, saying she would fetch some food for the child—and he was told that there were seven children of the marriage, but only one living—and from that day to this the parties had never seen each other. She was next heard of as being at Warrington, holding there a situation as cook. In March, 1880, she went to Penketh, where she called her- self Rebecca Maden, and engaged heraelf as housekeeper for Joseph Walker, who was a foreman platelayer on the line at Fiddler's Ferry, and whom she subsequently married. This man had been 'found drowned in the canal about a month ago, and the relations of the deceased found that he bad been entirely led astray by the prisonek The prisoner had been enquiring as to what money the second hasband would be entitled to from the company, but the relatives did not think she would use the money for the benefit of the children; and he had to press for a convic- tion, as they could then take out letters of administration and. claim everything for the children.-The first witness called was Edward Clarke mining contractor, Madeley, who said he had a brother Of the name of Walter Clarke, and he was present at his marriage with Rebecca Maden on the 28th July, 1581, at the Baptist Chapel, Madeley, in Salop. He signed the register. His wife was the other witness, and also signed the register. The prisoner and her husband lived together at Madeley for about two years, when his brother went to America on account of her dissolute habits. She subsequently followed him, and after about ten years' ab- sence Cal' returned together, taking a house at Hednesford, in Staffordshire.—Mr. Moore then proceeded to cross-examine the witness, and asked him if he knew that his brother had been married to another woman in America.—Mr. Davies: He cannot ask that question; this man is not charged with anything.—Mr. Rigby: He can ask that question. Sit you down.—Mr. Moore said the question must be asked to show that if the prisoner had committed bigamy she had done it under the impression that she was free.—Mr. Davies protested against the question being asked.—Mr. Rigby said it was a question that must be asked. They must get to know what was right and wrong so that the Bench could judge.--The Magistrates' Clerk remarked that they were not to try the case to-day.— Mr. Rigby: I hope the case will be laid before the public and that we shall administrate justice. We are not trying this man, but we are trying to elicit what might induce this ion ammaekn . mide a Thset amk ea gains tt a tgeest, herselfwom an ionrt ocaa uvseet ythis t I owuo9m apnt e dt Clerk: We are net trying the case.—Mr. Rigby: I know my position and I say that this question shall be asked.-- Mr. Davies said it was not just that charges should be brought againit a man who would have no opportunity of refuting them. He protested against it.—Mr. Rigby: Well protest against it. Go on Mr. Moore.—Cross examined by Mr. Moore, witness said be did not know that his brother had married a woman named Elizabeth Floyd, nor had anything been said to him about it. His brother left the prisoner with one child on her bands. He understood that his brother and the Prisoner were going to America together. His brother went away because he had no home to go to. He had seen prisoner drunk frequently.—Richard Hodge, platelayer, on the London and North Western Railway at Penketh, deposed to being present at the marriage of the prisoner with Joseph Walker, at the Wesley Chapel, Warrington, in July, 1880, and signing the register as a witness. div.head: DISHONEST ST. HELENS RELIEYING OFFICER.
div.p: THE DISHONEST ST. HELENS RE- LIEYING OFFICER.

PRESCOTT CONVICTED. At the Kirkdale Quarter Sessions, held in St. George's Hall, Liverpool, on Thursday, the Earl of Derby presiding, Jonadab Prescott was indicted for having on the Bth Sept., being the servant of the Board of Guardians of the Prescot Union, feloniously stolen Is. in money, the property of his masters, and with having, on the Ist December last, stolen a further sum of 4s. Mr. Sept., with whom was Mr. Shand, appeared for the prosecution; and the prisoner was defended by Dr. Corn- mine, M.P. (instructed by Messrs. Swift and Son, St. Helens). Mr. Segar said in this case the prisoner was charged with the theft of Is. on Bth September, and also of 4s. on the Ist December. The amounts were small, but he thought, after the jury had heard the facts of the case they would see it was a very important matter, not only because the manner in which the prosecution alleged the offences had been committed was very systematic, very deliberate, and to some extent ingenious, but also because it was very important indeed the jury should be quite certain the prisoner was guilty before they gave an ad- verse verdict. His character hitherto appeared to have been a very high one. The prisoner was appointed reliev- ing officer in July, 1879, and some time before he was brought before the magistrates appearei to have been doing double duty. Ills duties were onerous, and up to the time matters he was about to mention were discovered, implicit confidence was placed in him. He had in cases of out-door relief a considerable amount of discretion. The Board of Guardians met from time to time, and when they met they, as a rule, decided what applications were to be granted and what were not. But between the sittings of the El card of Guardians the relieving officer, Prescott, had a right to give relief it he thought fit, and the way in which relief was given was this, He had a book with counterfoils which con- tained printed forms, in which the name of the union was in print, and the name of the parish, and blanks were left for the name of the man who was to supply the provisions to the poor person; also the amount of relief, and the character of the relief that was to be granted. For instance. He had eleven tickets, and he would read one of them—" Prescot Union, Windle parish, to Mr. Wilcock "—that is the name of the provision dealer, then there is a blank place— " Please to supply bearer Stewart McLean, with bread, bat- ter, tea, and sugar, value 3s. 6d., 21st May, 1880." That was filled up by the prisoner who gave the order to the poor person, in this case Stewart McLean. Stewart McLean took it to Mr. Wilcock who gave him the bread, butter, and sugar. Mr. Wilcock supplied a considerable amount of provisions to poor people, and kept these orders on his file. That very ticket had been altered. It was originally of the value of 3s. Od. ;it was now of the value of 3s. 6d. He bad put sixpence after the three. After the goods were supplied prosecutor went to the shop of Mr. Wilcock and got his voucher orders for the previous week or fortnight as the case might be. These were added up by Mr. Wilcock or the prisoner and then the prisoner paid the provision dealer the total amount appearing upon the orders. Or Mr. Wilcock himself went to the parish office and obtained payment on the strength of these orders. What had really occurred in the case mentioned was this. Mr. Wilcock, the provision dealer, was paid the exact amount of the value as it was represented upon that and other tickets, and when Mr. Wilcock had been paid in various instances 3s the prisoner added 6d., and then when be gave the account to the Prescot Board of Guardians he got, instead of 35., 3s. 6d. That of course would be obtaining money under false pretences, and he might have been indicted for that; but he had only been indicted for stealing. And he lid not only obtain money under false pretences but put the money in his own pocket. and having spent it mis- represented the theft by adding (3d. to the vouchers and got from the Board of Gaardians a larger sum of money than he had paid, and thereby was enabled to conceal the theft. The amounfis were very small, but he was prepared to prove to the jury the following facts On the 21st May the prisoner gave an order to Stewart Mc- Lean for 3s. That Sc. was paid to Mr. Wilcock for goods which he had supplied, but the prisoner received the sum of 3s. 6d. He would ask the jury to look at that " six "to see whether it had not been altered. It seemed clear—bat he should call an expert of handwriting, and he would tell the jury that in his opinion the " six " had been written by the same person. But he thought the jury would see that it scarcely required an expert to come to that conclusion. Another person to whom he gave an order for 3s. worth of bread, butter, tea, and sugar was Sarah Brighouse. She got 3s. worth. Mr. Wilcock was paid 35., and then 6d. had been added in the account presented by the prisoner to the Board. It would appear that 3s. 6d. was the amount of 'relief which Sarah Brighouse got. He held in his hand a bundle of tickets, which amounted in all to £1 13s. 6d. That was the amount entered in one or two books kept by the prisoner. One was called the relief list, and the other the application report book. But he should show the jury he had only spent £1 12s. 6d. They charged the prisoner with having stolen is. He had another bundle of tickets which amounted to £3 Sc., but when Mr. Wilcock had them they amounted to £3 4s. That was a curious fact; but how did they account for it? It was not very difficult, because if they looked through those figures there was actually 4s. in sixpences added up and down. The offence was discovered by an accidental mistake. He entered in one of the books that he got 17s. 6d., and in another book he entered 17s. That at once made Mr. 'Hartley, tEe clerk to the Guardians, think it was his place to inspect the vouchers. ,He went into the matter minutely, and his attention was called to that "six." He said "This appears to have been altered. Somebody has put six over it. There I. another six; can you tell me anything about this ?" No; the prisoner could not give any explanation, whereupon Mr. Hartley said "If you suspect at all that these tradesmen are altering the tickets you must look sharp after them and not deal with them any more. Mr. Hartley did that thinking It was the tradesmen, and then said "What did you. pay Mr. Wilcock last week 7—Mr. Wilcock's name appearing on the order—and the prisoner said." I paid £3 45." Well, if those tffikets were added up they came to £3 Bs., and that was en- tered in the books as having been paid for the tickets. Accidentally the prisoner let'it out. There was no suspicion that the tradesmen had altered any of those bills. Mr. Wilcock was only one of the tradesmen, and he was a thoroughly honest man. He said distinctly he received £3 45., and Mr. "Wilcock's evidence was corroborated by his assistant. The prisoner was asked to give an explanation, abut he did not give any then, and subsequently a conversation took place in the presence of several persons, some of whom were members of the Board of Guardians. They asked the prisoner how much he was wrong, and he said he was about £25 wrong ; he thouzht £25 would cover all his deficiencies. He then asked Mr. Hartley to have mercy on him as he had a wife and family. That, he thought, an admission of guilt, but the prisoner defended himself before the magistrates to the utmost. The position of relieving officer was a position of trust, and it waemost important that people who had the giving of out-door relief to poor people and who had con- fided to them a considerablaamount of discretion, should be persons entirely above suspicion, and not guilty of stealing occasion sixpences from Boards of Guardians or the poor. Nobody bad any interest in altering the tickets but the prisoner, and therefore it seemed to him that the jury would be led to the conviction that they had only one duty in this case however painful it might be, and that was to find the prisoner guilty. Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Guardians, Mr. John Fidler, Wm. Wilcock, book-keeper to Mr. Wilcock, Sarah Brighouse, Lydia Cartwright, John Wm. Ralph, expert in hand-writing, Wm. Davies, clerk to Mr. Hartley, Samuel Wensley,.relieving officer, gave evidence in support of the indictment. Dr. Commins, for the defence, asked whether his Lordship thought there was any case to address the jury upon. Hie gettinge w eah contended they had not an atom of evidence whose servant the prisoner was, and that before the prisoner was found guilty it must be proved that the coins actually stolen were the coinsat oo nf a themfgsPiifiirtecshactaoi have enGbouefae rand nivausnemsa.b for The of evidencefh relief purpose tickets P I cki K:e offtvs d ht that fthalesriefi cwa money by false pretences, but the charge was for stealing is. and 45., and there was not an atom of proof that through the means of that falsification one farthing of the money found its way into the prisoner's pockets. His Lordship said the court entirely agreed that there was a cage to go to the jury. Dr. Commins then proceeded to comment on the evidence, and contended that altering the tickets was not stealing money, and that there was no evidence of the prisoner having carried away one farthing of the money of the Union.

div.p: Makes
ly

building. The main avenues and many of the stalls were covered with S/lIITI to the depth of a couple of inches. A snowdrift at Turton, many feet deep, and extending two or three hundred yards, bad to be cut through by navvies. The mail due in London at three o'clock from Carlisle, only reached Wigan at five, having to stop several times whilst gangs of men opened out a way. Luggage trains were stopped, and at places traffic was run on only one line. At Blackpeol, a strong easterly breeze prevailed, and the snow in many places drifted to a depth of several feet. The railway traffic between Lytham and Blackpool has been alto- gether stopped by the snow-drifts on the line, notwithstand- ing that extra locomotive power has been applied. The traffie between Lytham and Preston was discontinued, owing to the engines which worked the route being snowed up near South Shore station. On Tuesday afternoon, at the Wolverhampton County Court, while the court was sitting, and there was a large attendance, a considerable portion of the roof was suddenly blown in. It fell in that part where the public sit, and several persons were covered by the dibris. The alarm was great, and, thinking that the entire building was coming down, several people rushed to the balcony which overlooks the street at a considerable height. They were, however, restrained from clambering over it by the bailiffs. Tbe injured people were dragged from beneath the dill.* and three women and a man were removed to the General Hospital. Richard Thomas, of Temple,street, was found to have sustained a compound'fracture of the skull • and the women had received injuries to the ribs, shoulders, and skulls. The accident caused the suspension of the business of the court immediately. The weather throughout the Midlands was fearful. Trains were blocked, rivers frozen, and canal traffic suspended. Immense snow drifts, and consequent stoppage of traffic are reported from Bristol, Ryde, Dublin, Taunton, Ports- mouth, Cardiff, rtc. In Brighton many houses are completely blocked up, and the London and Brighton Railway is snowed up as far as Three Bridges. At Gloucester part of the roof of the Great Western Rail- way platform was bloWn away. At Birmingham' the wind blew down several chimneys and forced the windows out of several shops.

In addition to three blocks on the Stiuth-Western line, that on the Plymouth branch, that on the Holmsworth branch, and that below Barnstaple and Ilfracoinbe, the main up line was covered with snow to a depth of 15ft. Traffic *as stopped on the Ilfracombe and the Plymouth brandies of the South-Western line. The Devon and Corn- wall line is blocked near East Ansty, and the traffic between Barnstaple and Taunton is stopped. Several vessels are reported to have been lost off Felixstowe, Suffolk. One ship was seen to founder suddenly on Tuesday morning, leaving the crew no Hine to escape. At Dover a lugger went to pieces in the harbour, but the two men on board were saved. The signal box at the Admi- ralty Pier gates was washed away, and the telegraphic in- s.ruments damaged. Rails and lamp posts were washed away', and the houses in Waterlsto Crescent and on the Esplanade are swamped. At Harwidi several fishing vessels were driven ashore, and the sea was washing over them. A message was re- ceived that a vessel had sunk off Woodbridge Haven, that the masts were still above water, and it was thought men could be discerned clinging to them. It being impossible to launch the lifeboat from the beach, she was taken to the Great Eastern Company's pier, and launched from thence, proceeding towards the wreck alone, there being no tug available. While trying to make headway against the gale she suddenly capsized, throwing her crew into the water. Several boats put off to her assistance. One of the crew perished. At Yarmouth several vessels were wrecked, and there was great loss of life, several lifeboat men being drowned through the capsizing of the boats. Reports from Loadon, on Wednesday, say although it is deities( that a storm of equal severity has been experienced in the South of England, yet those who have charge of records say there is no record of one of any such intensity or of such duration. On shore business has been impeded, and traffic by road and rail practically suspended. The London and North-Western Railway was blocked by drifts of snow, and the company are unable to ensure punctuality in their train service throughout the whole of their system. On the London and South-Western owing to the block no London mail,had reached Launceston and other places in the West of England since Suaday morning. The Great Western traffic was so impeded on Wednesday evening, that newspaper and other parcels for Cardiff. Bristol, Exeter, and Plymouth were refused by Coe officials. Telegraphic communication thoughout the country has been almost entirely interrupted. Tne shipping disasters are very numerous, the principal one occurring off Great Yarmouth. Seven vessels were driven ashore and nearly 50 lives boat, including six of a lifeboat crew, who were •drowned when attempting to rescue the mate of the Guiding Star. The Coast Guard were occupied ' trying to save the crews of the various vessels by means of the rocket apparatus. With few exceptions, however, the vessels went to pieces so rapidly that no help could be I afforded. A brig, name unknown, was also lost with all I hands, being driven ashorg near the Wellington Pier. A I foreign barque, believed to be Austrian, was wrecked on the I Cross all the crew perished. At Southend the pier has ' been carried away. The piermaster and his family were I rescued by a boat's crew. Another boat, manned by 12 men, put off to their assistance, but it was swamped, and eight of the crew were drowned. At Harwich the hurricane has done a vast amount of da,nage to property both afloat and on land. Several smacks have been driven ashore, and the I beach is strewn with wreckage. A boat from H.M.S. Penelope, flagship of the Duke of Edinburgh, Commander- in-Chief of the Naval Reserve, is stated to have broken adrift and gone to pieces. Ashore, the railway companies have been the greatest 1 sufferers, most of the lines being snowed up. At Crediton, the snow drifts are in some places 20 feet in height. The 1 north mails of Tuesday night had not arrived in London up I to a late hour on Wednesday afteinoon. Five trellis were I snowed up at Ra.dley Junction for 20 hours, and the pas- I sengers, upwards of 400 in number, were compelled to I remain in the carriages. A road was dug from Radley to I Abingdon, a distance of three miles, in order to provide pro- visions for the imprisoned passengers. The efforts made to 1 extricate the down goods train snowed up at Brent, Somer- set, on Tuesday night, proved ineffectual, and all down passenger trains had had to be shunted on to the up ' line. The London am! North-Western main line was re- ported on Wednesday free from obstruetion. Off Yarmouth a French vessel sank, with a loss of 20 I hands. The brig Battle of Corunna, of Whitby, stranded, I and in spite of every effort the whole of the crew, eight in number, were drowned :Almost within a stone's throw of the pier. At Reading, on Wednesday night, the hotels ware filled with passengers who were unable to proceed on their journeys. At the junction for Weston-super-Mare the pas- sengers were compelled to walk in three feet of !mow. About 30 of the passengers, conveyed in one carriage and a van, were brought to Warminster from the snowed up train near Warminster about noon, but on the engine going back it was itelf embedded in the snow. A tree was blown down in the ; neighbourhood of Royston, aid a boy was killed. In the ' neighbourhood of Windsor Castle the snow Is six feet deep, and the Slough Road is impassable. The roads in the neighbourhood of Eton College were five feet deep in snow. The streets of Barnstaple were impas- sable during Wednesday, and business was suspended. At Bath snow had fallen without intermission for SC hours, and business was almost suspended. At Taunton great numbers of cattle bad been lost in snowdrifts. Two persons ! have been frozen to death at Warwick. Snow was falling ' thickly its Leeds, on Wednesday evening. The second half ' of the Scotch express went off the Great Northern line at ' Easendine, near Peterborough, and several persons sustained ! injury of a slight character. The Severn is full of masses of floating ice, and traffic is impeded. The collieries in the , Rhondda Valley were stopped owing to the severity of the ; weather. The overflow of the sea at Sheerness has done 1 considerable damage. The garrison were employed all night in placing bogs of sand in the sea wall cavities. The disaster is attributed to the wholesale cartage of shingle from the beach. A party of pantomime excursionists while driving from Okehampson to Lidford were upset by the ' force of the wind. When discovered, having failed to find their way, they were very much exhausted and seriously frost-bitten. In the Forest of Dean mineral and other operations had to be suspended, and County Court proceedings came to an abrupt close owing to the enforced absence of witnesses. Part of the Isle of Wight was for two days without mails or newspapers. A coal train on the Seahatn and Sunderland Railway was emtedded. A schooner was observed off Felixstowe with the crew in the rigging. The snow sub- sequently hid them from view, and their fate is unknown. In Dublin there were heavy falls of snow and hail. Tramcar traffic in the city was continued, but in the suburbs the lines were snowed up. Several trains were snowed up be- tween Dublin and Belfast. At the Skerries station, north of Dublin, on the Great Northern of Ireland Railway, a col- lision occurred between the down mail from Belfast and an ordinary train going north, in consequence of a snowdrift of the depth of 20 feet. A first-class carriage of the mail train was smashed, the guard's van was overturned, and the guard injured. A man was found frozen to death on the line. A considerable quantity of snow fell on the Highland line on Wednesday, and passengers were not booked north of Helms- dale. The weather in Ulster continued very severe, and was considered to be the severest since 1840. Op Wednesday night three vessels were reported ashore in the vicinity of the Barrow Sands, near Harwich. Minute guns and other signals of distress were observed, but it was impossible to render assistance. At midnight on Wednesday the the frost weatherhad t e iTv hi cee ssnwoewreb ls ot iel kl ibne tawsetae nt e co fh odri ae yr r aanngde mile no tr .w tinnorLeoanseddontnwina-s still of a severe character, and tensity. Vehicular traffic was suspended, and the local train ch station was overcome on Wednesday. The trains which had been stopped by the drift were cleared away, and gangs of work- men were employed throughout the night in clearing the line of the snow. Meanwhile the traffic was worked 'on a single line between Adlington and Horwich. The snow drift between Horwich Junction and I.ostock Lane station was over two miles in length, and Was occa- cloned by the snow being blown by a strong easterly gale from off Red Moss. One of the passengex trains from Bolton to Chorley was over eleven hours accomplishing a journey of ten miles. An engine of one ef the trains remained embedded in the snow all night. Many of the roads on Wednesday evening were almost impassable. Much interruptions to traffic has been occasioned in the Wigan district by the heavy snowstorm. Ile roads to Standish, Avian, and the neighbourhood were completely.

blocked. Trains on the Chorley branch of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway were much delayed, and on the London and North-Western no train from London arrived from nine o'clock on Tuesday night until seven o'clock on Wednesday night, when the limited mail reached Wigan, being over 17 hours late. On Wednesday the kitchen boiler at the residence of Mr. M'Clure, Swinley-read, Wigan, exploded. The outer wall- of the chimney was blown out, windows were smashed, and much damage done. The servant, Eliza Morris, was pre- sent in the kitchen at the time, and she received severe injuries. The two trains which were blocked between Lytham and South Shore have both been released.

-- The snow block in the vicinity of Heywood was some- what serious. The approaches to the town chiefly used by the farmers in bringing in milk were filled up in places With snow to a considerable height. One farmer had a horse almost buried in l'ilsworth' and had three hors is to drag his cart through the snow. On the Bury and Manchester old road, which runs thr. ugh Pilsworth, 20 men were on Wed- nesday engaged clearing a way through the snow for the farmers, several of whom. had not delivered milk since Tuesday. At Oldham on Wednesday?. thaw set in, anti traffic was resumed. Up to six o'clock on Wednesday night communication between London and Ireland via Chester and Holyhead was suspended on both the North-Western and Great Western routes. A slight snowstorm was experienced at Chester on Wednesday, and the cold was intense. In consequence of the hurricane on Tuesday night the Irish expresses were all about two hours late. On Wednesday the heavy gale continued on the east coast, and snow fell nearly the whole day. A large number of vessels have had to take refuge in the Humber, which is covered with large blocks of ice. Two men have lost their lives by the swamping of a boat in the river. Huge snowdrifts obstruct even the principal streets of Leamington. At Bristol the average depth of the snowfall has been at least DI inches. The drifts were everywhere very deep. Business was practically suspended, and those who opened did little business, only persons venturing out who must. The roads outside the city were impassable, and coal mer- chants notified that there would be no delivery of coal until the roads were cleared. The city was not only,deserted, but out off from communication with the rest of the country. Some cottagers outside the town of Cardiff had to be dug Out of their houses, being almost buried. At Plymouth, in some places from twenty to thirty feet of snow lie on the ground. The twelve hundred convicts at Princetown, Dartmoor, have run short of provisions. Several persons are reported lost, and some are beyond hope of being recovered alive. Nothing like the present block has occurred this century in the west of gnglaud. A telegram from St. Ives reports the almost total destruction of the new pier. Fifty feet length from the middle was washed away daring the storm, and the rest has succumbed tosthe heavy seas. This is a serious disaster for the town. .

___ .....--. 1 The snowstorm was renewed all ever Leicestershire, Rut- , landshire, and Northamptonshire on Wednesday, and the snow drifted in exposed districts to the depth of ten feet, completely stopping traffic. In many villages the people were snowed up, and had to dig their way out of their houses. At Blakeney a police constable, named Job Bennett, died from exposure while on duty. At Syston two lines were completely blocked, the snow having drifted on tile lines to the depth of five. feet, the drift extending a mile. Several trains got stuck fast, and could not get through, and at one time no fewer than 17 trains were standing unable to advance. In Leicester the streets were in places three feet under snow. On Tuesday and Wednesday snow fell throughout , Leicestershire without intermission for about 24 hours. In some parts of the country the drift is no leas than 12ft. deep; and some of the farmers who had attended Melton market were unable to return home, while others had to dig their way out. On Weunesday, Mr. James Bolt, North Shields, received a telegram from Southwold, stating that his barque, the Martino. Maria, had been wrecked at that place during the severe storm, and the whole of the crew, with the exception of the captain and two men, whose names are not given, had been drowned. , James Barrett, platelayer on the Midland Railway, was killed late on Tuesday night near Heathtown Station, Wol- verhampton. The storm was raging, and there was /ear of a collision at the junction of the North-Western with the Midland, and an obstruction at the points. Barrett was en- gaged in removing the snow as it accumulated, when a train struck him down and he was cut to pieces. At about seven o'clock on Tuesday night, as the workmen I at the Castle Ironworks, Birchille—an elevated and exposed 1 locality—were engaged in refilling one of the furnaces, a I wagon, which was descending the incline, was caught by a terrific gust of wind just as it had got clear of the shelter of the furnace, and was carried away off the rails. According to one account, two men, named George Meredith and Geo. Lake, who were in charge of the wagon, were carried away With it, bat according to another statement they jumped on discovering that the wagon had been displaced. Either way they fell from near the top of the incline, Meredith being killed on the spot, and Lake's skull being fractured, and his left leg severed from the body. The last-named poor fellow was at once removed to the Cottage Hospital. He died on the way thither. Great interruption to traffic on the Grea *Northern and Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railways was caused by a collision at Little Bytham, near. Grantham. The signal apparatus was disarranged by the storm, and a goods train, during the blinding drift, ran into a snow wreath several feet thick. While it was embedded a second goods train ran into the rear of the first. The line was blocked se effectually that the newspaper train due at Sheffield shortly before nine o'clock on . Wednesday-morning did not arrive till one o'clock. All traffic to Grimsby, except by Doncaster, was closed. Oa the Midland trains were running two hours late, the guard stating that trains had to force their way through wreaths many feet in thick- ness between Sheffield and Manton. They had little difficulty north of Bedford. Trains from the north on the Midland ran very fairly. The 5-20 p.m. passenger train from Don- caster to Grimsby was nearly wrecked on Tuesday night. Leaving shortly after time it proceeded beyond Appleby, and between that place and Elsharn, owing to the blocking up of the line by snow, it ran off the line. Considerable ex- citement prevailed among the passengers, of whore there was a large number. Fortunately no one was injured, nor was the rolling stock damaged, the only damage done being the breaking of a few "chair.." In consequence of the accident traffic was entirely suspended, and the line was not cleared until ten o'clock on Wednesday morning. SHOCKING ACCIDENT ON THE SHEFFIELD RAILWAY. TOUR OFFICIALS KILLED. SHEFFIELD, Wednesday night—Early this morning a serious accident occurred on. the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire line near Useelby, attributable to the heavy gale of last night. Reports having reached Mr. Nathan Smith, superintendent in the Retford and Grimsloy district, that the line between Barnetby and Lincoln Wall completely blocked up with snow, he last night proceeded to New Hol- land, in company with Mr. John Barber, locomotive superin- dent ; Joseph Weightman, foreman of the waggon repairs shed; and George Turner and John Hurst, two other officials, to go along the blocked line. In various places the snow was found to be two or three yards in depth, notwithstand- ing that there are but few cuttings. Shortly after midnight the snow plough became fast between Usselby and Market Rasen, and the officials got off the engine for the purpose of consulting as to the course to be adopted. They were stand- ing between the metals, and whilst they were here a light engine, coming from Lincoln towards Barnetby, and which was also engaged in clearing the line, dashed in amongst them without the sound of its approach, or indeed any warn- ing, being given them that it was near. Smith, Barber, Weightman, and Turner were killed instantaneously, their bodies being frightfully mutilated. Hurt, too, was shock- ingly injured, one of his arms being completely severed and his ribs and legs smashed. THE Corrrwetiv.—Heavy falls of snow are reported from the French provinces, and in many parts railway and tele- graphic communication has been stopped. It is stated that at the villages round Nimes the wolves have made their appearance in considerable numbers, and that hunting parties have been organised to exterminate them. Several villages and hamlets in France are snowed up. During three days Madrid has been without communication with the rest of Europe, and even with the rest of the Peninsula. Heavy rains, lasting almost the whole week, have stopped the trains in Northern Spain, detaining some of the mails forty-eight hours. In the Ebro Valley the country was ie several places flooded many leagues in extent. A vast amount of damage has been done to the agricultural districts and the live stock. Considerable damage has been done tethe telegraph and the railway bridges. Several towns, such as Burgos, Salamanca, and Cordova were invaded by the waters. Near Cadez and on the coast of Galicia, Asturias, and Biscay there have been wrecks and loss of life. Relief has been sent by the Government to several districts. MADRID. Tuessfay.—The foreign mails ef the 15th and 16th inst. have not yet arrived here in consequence of the accumulation of snow on the Northern Railway preventing the trains from running. MADRID, Wednesday.—The Guadalquiver has risen 24 feet. The quay at Seville is completely submerged; but goods which were lying there for embarkation were removed in time. A violent storm ie raging on the Mediterranean coast, and the mail to the Balearic Island has not left port. The floods in the south of Spain show no signs of sub- siding. AMSTERDAM, Wednesday.—A violent snowstorm is now raging here. The railways are blocked with snow, and traffic on the line is suspended. BouLoGenr, Tuesday.—The railway lines between Paris, St. Omer, and Calais have been blocked by snow since this morning. The sea off this port is rough, and the service of mail boats from and to England is suspended. The cold is intense. ,

div.p: RUNCORN AND THE WEATHER.

The town of Runcorn has, daring the past week, suffered in a variety of ways from the terrible character of the weather. The whole district has been ice-bound, and the view from the mighty bridge which spates the Mersey has been more like one of the wood cuts representing parties exploring for remains of the Franklin expedition at the North Pole than anything else. Far as the eye could reach there was nothing to be seen but snow. Snow everywhere, covering the tall masts of vessels in the ship-yards and causing nearly per- fect stillness where the busy hammer usually tinge from morn till night. Snow in "God's acre," wreathing the momnments with forms of beauty, and covering the spire of the pretty Parish Church with icicles. The river was everywhere covered with ice. This stream which is usually so busy at tide time, was apparently nothing but masses of ice, piled one upon another. Nothing was to be seen of the little ferry boat, and not a passenger or a waterman en "the slip." In the distance could be observed the powerful steam tugs of the Bridgewater Navigation Co., securely fastened in by the Ice King, and covered with their drapery of snow —silent as the grave—there being not a solitary fiat to pro- ceed to Liverpool. Few and far between were the foot pas- sengers- on the bridge, compared with the numerous pedestrians who generally pass over it. Railway traffic on Most days of the week was greatly impeded, and some of the passeug,ers uttered curses bothloud and deep on arriving at Ditton and finding that t' the connection" with the trains by which they had counted upon going forward, broken, and they left to contemplate the dreary landscape which stretches miles away in unbroken sameness. The porters and railway officials were not in any humour to listen sympathetically to the loud complaints of the weather- bound as they were too busy keeping fires goireg, thawing 4` points," and trying to make a way for the blocked traffic, ta attend to anything else. Some of the porters looked half asleep, and to be suffering considerably from their additional work, and they complained of having had to labour all night. On Wednesday—the day following the great aterm—the London newspaper express, which nese 29 through the station at such a fearful rate, instead of rushing past at about a quarter past ten, was not seen until far on into the evening, having been detained by snow which had drifted in huge mounds in various cuttings not very many miles from the metropolis. At Runcorn the news-lads be- longing to Messrs. Smith and the various agents who sell the London morning journals appeared quite bewildered on being told, hour after hour, that no metropolitan papers had reached the station, and there was quite a rush for dailies of all other descriptions—a copy of which it was impossible to find on sale during the afternoon. The evening papers went off with a rush, though in some cases additional sup- plies had been secured. On coming from the station at the early part of the week, a very busy scene met the eye of the spectator on arriving at Waterloo Bridge. The Bridgewater Navigation Co.'s servants were evidently doing all they could, by means of powerful ice-boats, drawn by large num- bers of horses, to keep open the canal communication; and large numbers of additional men were engaged in trying to keep the ice clear from the locks. The view from this bridge at night time was most picturesque, and would have proved not unworthy of the pencil of a Rembrandt. Large fires had been lighted by which to carry on the work, and these lit up the swarthy, earnest faces of the boatmen and boatwomen as they shouted to one another and their steeds, or occasionally gave vent to their overcharged feelings in adjectives more descriptive than polite. As the week wore on, the unequal fight with the frost was sus- pended, as it was found a contest in which victory was hopeless. At the corner of every principal street big unem- ployed men gathered, and many people were annoyed con- siderably by the pertinacity with which numbers of well clad lads beset them for ticket, to obtain liquid or other refreshments at the Cocoa Rooms. Early in the week, the great strike of Lancashire colliers began to tell its tale in Runcorn in the very rapid and extraordinary advance which took place in the price of coal As day after day went by, and the rumour got abroad that several of the large works would have to stop if a supply were not obtained almost immediately, a competition began on the part of householders in good position to get in stocks of coal, and the dealers in this particular article at once became the centre of interest to many whose cellars were empty. Some of the well-to-do sent their horses and carts to certain yards and offered a considerable advance on the ruling market price, but the dealers declined to sell to them, on the ground that they were not regular customers, and that had it not been for the temporary difficulty in which they found them- selves, they would not have honoured their small establish- ments with their presence. On Tuesday evening, a young man named Wm. Talbot, in the employ of the Weston Chemical Works, started from Sutton Dock for Weston with a horse, which he took along the towing path. It is supposed that whilst on his way he suddenly came upon a snow drift, and, in his efforts to make his way through it, he and the animal fell into the canal. As he did not arrive, a search was made en Wednesday morning, which resulted in the horse being found standing in the water, and alive. It was got out and taken to the works. Efforts were put forth to discover the body of Tal- bot, but they had to be given up, owing to the difficulties suet with through the frost. With the mid-day tide on Tuesday the boat Lord Stanley, belonging to Mr. G. Taylor, lime merchant, of Runcorn, was being brought from Widnes dock to the Old Quay, Runcorn, laden with burnt ore, for Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele. The vessel was being towed with several others by the tug Dart, when within a 100 yards of the pierhead the Lord Stanley filled with water, owing to the strong easterly gale which was blowing, and rapidly began to sink. There were only the captain and his wife on board the latter acting as hand; and the captain, discerning the state of affairs, lashed himself and wife to the tow rope, which was on the bow of the next flat. They were pulled through the water and taken on board the next flat and landed at the pierhead, They were much exhausted, and after some brand 7 had been administered they were able to proceed to their home in Canal-street. On Tuesday Mr. Yarwood's man proceeded to Weston with the beautiful new hearse which has just been pur- chased by the firm, and found that the drifted snow made the road nearly impassable. He, however, determined to force his way through, thinking he would be able to succeed in so doing with the pair of horses in his charge. The effort, however, proved a failure, and the hearse became completely blocked in the snow, and was only extricated with tard digging by a number of men. On Monday Mr. Alfred Norman, of Runcorn, had an adventure in connection with the storm. He left St. Helens by train at ten minutes past four in the afternoon, and when between Clock Face and Farnworth the engine ran into a snowdrift, and was only extricated by the combined efforts of six engines and 50 men. During the week the District Visiting Society connected with the Runcorn Parish Church have been very busy in an effort to, in some measure, relieve the great distress amongst the poorer members of the congregation. The vicarage has been besieged by people begging for help. The society have collected £l2 121. 10d., but this, it needs hardly be said, is a sum totally inadequate to deal with the present distress. A similar society in connection with Trinity Church has also been doing a good work, under the direction of the vicar (Rev. W. Preston) and the curate (Rev. W. Robinson). Good house coal has risen to about 21s. per ton, and the price for a very inferior description has been very little less during the last week. Some conception may be formed from this statement of the great difficulty experienced by many poor people in getting sufficient coal to keep the warmth in their bodies. Mr. Shaw, of the Mersey Mission to Seamen, has this year, as he did last, opened a soup kitchen at the Mission Room, and during the week he has supplied many of the poor boat people with eneals. On Monday, 137 persons were given soup and bread, and on Wednesday, 160 had a substantial dinner pro- vided. On Tuesday, Mr. Shaw gave a meal to 48 persons at Ellesmere Port, where the Mission haVe also a branch. Yesterday he provided a meal of soup and bread for 200 children. Mr. Shaw is entirely without funds to meet the expenditure he has been put to, and earnestly hopes that he will be supported by those who are able t 3 render assistance. He intends to keep open the kitchen as long as the frost continues. Mr. Bowyer, School Board Inspector, has been provided with a number of coal and provision tickets by the District Visiting Society before mentioned, and since the 7th instant he has given relief to 160 families. The School Board Officers have daily been visited by scores of persons anxious to receive a ticket, and the numbers at the disposal of Mr. Bowyer have been totally inadequate to meet the

requirements. Should the strike in Lancashire continue, about 350 men who have already had notice will be stopped at Messrs, Wigg Bros. and Steele's works. Nearly 200 hive also received notice at the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Co., aod these will -cease work to-day or to-morrow (Baturaay). Sixty men have also been thrown idle at Messrs. Brundrit and Co.'s shipbuildiag yard through the frost. The shipping trade is also in a very bad state, and large numbers of dock labourers are out of employment.

NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN. 1.0.G.T. HOPE OF EARLESTOWN LODGII.—At the usual weealy meeting of the above lodge, on Monday evening last, in accordance with arrangements made, the lodge-room was thrown open at 8 o'clock to admit the members of the Juvenile Temple, who were to give an entertainment, when upwards of 30 of the children attended, and went through an excellent programme of melodies, readings, recitations, dec., in a very creditable manner indeed. Brother T. O. Roberts, V.S.j.T., gave an address on the importance of the juvenile movement. An earnest letter was read from Sister A. M. Green, D.S.J.T., of Liverpool, regretting her inability to attend through illness, and urging the claims of the Temple upon the adult members. A hearty vote of thanks was tendered to them for their very enjoyable entertain- ment, and each of the children was . presented with an orange at the close of the meeting. There was a very large attendance of the adult members. Bro. Edward Newman, temple superintendent, presided. On Tuesday evening arrangements were made for a coffee suppat-when about 20 members attended. The evening was aftelrwards spent in singing, &c., and was much enjoyed. The very severe weather prevented many members from attending.

Mr. Sprigg, the Colonial has again expressed e very sanguine opinion of the Premier, pretty subjugation of the native tribes.
