div.head: DISTRESS IN RUNCORN.
div.p: THE DISTRESS IN RUNCORN.

PUBLIC MEETING YESTERDAY. Yesterday, a public meeting was held in the Commissioners' Boardroom, at the Town Hall, Runcorn, " for the purpose of considering what steps shall be taken to relieve the distress now prevailing, in consequence of the inclement weather and depression of trade." There were present the Revs. Canon Barclay, M.A. and W. Robinson, (Established Church) J. Nowell (superintendent Wesleyan) and Henry Valentine (Wesleyan Methodist); J. D. Thomas (Congregationalist); and Evan Williams (Calvinistic Methodist; Messrs. Gorge Marshall, Philip Speakman, John Ashton (magistrates' clerk), G. S. Hazelharst, Thomas Norman, Joseph Burton, Francis Fairhurst, J. 0. Jackson,, J. Percival, Edward Imison, William Sutton, R. H. Mouritz, and John Mack. The entrance to the room was completely blocked by about two hunvlred poor people, who had as- sembled in the hope of obtaining some immediate relief for their sufferings. The Itev. Canon BARCLAY was voted to the chair. He thanked Mr. Marshall for the promptitude with which he had called the meeting, as the time had come when the dis- tress had gone far beyond the reach of private benevolence, and when something of a public nature must be done in order to deal with it. (Hear, hear.) The extensiveness of , the present distress surpassed anything he had ever known I during the course of a long experience in the town. (Hear, I hear.) They might make up their minds that if they could escape with about ten per cent. of imposition they would escape very well; and it would no doubt be the earnest 1 endeavour of the committee to do all they possibly could to prevent the funds being wasted upon undeserving cases, If one person out of ten imposed upon the fund, that was no reason why the other nine should be left' to starve. The distress existing in the place was patent to every one for there was hardly a person in any position in the town Whose door had not within the past few days been besieged by applicants for relief. He had pleasure in moving that a relief fund be established in Runcorn, in order to assist those who, through scarcity of labour at great works in the town, or from the stoppage of the canal, and the inclemency of the weather, were at the present time reduced to great distress. Mr. Martsrum. said he thought it behoved them to do what they could in order to help those who were really in need. He had pleasure in seconding the motion. The resolution was carried unanimously. On the motion of Mr. MARSHALL seconded by Mr. Tnomes NORMAN, Mr. G. S. Hazfehurst was elected treasurer. Mr. Plum? SPEAKMAN moved that Mr. Edward Imison be appointed secretary to the relief committee, and the motion was carried with acclamation. The CHAIRMAN said that during the last week be had been distributing through the district visitors, between £3 and £4 a day in connection with his own congregation; but much difficulty had been experienced through the impractability of visiting all the applicants. Ifo doubt Mr. Shaw, the seamen's missionary, and Mr. Bowyer, the school atten- dance officer, would be able to render the Relief Fund Com- mittee excellent help—(hear, hear)—as they were thoroughly acquainted with most of the people who would apply for assistance. He thought it would be wise to refer any Roman Catholic applicants to the Rev. Father Fennelly. Rev. J. NOWELL said his experience of such work, had led him to the conviction that on such occasions as the present, the greatest distress was found amongst families the mem- bers of which would rather starve than make public appli- cation for assistance. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN quite agreed with Mr. Nowell, but said that on such occasions the greatest difficulty was always experienced in finding volunteers who would undertake the visiting work. Mr. Hazr EIIITST considered it would be a wise plan to give each of the ministers in the town a supply of relief tickets.

Rev. E. WILLIAMS remarked that on the last occasion when there was distress in the town, he found that appli- cants came to him who had previously been to three or four other ministers. (Laughter.) Great complaint was made by some gentlemen in the town, at that time, about the in- discriminate manner in which the relief was administered; and he was afraid that unless they went about their work systematically, considerable difficulty would be experienced in getting some persons to subscribe. Mr. HAZLEHIIIIST said that what he meant was that the ministers should relien only those with whom they were acquainted. Mr. Msasturs, believed that the indiscriminate distribu- tion of tickets by the ministers would only add to the evils experienced in past years. Mr. HAZUMIIIIST: But the ministers might distribute , only to those who were members of their own congrega- tiens. _

Mr. Nonntats : Oh, some of them will be members of any congregation you like, if they can only manage to secure a contribution. (Laughter.) Rev. J. NOWELL : If I had one person at my doer yester- day, I had fifty. Rev. W. ROB/NSON : I had several at mine, and they said that the Chairman had sent them there. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN (laughingly) : Well, I have never sent a single one to you. I have stated that in distributing our relief we bad nothing whatever to do with Trinity Church district; but I have only said so in general terms. (Renewed laughter.) Rev. J. Nowm.r. : I had some, 'Mr. ' Chairman, at my house, who said you had sent them. (Laughter).. The CHAIRMAN: All that I have said has been that if they went to a Wesleyan chapel, they m.st get the minister of that chapel to relieve them.

- Mr. HAZLEITTIRST moved that each minister in the town should be provided with a certain number of tickets, for distribution amongst the members of his own congregation who were not likely to apply to the General Committee.

Mr. NoRNAN seconded .the resolution, and it was passed unanimously. On the proposition of Mr. MARSHALL seconded by Mr. JACKSON, the gentlemen present were constituted a relief committee, with power to add to their number. Mr. AsaxoN said that during the distribution of relief at Frodsham it was found prudent to have two descriptions of Contributions, some being ,freekly subscribers and others giving a donation. The CHAIRMAN said that a leading official of the Weston works had told him that that day 500 men would be thrown out of work there, one third at least of whom it might be expected would need relief as dwellers in Runcorn. Rev. E. WILLIAms : I believe the Runcorn Soapery Works stop to-day. Mr. NORMAN': Mr. Lyon's place stopped yesterday, and Messrs. Steele's will cease work on Saturday. On the motion of Mr. MARSHALL, seconded by Mr. NOR- max, it was agreed that a circular, soliciting help, should be sent out by the secretaty, who should be assisted in his duties by Mr. Sutton and Mr. Brookes. After some discussion, it was agreed that the relief should not be extended to Weston, but confined to Runcorn. The following is a list of the weekly subscriptions to the fund, promised in the room :—Canon Barclay £1 Is., Joseph Burton (solicitor) 10s. 6d., George Marshall 7s. 6d., Frances Fairhurst 10s. 6d., Dr. Mouritz £1 Is., Thomas Norman £1 Is., John Ashton £1 is., J. 0. Jackson £l. is. The rest are donations :—Mr. Philip Speakman £2 25., Wm. Sutton £1 Is., Mrs. Thomas Hazlehurst £lO, George S. Hazle- burst £lO, Evan Williams 10s. 6d., John Nowell £1 Is., Imison £2 25., J. D. Thomas Sc., H. Valentine Sc., and Mrs. Lea 10s. The proceedings then terminated, and the committee immediately commenced to administer relief to the crowd in attendance.

WARRINGTON HIGH WAY BOARD. A general meeting of the members of this Board was held on Wednesday, at the Masonic Chambers, Sankey-street. There were present Messrs. Joseph Hartley (chairman), Jno. Fairclough, Henry Bate, John Stanier, Wm. Royston, Reginald Owen, jun., Joseph Pennin ton, James Houghton, Joseph Humphreys, White (law clerk), and Thompson (surveyor).

THE WIGAN JUNCTION RAILWAY. The SURENYOR reported that he had received a notice stating that application was intended b be made to Parlia- ment to authorise the abandonment of the whlle of the railway D, which was authorised by the "Wigan Junction Railways Act, 1875." This railway was intended to he made from Wigshaw to Padgate. He had also received a letter from Mr. Babe, of Liverpool, in which he declined to accede to the full request of the sub-committea with re- ference to the screens required for the various bridges, although the committee had agreed not to enforce the lengthening of the wing walls of the Bolton-road Bridge, which would entail a great outlay on the part of the com- pany. The Surveyor7suggested that he should be asked to re-consider the matter, and reminded of the conditions con- ained in the agreement. Oa the motion of Mr. PENNINGTON, seconded by Mr. Owart, it was resolved that the Clerk write to Mr. Beloe concerning the matter, and if no agreement could be COM 2 to, that the Surveyor and the Clerk have a personal inter- view. WIGSHAW BRIDGE. _ . . .

The SURVEYOR said he had had an interview with Mr. R. Stone with reference to the western approach of the Wig. sbaw Bridge. Mr. Stone had pointed out that the company had made the approach a little steeper than it ought to be on account of allowing for settlement at the deepest part of the embankment, but to counteract the effect of this he agreed to find materials to raise their own and the Board's length at the end where there was a depression. The Sur- veyor considered this satisfactory, and the work will be pro- ceeded with. TUE moons. The SURVEYOR reported that since the last meeting of the Board there had been some very high floods, and in conse- quence the county roads at Houghton Court and Spittal Bridge had been submerged to a dangerous extent. At the latter place a horse got off the roadway and was drowned. He thought a representation should be made to the county authority that these roads required raising and otherwise improving, so as to avoid the frequently recurring nuisance caused by the floods. Mr. Owe r inquired if the Board were not liable to an action for the loss of the hcrse. Mr. WHITE: No. Mr. OWEN said it was very hard that an individual should have to lose a horse in that manner when he paid rates for the repair of the road. A MEMBER: Very hard indeed. The Surveyor was instructed to write to the authorities as to the state of Houghton Court. This ooncluded the whole of the businem.

div.head: TEE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY -22, 1881
div.p: TEE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JANUARY -22, 1881

THE CAPTURE OF AN ALLEGED GANG OF WIDNES LEAD STEALERS. At the Widnes Police Courdipn Saturday, before Mr. P. Gossage, Julia Tobin, Tobin, Ellen Hunt, and Mary Clarke were charged, on remand, with stealing 3 cwt. of lead, the property of Messrs. T. Snaps and Co., of the Phcenix Chemical Works. Paul Kerley, a marine store dealer, who has been in business some years in Cholmond- ley•street, was chaged with receiving the lead, well know- ing it to have been stolen. Mr. Swift, sen., St. Helens, ap- peared for the prisone - Kerley, and 'the case occupied most of the afternoon. Much of the evidence was a recapitula- tion of what was stated at the heating last week. James Hunt said that during the last three months they had missed large quantities of lead from the works. On the Tuesday after Christmas Day they commenced to repair a ,1 leaden tower, and the men had to cut portions of the old lead out, and put new in. The old lead was placed in the yard, where there were also some pigs of new lead. On the 11th inst. he looked at the scrap lead, and found it all right. On the following day, from what was said to him, he ex- amined the scrap again, and missed some of it. He went to the police station the same night, and was shown an amount of lead. The steam jet produced was connected with a vitriol chamber. The other pieces produced were portions of the cellar of the tower. The last piece bad been used as a plenisher. The piping in court (which had been cut) was part of an overflow pipe to the salt cake; the other pieces were from a powder chamber. On the sth inst. he saw Kenna and the two Tobins near the works, each with a bag in her possession. On going towards them they ran away, leaving the bags. He examined:them, and found lead in them, four pieces of which he now identified. He had them carried into the works, and afterwards handed them to P.C. Pitt. They never sold small amounts of the lead belonging to the works; though it was quite true that they melted the scrap lead down and disposed of it to the wholesale dealers. Thomas Pende, plumber at the Phcenix Works, said on the 12th inst., from what was said to him, he went to the scrap heap and missed part of the leaden cellar. He also identified ilhe piping produced. which was in eight pieces, but was only in one piece when he first saw it. He likewise identified the plenisher, and a piece of old sheet lead. Gerald Newman, labourer at the works, said he lived at 42, Barn-street, and on Wednesday, the 12th instant, he was near to West Bank dock during the morning, and he noticed the prisoners Kenna and Hunt coming from the direction of the top gate of the works. One of them had a bag with her, and he gave information to the people at the works of what he had seen. He found the top yard gate, which was usually shut, open. P.C. Clarkson stated that on the 12th instant he went with Sergeant Eastham and P.C. Pitt into Queen-street, and visited the house of the prisoners Hunt and Clarke, who live together. In a closet underneath the stairs he found the three sacks produced, which were marked with some kind of lead, and appeared to have been recently used. He appre- hended the prisoner Hunt. On the way to the station she said she never stole or sold any of the lead, but "she had eaten some of it." He then went with Eastham to Chol- mondley-street, where the prisoner Kerley keeps a marine store. He asked Kerley if he had bought any lead that day, and he said "No; I have no lead on my premises.' Eastham next followed, and in the sergeant's presence the man made a similar statement. He (witness) then searched a stable in the yard, but found nothing there. He next went into the house again, and Sergeant Eastham called his attention to the book lying on the desk, in which the pri- soner ought to enter any articles pnrchased. Eastham said, "I see no entry of any lead having been bought to-day, nor for this last week." Prisoner answered, "All is in that 1 have bought." He then went with the prisoner upstairs, and agaip searched for lead, but found none. He proceeded downstairs, and then heard Ssrgeant Eastham call to him from the cellar, and requiring him to bring a light. He lighted a candle and took Kerley with him into the cellar. Underneath the cellar steps, in a dark corner, the sergeant found a quantity of lead. Eastham said to Kerley, "What about this lead ?" He made no reply, and gave no expla- the nsHtaaet stepstiitoohnnKe station. iaboutaHapyep said,trit oe apprehended bkee nede, gt possessionht ahttKnneodirde o'clock . ayeopyca Wpnko appeared htalnhretdheehndaesttdaohtmolboe e akyoe andehgwavihyeemwtrne eihnbentigoingnogeenh, erwetae weighed police pgoanhl about four and a half cwts. The pieces lying at the top of n thet th alreaa d wereilln n appre- hendedin the the presence and H e echargednna the prisonerunt r epli neverannaand t stole i” aor sold any chargedlead . Clarke MaryMary Clarkewith d Man anraye rAn n K beingco d in stealing the lead, and selling some of it to Kirley that day. She answered" She sold a bit of it, but had no hand in stealing it." He charged Kerley by himself, with re- ceiving the lead some time during the last three months, knowing it to have been stolen. Kerley said "I did not know It was stolen."

In cross-examination, the witness said he had known Kerley about five years—in fact, since he came into Widnes. He believed that Kerley had never been charged with any- I thing of this kind before. When they went to search his premises, the prisoner did not offer any objection. Sergeant Eastham gave evidence corroborative of that of Clarkson generally, as to what took place at the marine store dealer's. He also detailed very fully the questions he asked the marine store keeper as to having bought any lead that day or for some time. He added that he found the name of Mary Kenna in the book kept by Kerley, twelve times during the last three months, Mary Tobin's nine times, and Clarke's four times, all as having sold scrap iron to Kerley. P.C. Ross gave corroborative evidence.

P.C. Pitt said he took Kenna into custody, and on charg- ing her she deaied having stolen any of the lead. He apprehended the two Tobins on the 13th inst., and on being charged they made no reply. He also charged them, in the presence ef Kerley, on a day afterwards, with stealing four particular pieces of the lead on the sth inst. Kenna first replied that she did not take any lead that day, but after- wards said, "I sold these two pieces, or two very like them, to Kerley yesterday." Mary Tobin denied having anything to de with stealing the lead mentioned, and remarked that she was not out the house during the week of ..the robbery.

This concluded the case for the prosecution. Mr. Swift asked Mr. Gossage if it would be any use to address him on the case or had he made up his mind to commit his client for trial. Mr. Gossage: There is no doubt in my mind that there is a very strong ease against Kerley. Mr. Swift: Then it would be useless for me to occupy I your time with any remarks. Mr. Gossage: Yes, I think it would. I do not see that anything you can say would disabuse my mind of the con- viction that there has been a regular system of robbery going on, and that this man has received the lead. The prisoners were then each formally committed to the "Liverpool Quarter Sessions for trial. The prisoners were indicted at the Liverpool Quarter ISessions on Wednesday, and found guilty. Lord Derby, in passing sentence, said: In the case of the two young girls—Mary Tobin who is aged 14, and Julia Tobin, who is aged 12—we gave determined, considering their youth, :and considering that they have been led into temptation by other parties, to give them another chance. The sentence of the court will be, therefore, that they be imprisoned severally for two days—that is to say. they will be released at the expiration of these sessions. They must seriously remember that if they ever come here again they cannot get the same kind of indulgence shown them. In regard to the case of Mary Kenny, whose age is 12, we can- not deal with her in the same way, but still the sentence will be a light one. The sentence of the court on you Mary Kenny, is that you be imprisoned and kept to hard labour for three calendar months. Now, we come to the case of Paul Kerley. the marine store dealer, and I am bound to say that we think it our duty to deal with that in a different manner. It is clear he has been dealing at times with these young people, and it is clear he has not only committed crime himself, but has instigated others to do so. The sentence of the court on you, Kerley, is that you be imprisoned and kept to hard labour for 15 calendar months.
WIDNES TRADERS' ASSOCIATION,

IMPORTANT MEETING YESTERDAY. Yesterday afternoon the annual meeting of the Widnes Traders' Association was held at the Officers' Room. the Volunteer Hall. Mr. E. K. Muspratt presided, and there were also present Messrs. Eustace Carey, H. Brunner' T. S. Timmis, Major Cress, Sidney Muspratt, John Clare, J. W. Carlile, and H. W. Deacon (secretary). Mr. DEACON read the report cf the Executive Committee during the year, which stated that the memorial against the Staffordshire Railway Company's Bill of last session was presented, protesting against the alterations of the maximum rates of charge which were proposed. The Bill, however, was passed with only slight modifications of its original proposals. An interview was obtained with Mr. Kay (L. Jr, N.-W), and the recent traffic block and the diffi- culty of entra ice to the canal and dock were brought before his notice. On the first subject, he mentioned that the block was owing to the insufficient siding accommodation pos- sessed by many traders; and he suggested that the Associa- tion should use its influence to get the traders to increase their siding accommodation. It was pointed out to Mr. Cross that the Association could not do anything of the kind, and that it was emphatically the duty of the railway company to see that prsper sidings were provided. He eventually admitted that this was the duty of the railway company, and he undertook to give the subject his personal attention. Since that time the committee had heard of no complaints from the manufacturer on. the subject, and the traffic seemed to have been better worked. Mr. Kay, Mr. Worthingron, and the committee then visited the canel and dock entrances, and the subject was discussed oil the spot. Mr. Kay. promised to bring the matter before his directors, and said that he would use his endeavours to get them to make bye laws, and to undertake a scheme for a new and batter water entrance. Mr. Worthington promised to " flush " as regularly as possible, and to put men on to I "scuttle," if opportunity offered. This that gestleman had since done, but the effect was very temporary, as the real cause of the silting up of the gut from the channel to the entrance, seemed to be further up the river, and to arise from the channels and the formation of banks. The com- mittee also communicated with the Upper Mersey Commis- sioners, with the object of getting them to take action in the matter, if possible; but, in reply, they stated they had no powere to take any step for deepening the gut. The committee had authorised Major Cross, civil engineer, to prepare plans, at a cost not exceeding £lOO, for a new entrance to the canal and dock. These plans were in course of preparation' and when they were completed it was the intention of the committee to lay them before the directors of the London and North-Western Railway Co., who had expressed their willingness to receive a deputation and con- sider the subject. The committee had examined the bye- 'laws which were of interest to this neighbourhood, and, with the exception of a clause in the Midland Railway Com- pany's Bill, there appeared to be nothing affecting the in- terests of the traders. In their Bill the Midland Railway Company asked for powers to make certain charges in ad- dition to any rates and tolls which they were at present authorized to charge for a supply of wagons by them for the conveyance of coal, coke, dtc. It appeared to the committee that the clause in question would not be unreasonable, under certain conditions and they had written to the railway company and suggested that a proviso should be added to the clause, to the effect that nothing therein should interfere with any existing rights of traders to provide their own wagons, if they wished ; and also that the short distance clause should be altered. A Bill was being introduced into Parliament this session en- tituled "The Garston Dock and Railway Bill," the objects being to construct a new dock at Garston and a short rail- way connecting the dock with the Cheshire Lines Railway. The promoters would not object to put in clauses classify- ing chemicals according to the wishes ef the traders, on the understandiag that the latter would give their support to the measure. The committee had, therefore, instructed their solicitors to draw up a petition, and it would be sent round for signatare as soon as possible. The statement of accounts , up to December 31st, 1880, showed that at that time the out- standing liabilities were about £lBO. When these were made up, there would be a balance of about £lO7 to the credit of the association. . _

On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. T. Strrrox TIMMIS, the report was adopted. Mr. CAREY said he did hot consider the London and North-Western had acted with sufficient diligence in clearing the canal from ice. They had had experience during the last few days of the difficulties incident to a block of traffic. The meeting decided that the secretary should write to the company' on the subject. On the proposition of Mr. Timms, seconded by Major Cnoss, it was resolved that Mr. H. Brunner be appointed a member of the Executive; after which the proceedings terminated.

LICENSING Marrana.—.The application of Mr. John Knowles, of Wilson's Hotel, for an extension of hours from eleven at night until three or four o'clock in the morning of the following day, at the Bachelors' Ball, was granted.—Mr. Barthold Rethbery, a German, applied for permission to sell at the Castle Hotel, Halton, until next transfer day. The information as to the defendant's character was not suffi- ciently full for the satisfaction of the Bench, and the hearing of the application was adjourned until next week.

LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Wednesday morning in the reading room of the Library, Mr. W. H. Lacey, presiding.

BAROMETER FOR THE READING ROOM. The LIBRARIAN (Mr. Chambers) laid upon the table the barometer which has been supplied by Mr. J. Cotton, chemist, Church-street, and after some conversation as to where it should be fixed, it was resolved on the sugges- tion of the Librarian, to !place it on the centre pillar in the room, and immediately over the large globe.

VALUABLE ADDITION TO-111-E LIBRARY. The books ordered to be obtained by the committee at a previous meeting, had, the Librarian reported, all been re- ceived, making an addition of 407 volumes. Of these 124 were received in December, and the remainder, 233, had arrived this month and will be available to the public as soon as they have been catalogued.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE. The LIBRARIAN reported that the Sunday attendance on the 12th December (weather fine) was 102; on the 19th December (frosty and snow) 112; on the 26th December (fine) 59 only, the comparative smallness being due to the fact that the day was the one succeeding Christmas day; on January 2nd (fine) 116.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. S. Rigby and G. Artingstall. ALLEGED BREACH OF THE LICENSING Am..—Samuel Taylor, keeper of the Boat House public-house, Hollins Green, was summoned for selling liquors during prohibited hours; and Joseph Clare, William Wright, and John Owen, young men, with aiding and abetting.—Sergeant Pattison said he, accompanied with P.C. Macfarlane, were going in the direction;of the Boat House, on Sunday morning, the 9th instant, about 10-30, and he saw three men enter the beer- house. The officers followed, the sergeant going in at the back door and the constable entering at the front. The men Were found in the kitchen, Owen having a pint jug con- taining about a gill of beer in his hand. It was fresh drawn. Clare and Wright exclaimed "You haven't seen us with anything." Mrs. Taylor, the landlady, then came into the room shouting "The sergeant is coming, be quick." The landlord stated that the men had not been served with any beer.—By Mr. Moore, who defended : Never saw any of the men drinking in the house.—P.C. Macfarlane gave corrobo- rative evidence.—Mr. Moore having addressed the Bench for the defence the defendant was sworn, and said that the three men went into the house to hire a boat to cross the river. None of the men were served with liquor.—Defen- dant Clare said he and his companions were going from Cadishead to Lymm on the day in question, and went to the beer-house to get a boat to be ferried across the river, that being the nearest way.—The other defendants confirmed this statement, and the Bench dismired the case. MESSRS. GRACE AND THEIR CARTERS.—Thornas Canary was charged with being asleep in charge of his horse and cart, at Sankey, on Saturday morning.—Fined 2s. 6d. ignd costs.—Defendant said he worked at Grace's, and Mr. Arting- stall enquired whether all these kind of offences were com- mitted by the carters of Messrs. Grace.—The officer said they were.—Mr. Artingstall remarked that some notice ought to be given to them.

THE REV. JOBEPH AGAR REX; Wesleyan Minister, , Warrington, has just issued the second edition of his " Com- , mentary on the Romans," a work that has elicited the highest praise from some popular divines. P. RTIANDS'EI MOTION ON THE TRANSVAAL.— The following are the terms of the motion given notice of by Mr, Rylands, M.P., for the 21st inst.: That this House is of opinion that the annexation of the Transvaal was impolitic and unjustifiable, and would view with regret the adoption of any measure by Her Majesty's Government for the purpose of enforcing British snpremacy over the people of the Transvaal, whohrightfully claim their national independence."

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

DRVNE.—David Rogers, who did not appear, was fined 50. and costs for being drunk on the Ist inst.—P.C. Brydges proved the case. REMOVING GOODS TO AVOID PAYMENT OF RENT.—Walter Bushell, John-street, who was represented by his wife, was summoned by Mr. John Dickson for fraudulently removing gocds to avoid a distress for rent.—The complainant said he was the owner of a house formerly occupied by the defen- dant, who was 275. in arrear with his rent. Between the Bth and 10th inks, the goods were removed, though he had behaved very leniently to him.—The Bench made an order for payment of the arrears and costs. A MissiNct WITNESS—Mary Loftus about 18 years of age, was charged on remand with stealing a can of con- densed milk, value 6-0., the property of Mr. Lawrinson, shopkeeper, Widnes-road. The prisoner was remanded, and in the meantime the assistant who should have given evidence, was discharged, and left the town. The Chairman said the prisoner had had a very narrow escape, and he hoped it would be a warning to her in future not to give way to any temptation to be dishonest. AN UNGRATEFUL THIEF STEALING A COAT AND VEST. —Wm. Leach, a young man, was charged with stealing a coat and vest, the property of John Fender, a foreman in the employ of Messrs. Gaskell and Deacon. The evidence was to the effect that the prosecutor put his coat in the cabin on going to the works, upon the previous evening, at five o'clock. During the night the ',Boner visited him and told a very pitiful story, on which he gave him part of his food. He (witness) saw the articles at three in the morning, and missed them at four. He afterwards found the house where the prisoner was lodging, and it was discovered he was wearing the vest.—The Chairman said the prosecutor ought to know better than harbour men on the works at the dead of the night. He must not do anything of the kind in future. Prisoner would be sent to gaol one month with hard labour.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. A. Thomas.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. A. Thomas.

A WIDNES MAN CHARGED WITH NEGLECTING TO SDE.- PORT Ins MOTHER.—Wm. Stanley, a black ash man, working at Messrs. Gossage's Widnes, was charged with neglecting to pay to the support of his mother, who is chargeable to the Runcorn Union.—Mr. Thomas Houghton, collector, said the Guardians were paying the defendant's mother 3s. per week, and they had made an order upon the son to contribute Is. weekly.—Defendant said he was quite willing to pay his share of the relief if his other brothers were likewise sum- moned. They were quite as well able to pay as he was. One of them had no children of his owri, but was living in adul- tery, and keeping the woman's children.—The Chairman said it was highly probable the position of the defendant's other brothers would be fully enquired into by the Guardians. All the magistrates bad to do was to make an order upon him to pay Is. per week towards the support of his mother, and Is. ed. costs. ASSAULT ON A GIRL BY • MARRIED WONAN.—A power- ful looking woman named Jane Lucas, of Brook-street, was summoned for assaulting Elizabeth Sampson, a girl about 14 years of age, living with her parents in Lyon-street.— Mr. Lewin appeared for the complainant, who said that on the 11th inst. she gave the husband of the defendant a letter as he was coming from work, asking him "to keep his wits quiet." Whilst on her way borne, she and her companion, whose name was Ellen Rigby, stopped to look into Mr. Houghton's shop window, when the defendant came up, seized her (witness) by the hair, which she twisted round, and then dragged her by it to the corner of Brook-street. Defendant also smacked and scratched her face, and said that if she came upon her premises again she would knock her brains out.—Ellen Rigby, aged 18, gave corroborative evidence.—Defendant said the complainant had annoyed her very much by coming to her door, hammering it savagely, and then running away. Mrs. Sampson had written several letters of a very insulting natyre to her husband about her. She was aggravated by the con- duct of her mother, that when she saw her in the street she got hold of her, but she had no knowledge of having scratched her face.—Mr. Brundrit said that Mr. Lewin, in opening the case, Was quite satisfied in calling the assault an unprovoked one. Whatever the parents had done, she had no right to attack the girl.—Defendant would have 103. and Ils. costs to pay, or in default, be sent to prison 14 days, with hard labour. They hoped the fine they had in- flicted would be a warning to her to keep her temper in the future.

DI2I7NE AND DISOHDERLY.—Sarah Clarke and Thomas Clarke were convicted, the former of having been drunk, and the latter drunk and disorderly, in Halton-read, at about 12 o'clock at night on the 10th inst.—P.C. Hibbert proved the case, and each defendant had 10s. and 9s. 6d. costs to pay, or be imprisoned 14 days. SMART CAPTURE OF MIDNIGHT FOWL STEwins.--Joseph Hayes and George Haves, two relatives, !were charged by Mr. Horsfall, cashier, Irwell-lane, with stealing four hen; value 10s., on the 14th inst.—The prosecutor said the hens produced were his property, and he saw them safe on the previous Thursday, about noon, in the cote inthe outer yard of his premises, where they were kept.—Charles W. Hors. fall, aged 14, son of the previous witness, said he made the cote up, and locked it, at about four o'clock on the after- noon of the day named;—Sergeant Handford stated that about 20 minutes past midnight, on Friday morning, he was on duty at Grosvenor-street, near the end of the prosecutor's house, in company with Sergeant Michael, when be saw some one come along the street and lump over some boards into the yard where Mr. Horsfall keeps hens. The men remained there about five minutes, and then went in the direction of Messrs. Wigg's works, and ultimately into a yard where was a house occupied by one of them. He and the other officer followed, and arrived in time to see the prisoner, Joseph Hayes, killing one of the stolen fowls. They took the prisoners in custody, after which he said to them "What sort of a game do you call this ?" Joseph Hayes

div.head: WARRINGTON UNION INDUSTRIAL
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION INDUSTRIAL
SCHOOLS. - - - UNVEILING THE TABLET STONE.

The ceremony of unveiling the tablet stone at the new Union Industrial Schools, which are in course of erection at Padgate, took place on Tuesday afternoon. The greater nnmber of the persons present at the ceremony, left War- rington by train about two o'clock. On arriving at the schools the party proceeded under the charge of the archi- tects, Messrs. John Pierpoint and Son, and the builder, Mr. G. Napier, to inspect the premises which have made rapid progress towards completion. By three o'clock, the hour appointed for the ceremony, several other Guardians had arrived and there were present Mr. W. Derbyshire (chair- man,) Messrs. Brown, Longshaw, Houghton, Gibson, Fair- burst, Woolfall, Loughlin, J. C. Sutton, J. Caldwell (New- ton,) J. Pierpoint, T. Pierpoint, G. Napier, and J. Siddeley (clerk of works.) A strong and bitter cold wind blew from the east which rendered it most disagreeable to be out of doors, and it was wisely decided that the ceremony at the building should be as brief as possible. Mr. W. DARBYSHIRII, by whom the ceremony was per- formed, stepped forward, and remarked that owing to the boistorous state of the weather it had been decided to lose no time there, but to adjourn to the Stocks Inn, where same remarks would be made. Mr. Derbyshire then pulled a cord and the veil fell. It revealed the tablet stone which bore the following inscription "Warrington Industrial Schools, erected 1881, William Derbyshire, Esquire, chairman." Three hearty cheers were then given, and the unveiling ceremony was completed. An adjournment was made to the Padgate Stocks Inn, where the party were joined by Messrs. J. Harrison, and Jas. Pennington (vice chairman,) W. E. Winstanley, and Balharry, who had been delayed on the way, owing to the roads being blocked by snowdrifts. The company then partook of a capital dinner, which was excellently served by the landlord, Mr. Dainteth. _ .

After dinner the senior VICE-CHAIRMAN (Mr. Harrison) presided and gave the health of the Queen; remarking that the Queen was sometimes blamed, and he confessed that he had a little grievance against her himself, as she did not mix quite sufficiently with her peeple ; but they could say perhaps that a more noble monarch never presided over a people. The CHAIRMAN next proposed the health of Mr. Derby- shire, the Chairman of the Board, and said he had pleasure in doing in because, as they were aware, they had met together that night to do him such honour as they could to commemorate the unveiling of the tablet stone which would ornament the building that was being erected in that neigh- bourhood. It certainly was important even as an erection in that place •, and notwithstanding that considerable opposition had been manifested towards it by a good many people, he was not without hope that they would live to see that the erection of those schools, and the taking away of the children from the bad influence of the paupers in the Workhouse, would be a move in the direction of human pro- gress,ewhich every lover of this country wished to see carried out. (Hear, hear.) He believed that would be the effect of it,—(hear, hear,)—and the unveiling of the tablet, to ornament the front of those schools, was a little event in the history of the life of their chairman, which he thought it was very proper, becoming and fitting should not pass with- out some little demonstration of their feeling on that occasion. (Hear, hear.) They had been to look at the stone and had seen the inscription placed upon it, and they knew the name which was placed upon that stone was worthy of being there recorded,--(hear, hear,—for he did not think a more indefatigable Chairman of a Board of Guardians existed in England than Mr. Derbyshire was and had been. (Applause.) He thought he should be right in saying that Mr. Derbyshire had never missed one meeting since he be- came Chairman of the Board. He had the honour orbeing senior vice-chairman, but like Othello his occupation was gone. When he acted as senior vice-chairman when other gentlemen preceded Mr. Derbyshire, he was frequently called upon to act in that capacity—(hear, hear); but Mr. Derbyshire bad not given him the opportunity of distinguishing him- self. Mr. Derbyshire had not missed once. That was say- ing a great deal, but he believed, if he were chairman for several years they would find him equally regular in the discharge of his duty. They must congratulate themselves on having built these schools, and he hoped it would be the privilege of everyone of them to see them in working order, and those who lived in the schools would recognise the ad- vantages of being educated apart from the workhouse. He hoped the inhabitants of Warrington, who would be called upon to pay for the schools would feel that the investment was a good one, and that they had done much to snatch the children from a position which was considered anything but satisfactory. He trusted their exertions would triumph over prejudice, and that the result would be the welfare of tie poor children who were entrusted to their care. (Applause.) Mr. DARBYSHIRE, iii response to the toast, thanked them for the cordial way in which they had drunk his health, to- gether with that of his wife and family. In coming to un- veil the tablet stone of the Warrington Union Industrial Schools he found more Guardians at the premises than he expected to be there considering the weather. It was sug- gested there that they should not lose any time but simply unveil the tablet according to announcement, and adjourn there to give an opportunity for any Guardian to express his feelings. It had afforded him great pleasure to unveil that stone and to be asked by his fellow Guardians to do so. It gave him pleasure also to see the building so far advanced as to require the unveiling of the tablet. He thought it had proceeded very quickly indeed recently, and he hoped it would soon be completed. They all knew now that every child had to be educated according to law. That was not so a few years ago. All children must be educated if the School Inspectors could lay their hands upon them. The Board of Guardians of Warrington had only carried out the intention of the law in providing more accommodation for educating the children of the poor people. Guardians were the guardians of the poor, and it was their duty to do the best for those poor children that they possibly could; and if every body or committee of management in connec- tion with other public schools in Warrington had tried to increase their accommodation for educating children as much as the Guardians had, there would be no necessity whatever for a School Board in Warrington—(hear, hear)— of which they had heard so very much lately. He thought Warrington would regret having a School Board. (Hear hear.) He was connected with one or two—one in Cheshire and the other in Lancashire—and his friends in both places regretted that they had ever had any thing to do with a School Board; and if they had to do the work again they would rather provide more school accommodation in the ordinary way, than establish a School Board. (Hear, hear.) He had no doubt that was pretty much the feeling in Warrington. He had no doubt the view of the Government in making education compulsory, was to do away as much as possible with crime and pauperism, and he had no doubt that results would be seen in a few years. He hoped, at any rate, if the measure had not at first the full effect anti- cipated, it would have some influence upon the character of the poorer classes. It had been the practice of the Guar- dians recently, and he thought it was the correct view to take, that where there was a family of 5 or 6 children and father and mother,—who might be thrown out of work through some unavoidable circumstances—to give them an order to send their children to the schools, instead of a few shillings for relief. If there was any stigma in being sent to the workhouse school it would certainly be removed when that building was completed, because the schools would be away from the workhouse, and would be conducted upon a principle which would not in any way taint those who were educated at those schools with pauperism, but, he hoped, on the con- trary, would strengthen them with purpose to proceed through life without help. (Hear, hear.) There had been a great deal said about the expense of the new schools. He could not for the moment say what would be the difference between educating the children at the new schools, and edu- cating them in the old schools at the Workhouse; but he could say it would not take altogether id. in the .£ to manage the establishment. He should think it did not cost very much less when they were educated at the barracks. He had no doubt they were all aware of the kind of instruc- tion that would be given at the schools. He should suggest that the teachers of the school should be governed by the fundamental consideration that the main aim should be net so much to impart knowledge as to impart the power of it,—(hear, bear)—to train up the children so as to enable there to acquire easily whatever particular knowledge their future position in life might chance to demand; in short, to supply them with suitable tools, and the requisite skill to which they must then be left to carve out their own future. This, he hoped, would be something better both fer them.and their children than being a burden upon the rate- payers. (Hear, hear.) If they imparted an education of that character to the children he hoped It would do away with hereditary pauperism, and fit them to earn their own living without being a burden upon the ratepayers. (Ap- plause.) The CHA111714.11 proposed the health of Mr. Winstanley, one of the oldest members of the Board. Mr. WINSTANLEY suitably responded, and contended that the Board had acted wisely in building those schools. The healtha of the junior 'ice-chairman (Mr. Jos. Pen- nington), the chairman' and the clerk having been drunk and suitably responded to, the proceedings terminated. The workmen engaged at the schools were afterwards entertained to dinner.

div.head: BOONS ISSUED DURING TEE MONTH.
div.p: BOONS ISSUED DURING TEE MONTH.

Mr. CHAMBERS reported that 7,933 books were issued from the Lending Library from the 12th December, 1880, to the 15th January, 1881 (five weeks), out of which 71 were handed out for reading in the reading room. He also reported that there were 2,257 members in the lending department. The 7,933 books were classified as follows :—His- tory 292, biography 277, travels t3OB, natural history 126, sciences 313, theology 126, poetry 134, fiction 5,948, politi- cal economy 22, fine arts 22, general literature 365, total 7,933, as compared with 6,896 in the five weeks of last month.

A GIFT. During the past month there had been presented to the Library "The Coalfields of Great Britain: their history, structure, and resources, by Edward Hull, M.A., LL.D., F.R.5.," presented by the author.

THE LIGHTING OF THE 12001 f. It was decided to place "Manchester burners" in the chandaliers in the reading room, and place over them globes similar to those at present ia the library. PAVING COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting Of—thi—s—c-Otn—Q;;;as held on Wed- nesday afternoon, Alderman Johnson (ex-mayor) presiding. There were also present Aldermen Gamble and Cook, Councillors Walker, Bishop, Mr. Brewis (town clerk), Mr. Craik (deputy town clerk), Mr. Hart (borough engineer), and Mr. Johnson (borough treasurer.) Mr. HART said he had gone into the question whether the Primitive Methodist Chapel Trustees should be exempted from the payment of cost incurred in the Corporation draining the passage adjoining the chapel in Kirkland- street. Both be and Mr. Craik were satisfied that the Cor- poration could not recover. The claim was £6 for sewer. Alderman GAMBLE: What is the .resolution of the com- mittee about that?
The CHAIRMAN : But it is not used as a place of wor- ship. . .
Mr. CRAIK said that when a similar thing was discussed a while ago the claim was allowed. Tho TREASURER: But the new chapel was not built then.
Mr. WALKER Slid it was used for !week day services and he thought it was even more used than the new chapel. Alderman GAMBLE: It is used for nothing else. The TREASURER : It is used for schools.

Mr. BREW'S then read the Act relating to the question, front which it appeared that all "churches or chapels or meeting houses appropriated for public or religious service" should be exempt from payment but that such should be certified and recorded according to law. The CHAIRMAN: ; think they can get over it if it is used for service.

Alderman GAMBLE: You won't exempt schools from pay- ment of highway expenses when they are used for prayer meetings once or twice a week? Mr. Buswis : But the place requires to be licensed. You require a certificate that the meeting-house, or whatever it is, is appropriated to public and religious worship. The CHAIRMAN: They have to get a certificate. They have to produce one, then? The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK: They produced it some time ago.. _ .
The TREASURER: I had the certificate a month or so; it was .from the Registrar-General.
Alderman Coorc : Was it registered as a place of worship? The TREASURER: Yes.

Alderman GAMBLE : If it is a school employed occasionally for religious services I think it is exempt. Mr. BREWIS : But have they kept the license going after they built the new one? The CaanimAN said to all interests and purposes it was a schoolroom, and he thought there was scarcely a school in the town but which had religious service conducted in it from time to time.

Mr. HART: It was formerly used as a chapel, but they have now made use of it for nhool purposes. Alderman Gamma thought, however, it ought to be exempt, seeing that it was originally a chapel, and that it was now converted into a school.

Mr. BREWIS did not think it should be exempt. The TREASURER raid it was exactly in the same position as the Independent school, which was exempt. It was ultimately decided that Mr. Wilshaw be seen and asked to produce the certificate with license.

div.head: TRAMWAYS AND THR RAILS.
div.p: THE TRAMWAYS AND THR RAILS.

A letter was read from Mr. Joseph Speight, tramways' con- tractor, dated 15th January, stating that the tramways' directors had sent him a letter lis reference to the rails in Westfield-street, drc., stating that they trusted they would be able in a few days to give him an order to proceed with the work in St. Helens. Before putting the rails down he asked for' and obtained the consent of the borough surveyor; and he trusted the committee would exercise a little indulgence in the matter.

Mr. HART denied 1:n. foto that he gave any permission,. but he said that if Mr. Speight chose to put down the rails in the street he would have to be responsible for them. Alderman COOK : Well, that is a plain sentiment. There has been complaints of accidents arising from these rails.

Alderman GAMBLE thought something should have been done, but at present it was frosty weather. The CHAIRMAN : But it is not at all necessary that the rails should be laid down so long before they are wanted. The people in the dark trip over them. Mr. WALKura: There has been a good many falls; my wife fell over some one night. The TIMM:TRIM : I fell myself one Sunday night. Alderman Cool{: I suppose they want to lengthen their Act to two more years. Their present Act says they must complete in a short time. The CHAIRMAN: Well, now, what should be done with respect to these rails ? If they go in for an extension of time, the rails ought to be .retuoved. Mr. HART: The police can make them remove the rails. If they put one on one side of the road and another en the other, and not place them upon one another, there would be but little danger. But it is very awkward sa they are now placed. The CHAIRMAN : If they placed them upon some waste land it would be all right. What action can we take? Mr. BRENVIS: You can summon them, but give them seven days' notice. Mr.Cusuc said he had already written to the company requiring the removal of the rails. It was decided to give them notice to remove them, and if they were not removed proceedings would be taken against them.

THE BORROWING OF HONEY. :7.1,0Cal Government Board, Whitehall, B.W , 15th December, 1880.--Eir,—l am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter on the 2nd inst. as to the proposed borrowing, by the Town Connell of St Helens, of £3,200 for works of street improvement, and to state that if the Town Council apply for sanction to a loan for the works, the Board will be prepared to give consideration to the matte Having regard, however, to the character of the works, it would not be in with their practice to allovr so long a term rq thirty years for the repayo.m.i, of tho loan, lam to add that the 80.:.rd presume that all the strees intended to be paved are highways. repairable by the inhabitants at large.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, F. F. ROTTON, assistant secretary. No definite resolution was come to by the committee.

THEI CORPORATION AND THEIR CHARGES. The following letter was read We are in receipt of an account frem the Corporation for the severing of Escleston-street, the charge for which we consider to be most excessive, and do not think it equitable that we should be charged with the expenses of the construction of an exti aerdinary sewer which has bean made for the carrying of the sewage of an outlying district, and of a larger size and greater depth than would be necessary for this read only. We therefore ask you to reduce the cbsrge to that of an ordinary sewer, such as would have been required for this property, and for which we shall have no objections to pay. We have been aware for some time that you have made reductions under pre- cisely similar circumstances, and hope you will give to us the Same consideration and abatement.—Remain, gentlemen, yours obediently, JINX WIWDUS, WIT [IAN LEIGH, WrufAM TAMER, ELLER TASTIER, GEORGE GESKETE, and .TORN MATHER."

Mr. HART said the total amount of the expenses claimed was about .£250. The CHAIRMAN: This is a similar case to that of the alkali manufacturers, Messrs. Lockwood and Leiths. The committee decided to arrange with the above pro- perty owners on terms similar to those in the case referred to, A letter was read from Mr. Oppenheim, solicitor, Hard- shaw-street, saying that his client, Mr. George Melling, had instructed him to inform the committee that he disputed the ,£BO 18s. 7d. demanded from him as his apportionment of the cost incurred in awning Ecdeston-street, and he die- puted his liability to the payment of any sum whatever. It was agreed to offer Mr. Melling the same terms as had been cvnceded to the other property owners.

V. ••‘. - - /-1111.. i. • ESTABLISIIMENT, DOG and WINE LICENCES.— The Commissioners of Inland Revenue remind those who keep Carriages, or Male Servants, or who use Armorial Bearings, that their Licences must be renewed in the month of January. Dog Licences must be renewed' at the same time, and when- ever any additional Dog is kept a Licence must be immediately obtained. Farmers and shepherds may obtain exemptions for Dogs kept and used solely for tending sheep or cattle on a farm, but a declaration that the dogs are so used must be made to the Supervisor of Excise for the district. Licences or exemptions are not transferable from one person to another. The penalty for keeping a dog without licence or exemption is es. TAKING ORDERS you WINE, &c.—The Commissioners also give notice that no person may solicit, take, or receive any order for wine or spirits unless he holds a licence for that pur- pose or is the bona fide traveller for a firm duly licenced in the United Kingdom. The penalty for so acting without licence is moo. When the residence of the offender is not known, or is out of the United Kingdom, the summons will be left at the house or place where the offence was committed. London, Ist January, 1881.

THE BURIAL BOARD for the TOWNSHIP of RUNCORN REQUIRE £2,000 at 4 per cent, per annum, to replace a loan falling due on the 30th of March, in one or more sums of not less than £2OO each, and for a term of seven years. The security is the Poor Bate of the Town.—Apply to W. B. SALRELD, Secretary. Burial board Uffice, January 13th, 1881.

THE RUNCORN PROPERTY AND INVESTMENT CO., LIMITED, are prepared to receive Deposits as under :—On sums at one month's notice, 4 per cent, per annum; on sums at three months' notice, at 5 per cent, per annum. Interest payable half-yearly, on the 24th June and the 24th December. The security to investors consists of the valuable freehold estates and properties owned by the Company, proper- ties in mortgage to the Compmy, and the large margin of un- called capital. Deposits can be paid at any time to Mr. James Pritchard, Leinster-read ; Mr. William Handley. Church- street ; and at Bethesda Schoolroom, on the first Thursday in every month, from 7-30 to 8-30 p.m.

COWLEY'S TRUST.—NEW SCHOOLS.—TOWNS- MEN interested In the completion of oowley's New &tools are INVITED to MBET ME and the GOVERNORS of the Trust in the MAYOR'S PARLOUR, TOWN HALL, On THURS- DAY, the 27th JANUARY inst., at Three o'clock p.m., to con- sider what steps can be taken to facilitate that object. JAMES HARRISON, Mayor. Town Hall, St. Helens, 19th January, 1881.

NOTICE.—Grinding for Hire.—The ST. HELENS CORN MILLS, College-street, are prepared to Grind or Crush for hire, Beans, Oats, and Indian Corn, on mlst rea- sonable terms. TAMES R. WILLAOY (late of the fit. Helens Corn Mills), 'respectfully announces that he has commenced business as a Corn, Flour, Provender, and General Commission Agent.
